Alternate_Names: Abhor, Abor, Boga’er Luoba, Bori-Karko, Lhoba, Luoba
Location: Arunachal Pradesh state: East, West, and Upper Siang districts, Upper Subansiri and Dibang Valley districts; Assam state: Assam valley north hills, between Bhutan and Buruli rivers.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Central Tibeto-Burman, Tani
Dialect_Names: Ashing, Bokar (Boga’er Luoba), Bori, Karko, Komkar, Milang (Milan), Minyong, Padam, Pailibo, Pangi, Pasi, Ramo, Shimong, Tangam

Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Khamba [kbg], Tshangla [tsj].

Scripts: Latin script [Latn]. Tibetan script [Tibt], used in China.
General_Remarks: A Scheduled Tribe with several subgroups. ‘Adi’, hillman, is a cover term for eastern Tani languages.

Location: Arunachal Pradesh state: East Siang, Lepa-Rada, West Siang, and Upper Subansiri districts.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Central Tibeto-Burman, Tani
Relationships: Lare is the main dialect and is accepted by all Galo.

Language_Use: Home, community. Used by all.
Language_Contact: Most also use Assamese [asm]. Most also use Hindi [hin], especially with the military. Many also use English [eng], especially the educated and the young.
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 60%. More men can read than women but more girls and women are learning.

Location: Assam state: Kamrup district, Basbistha, Chandubi, Jalukbari, Jorabat, Kahi Kusi, Khetri, Loharghat, Pandu, Panikhaith, Rani block, Sonapur, and south of Brahmaputra river; Meghalaya state: Ri-Bhoi district, Nongpoh area, Barni Hat and Umling.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Karbi
Relationships: Reportedly unintelligible with Karbi [mjw]; intelligibility testing inconclusive regarding whether Guriaghuli area dialect is well understood in Meghalaya. Lexical similarity: 57%–68% with Karbi; 70%–86% between dialects.
Language_Use: Many ethnic group members no longer use Amri Karbi. Much borrowing from Assamese [asm] (in Assam) and Khasi [kha] (in Meghalaya). Some Amri Karbi villages shifted completely to Assamese due to intermarriage and the perception that Assamese is preferred for children to do well in school. In the remote and isolated border area, the language is still strong. Home, village, religion. Some of all ages. Positive attitudes. Strong feelings of separateness from the dominant Karbi group in Karbi, Anglong District.
Language_Contact: Most also use Assamese [asm]. Many also use English [eng].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 20%—60%.

Alternate_Names: Anāl, Anal Naga, Namfau, Pakan, Pakan Naga
Location: Manipur state: Chandel district, Chakpikarong, Chandel, and Engnoupal sub-districts, on Chakpi river banks.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Kuki-Chin, Northwestern
Relationships: Reportedly most similar to Lamgang [lmk] (Kuki Naga).
Typology: SOV.
Language_Contact: Many also use English [eng]. Also use Meitei [mni].
Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Moyon Naga [nmo].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L1: 74% (2001 census).
General_Remarks: Declared themselves Nagas (ethnically) in 1963.

Location: Andaman and Nicobar Islands union territory: Port Blair, 40 villages south of Port Blair.
Classification: Creole, Hindi based
Relationships: A creolization of Hindustani, Bengali [ben], and Malayalam [mal].
Language_Use: Home. Used by all.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin], especially with outsiders. A situation of diglossia.
Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Mixed Great Andamanese [gac].
General_Remarks: Spoken as L1 by mixed generations of communities. Contains elements of Indo-Aryan and Dravidian grammar. No literature exists in the creole. Standard Hindi literature is used.

Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Marathi [mar].

Location: Bihar state: Banka, Bhagalpur, Katihar, and Purnia districts; Jharkhand state: Godda and Sahibganji districts.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Outer Languages, Eastern, Unclassified
Relationships: 79% inherent intelligibility of Brahmin Maithili. Lexical similarity: 81% (Brahmin) to 87% (non-Brahmin) with Darbhanga Maithili.
Typology: SOV; postpositions; noun head final; content q-word in situ; clause constituents indicated by case-marking; passives and voice; nontonal.
Language_Use: Use declining (Van Driem 2007). Home, community. Used by all. Negative attitudes.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin], especially for trade, government, and prayer.

Relationships: May be intelligible with Nyishi [njz].
Language_Contact: Also use Assamese [asm]. Also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin]. Also use Nefamese [nef].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 71% (2001 census).

Location: Andaman and Nicobar Islands.
Classification: Andamanese, Great Andamanese, Central
Afro-Asiatic, Semitic, Central, South, Arabic

Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Maldivian [div], Mewati [wtm], Urdu [urd].
Scripts: Arabic script, Naskh variant [Arab], primary usage. Braille script [Brai].

Location: Kerala state: Kozhihkode district, Ernad sub-district; Malappuram district, Nilambur sub-district; Palakkad district; Karnataka and Tamil Nada states.
Classification: Dravidian, Southern, Tamil-Kannada, Tamil-Kodagu, Tamil-Malayalam, Malayalam
Relationships: Lexical similarity: 63%–69% with Malayalam [mal], 53%–55% with Tamil [tam].
Language_Use: Vitality in Malappuram District questionable due to small population, no separate settlements, living with Malayalis. Low education level helps keep language stable. Home, community. Some young people, all adults. Negative attitudes.
Language_Contact: All also use Malayalam [mal]. Many also use English [eng].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 70% in Malayalam [mal].

Location: Arunachal Pradesh state: Changlang and Lohit; Assam state; Meghalaya state: west Garo Hills; Nagaland state: Dimapur, Kohima, Mokokchung, Wokha, and Zunheboto; West Bengal state: Jalpaiguri and Koch Bihar.

Dialect_Names: Jharwa (Pidgin), Mayang, Standard Assamese, Western Assamese (Kamrupi)
Typology: SOV; noun head final; gender (masculine/feminine); case-marking (6 cases); verb affixes mark person, number, gender of subject; passives; tense and aspect; 21 consonant and 16 vowel phonemes; non-tonal; free stress; honorifics.
Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Adi [adi], Aiton [aio], Amri Karbi [ajz], Angami Naga [njm], Ao Naga [njo], Apatani [apt], Bawm Chin [bgr], Chang Naga [nbc], Deori [der], Digaro-Mishmi [mhu], Dimasa [dis], Galo Adi [adl], Hajong [haj], Hmar [hmr], Hrangkhol [hra], Hruso [hru], Idu-Mishmi [clk], Kachari [xac], Kamtapuri [rkt], Karbi [mjw], Khamti [kht], Khamyang [ksu], Koch [kdq], Kok Borok [trp], Kurmukar [kfv], Lyngngam [lyg], Miji [sjl], Miju-Mishmi [mxj], Mising [mrg], Nocte Naga [njb], Phake [phk], Puroik [suv], Singpho [sgp], Sumi Naga [nsm], Tangsa Naga [nst], Tiwa [lax], Turung [try], Tutsa Naga [tvt], Wancho Naga [nnp].
Education: Taught in primary and secondary schools through grade 5 and as subject thereafter in Assam state.
Literature: Literature. Newspapers. Periodicals. Radio. TV. Videos. Dictionary. Grammar. Bible: 1833–1995.

Location: Chhattisgarh state: Raigarh district, Jashpur area; Jharkhand state: Gumla, Lohardaga, southern Palamau, and northern Ranchi districts of Chotanagpur Plateau; Maharashtra state; Odisha state: Sambalpur district; West Bengal state.
Classification: Austro-Asiatic, Munda, North Munda, Kherwari, Mundari
Language_Contact: Also use Bengali [ben]. Also use English [eng]. Also use Sadri [sck].

Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Sal, Boro-Garo, Koch
Relationships: Related to Koch [kdq] and Rabha [rah].
Language_Use: Some young people, all adults.
Language_Contact: Also use Garo [grt]. Also use English [eng].

Alternate_Names: Abadi, Abohi, Ambodhi, Avadhi, Baiswari, Kojali, Kosali
Location: Bihar state; Delhi; Madhya Pradesh state; Uttar Pradesh: Allahabad, Bahraich, Bara-Banki, Faizabad, Gonda, Kheri, Lucknow, Pratapgarh, Rae-Bareli, Sitapur, Sultanpur, and Unnao districts.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Intermediate Divisions, Eastern, East Central
Relationships: Dialects are generally mutually intelligible. Lexical similarity: with Bhojpuri [bho], Rana Tharu [thr], Maithili [mai], Nepali [npi], Hindi [hin]. Also Sanskrit [san] borrowings.
Typology: SOV; postpositions; noun head final; 2 genders; clause constituents indicated by case-marking; verbal affixation marks person, number and genders of subject and object; no ergativity; tense and aspect; passives and voice; 30 consonant and 8 vowel phonemes; nontonal.
Language_Contact: Many also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L1: 50%–75%. Education is in Hindi [hin]. Considerable epic literature. Hindu holy book, Ramcharitmanas, by Tulsi Das.
Literature: Literature. Newspapers. Periodicals. Radio. TV. Videos. Grammar. Texts. Bible: 2000–2005.
General_Remarks: ‘Kosali’ is a name used for the Eastern Hindi group.

Language_Contact: Many also use English [eng].
Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Irula [iru], Kota [kfe].
Scripts: Badaga script [Qabq], in development. Kannada script [Knda], no longer in use. Latin script [Latn]. Tamil script [Taml], used since 2009.

Alternate_Names: Bagelkhandi, Bhugelkhud, Gangai, Godwani Kawathi, Kenat, Kevat Boli, Kevati, Kewani, Kewat, Kewati, Kewot, Kumhari, Mandal, Mannadi, Riwai
Location: Chhattisgarh state: Bilaspur and Koriya districts; Madhya Pradesh state: Anuppur, Chhindwara, Dindori, Jabalpur, Mandla, Panna, Rewa, Satna, Shahdol, Sidhi, and Umaria districts; Uttar Pradesh state: Allahabad, Banda, Mirzapur, and Hamirpur districts.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Intermediate Divisions, Eastern, East Central
Relationships: Godwani (refers to Bagheli-speaking Gonds), Kumhari (refers to Bagheli-speaking Kumhar). Though geographic and caste variation is found in Bagheli, no dialect is prevalent. Rewa area variety is considered standard. Lexical similarity: 79%–99% between all Bagheli varieties; 72%–91% with Hindi [hin].
Language_Use: Vigorous. All domains. Used by all. Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Many also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin], using it widely but not displacing Bagheli in any domain. 35% of Bagheli speakers have at least good general proficiency.
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 49% in Hindi [hin]. Had literature since 16th century.

Location: Punjab state: Fatehabad, Firozepur, Hanumangarh, Haryana, Rajasthan, Sriganganagar, and Sirsa districts.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Intermediate Divisions, Western, Rajasthani, Unclassified
Relationships: Lexical similarity: 81%–95% between all varietes of Bagri, 58%–63% with Eastern Punjabi [pan], 56%–69% with Hindi [hin], 56%–70% with Haryanvi [bgc], 51%–66% with Marwari [rwr], 58%–69% with Merwari [wry], 69%–76% with Shekhawati [swv], 47%–63% with Godwari [gdx], 63%–65% with Dhundari [dhd], 60%–66% with Mewati [wtm], 74% with Jandavra [jnd].
Typology: SOV; tonal, 3 tones.
Language_Use: Vigorous. Home, village, school, market, religion. Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Most also use Hindi [hin]. Educated people and men have greater proficiency. Many also use English [eng].
Literacy: Most Bagri live in rural areas and are illiterate.
General_Remarks: A Scheduled Caste.

Location: Bihar state: Muzaffarpur, Samastipur, Shivahar, Sitamarhi, and Vaishali districts; Dharbhanga district, Singhwara block; Purba Champaran district, Dhaka block.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Outer Languages, Eastern, Bihari
Relationships: Lexical similarity: 51%–65% with Maithili [mai].
Language_Use: All domains. Used by all.
Language_Contact: Many also use Hindi [hin] (Kashyap 2014). Also use Bhojpuri [bho]. Also use Maithili [mai].
Scripts: Devanagari script [Deva]. Kaithi script [Kthi], used until the turn of the 20th century.

L1_Full: 800 in India (2007). Possibly L2 speakers only.
Location: Punjab state: Firozpur district.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Iranian, Western, Northwestern, Balochi
Typology: SOV; both prepositions and postpositions; gender (masculine/feminine); no articles; case-marking (5 cases); ergativity; passives; tense and aspect; 23 consonant and 8 vowel phonemes; non-tonal.
Language_Contact: Shifting to Urdu [urd].
Scripts: Arabic script, Naskh variant [Arab]. Arabic script, Nastaliq variant [Aran], primary usage. Latin script [Latn], limited usage in the early 1900s.
General_Remarks: Distinct from Western Balochi [bgn] of Pakistan, Afghanistan, Iran, and Turkmenistan; and Southern Balochi [bcc] of Pakistan, Iran, Oman, and United Arab Emirates.

Alternate_Names: Baltistani, Bhoti of Baltistan, Byltae, Sbalt
Location: Jammu and Kashmir state.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Western Tibeto-Burman, Bodish, Central Bodish, Western
Language_Use: Some young people, all adults.
Language_Contact: Many also use Purig [prx]. Also use English [eng]. Also use Shina [scl]. Also use Urdu [urd], with high proficiency in some places, except among women and uneducated populations.
Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Purig [prx].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 62% (2001 census).
Scripts: Arabic script, Naskh variant [Arab], used since the 17th century. Arabic script, Nastaliq variant [Aran], used since the 17th century, primary usage. Balti script [Qaab], no longer in use. Tibetan script [Tibt], used between 8th and 17th century, recent efforts to revive usage.

Alternate_Names: An Yüng, Bantaba, Bantawa Dum, Bantawa Rai, Bantawa Yong, Bantawa Yüng, Bontawa, Kirat Khambu, Kirat Khambu Rai, Kirawa Yüng, Rai
Location: Sikkim state: Lingdum, Rolep, and many other parts of the state; West Bengal state: Darjeeling.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Western Tibeto-Burman, Himalayan, Kiranti, Eastern
Typology: SOV; postpositions; noun heads initial; no noun classes or genders; content q-word in situ; genitives, adjectives, numerals before noun heads; polar questions marked only with rising intonation; content questions same word order as assertive sentences or question word directly before the verb; up to 2 prefixes, 10 suffixes; clause constituents indicated by word order; affixes indicate case of noun phrases; verbal affixation mark person, number, object—obligatory; tense and aspect; no passives or voice; split ergative; comparatives use Nepali word, bhanda; 25 consonant and 6 vowel phonemes; numbers above 3 are borrowed from Nepali [npi]; CV, CVC, CVCC; nontonal.
Language_Use: Some shift to Nepali [npi] evident, especially among young generation. Home, friends, religion. Some young people, all adults. Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Most also use Nepali [npi]. Also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin], especially among ex-soldiers.
Literature: Literature. Newspapers. Periodicals. Radio. Videos. Dictionary. Grammar. Texts. NT: 2020.
Scripts: Devanagari script [Deva]. Kirat Rai script [Krai], used in Sikkim.

Location: Madhya Pradesh state: Barwani district, Rajpur and Barwani sub-districts; Khargone district, Jhirniya sub-district; Maharashtra state: Jalgaon district, Yawal and Raver sub-districts; Dhule district, Shirpur sub-district.

Relationships: Dialect center is Madhya Pradesh, Barwani District, Choutharya village of Rajpur tahsil. Lexical similarity 62%–66% with Pauri Bareli [bfb], 67%–73% with Rathwi Bareli [bgd].
Language_Use: Vigorous. All domains except education. Used by all. Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Also use Ahirani [ahr]. Also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin]. Also use Marathi [mar]. Also use Nimadi [noe].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: Below 10%.

Location: Maharashtra state: Nandurbar district, Dhadgaon, Shahada, and Taloda sub-districts; Dhule district, Shirpur sub-district; Madhya Pradesh state: Barwani district, Pansemal sub-district, Nivali and Pati blocks.

Relationships: Pauri Bareli not intelligible with Rathwi Bareli [bgd] or Palya Bareli [bpx]. Dialect center in Maharashtra, Nandurbar district, Dhadgaon tahsil. Lexical similarity: 81%–88% with varieties of Pauri Bareli; 68%–79% with Rathwi Bareli [bgd]; 62%–66% with Palya Bareli [bpx].
Language_Use: Vigorous. All domains except education. Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Also use Ahirani [ahr]. Also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin]. Also use Marathi [mar]. Also use Nimadi [noe].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: Below 10%.

Alternate_Names: Barel, Barela, Paura, Pauri, Pawari, Pawri, Rathi, Rathia, Rathwi Pauri
Location: Madhya Pradesh state: Barwani district, Barwani, Sendhwa, and Rajpur sub-districts; Khargone district, Bhagawanpura, Jhirniya, and Bhikangaon sub-districts; Dewas district, Bagli sub-district; Khandwa district, Burhanpur sub-district; Dhar district, Dahi block; south Jhabua district, Rathia Bhilala; Maharashtra state: north Dhule district, Shirpur sub-district; Jalgaon district, Chopda, Raver, and Yawal sub-districts.

Relationships: Pauri Bareli [bfb] and the Rathwi Pauri dialect not intelligible with Vasavi [vas] or Bhilori [noi]. Dialect center is Madhya Pradesh, Barwani District, Chiklia. Language_Use: Vigorous. All domains except education. Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Also use Ahirani [ahr]. Also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin]. Also use Marathi [mar]. Also use Nimadi [noe].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: Below 10%.
General_Remarks: A Scheduled Tribe.

Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Outer Languages, Northwestern, Dardic, Kohistani

Alternate_Names: Babri, Badak, Baori, Basria, Bawari, Bawaria, Bhoria, Vaghri
Location: Chandigarh, Haryana, Himachal Pradesh, Punjab, Rajasthan, and Uttar Pradesh states; Delhi.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Intermediate Divisions, Western, Bhil
Language_Contact: Many also use English [eng]. Also use Eastern Punjabi [pan].
General_Remarks: A Scheduled Caste.

Location: Haryana state: Ambala, Kaithal, Karnal, and Kurukshetra; Punjab state: Fatehgarh Sahib district and Patiala; Uttar Pradesh state: Muzaffarnagar and Saharanpur.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Unclassified
Language_Contact: Shifting to Eastern Punjabi [pan]. Many also use English [eng].

Location: Karnataka state: Mysore district; Kerala state: Wayanad district; scattered in Tamil Nadu state.
Classification: Dravidian, Southern, Tulu
Relationships: Related to Tulu [tcy] and Koraga [kfd].
Language_Contact: Shifting to Kannada [kan].
General_Remarks: Bellara is a Scheduled Caste in Karnataka, Kerala, and Tamil Nadu. Speak a dialect of Kannada [kan] (Singh 1995b).

Location: Assam state: Goalpara district; Bihar state; Jharkhand state: Dhanbad, Manbhum, Santal Parganas, and Singhbhum; Odisha state: Bales and Mayar; Tripura and West Bengal states.
Official_Recognition: Statutory provincial language in West Bengal, Tripura, Assam states (1950, Constitution, Schedule VIII).
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Outer Languages, Eastern, Bengali-Assamese
Dialect_Names: Barik, Bhatiari, Chirmar, Kachari-Bengali, Lohari-Malpaharia, Musselmani, Rajshahi, Samaria, Saraki, Siripuria (Kishanganjia)
Typology: SOV; postpositions; noun head both initial and final; 3 genders: male, female, neuter; content q-word initial and final; clause constituents indicated by case-marking (5 cases) and word order; verb affixes mark person, number; definite article affix; tense; passives and voice; causatives; comparatives; non-tonal; 35 consonant and 5 vowel phonemes; stress on first syllable.
Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Asuri [asr], Bishnupuriya [bpy], Chakma [ccp], Dimasa [dis], Hajong [haj], Kamtapuri [rkt], Kharia [khr], Kharia Thar [ksy], Koch [kdq], Kok Borok [trp], Kudmali [kyw], Kumarbhag Paharia [kmj], Lodhi [lbm], Mahali [mjx], Maithili [mai], Mal Paharia [mkb], Panchpargania [tdb], Pnar [pbv], Rabha [rah], Sadri [sck], Sakachep [sch], Toto [txo], Urdu [urd].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L1: 85%.
Education: Taught in primary and secondary schools through grade 5 and as subject thereafter in Assam, Tripura, and West Bengal states.
Scripts: Bengali (Bangla) script [Beng], primary usage. Braille script [Brai]. Newa script [Newa], no longer in use.

Alternate_Names: Baderwali, Badrohi, Bahi, Bhadarwahi, Bhaderbhai Jamu, Bhaderwali Pahari, Bhadrava, Bhadri
Location: Himachal Pradesh state: small border area; Jammu and Kashmir state: Doda district, Bhadarwah town and surrounding villages.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Intermediate Divisions, Western, Pahari, Western Pahari
Relationships: Lexical similarity: 45% with Pangwali [pgg].
Language_Use: Vigorous in spite of high bilingualism; L1 seen as important. Home, village, religion. Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin]. Also use Kashmiri [kas]. Also use Urdu [urd].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 70% (84% for males, 53% for females).
Scripts: Arabic script, Naskh variant [Arab]. Devanagari script [Deva].

Location: Madhya Pradesh state; Maharashtra state: Amravati district.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Outer Languages, Southern, Unclassified
Relationships: Lexical similarity: 91%–95% with Gowlan [goj], 61%–62% with Hindi [hin], 33%–34% with Marathi [mar].
Language_Use: All domains. Used by all. Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin]. Also use Marathi [mar].
General_Remarks: Bhalay probably an alternate spelling of Balahi (Balai), a Scheduled Caste found in Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Rajasthan, and Uttar Pradesh.

Location: Chhattisgarh state: Bilaspur, Durg, and Surguja districts; Madhya Pradesh state: Chhatarpur, Chhindwara, Datia, Jabalpur, Mandla, Panna, Rewa, Sidhi, and Tikamgarh districts; Uttar Pradesh and West Bengal states.
Classification: Dravidian, Unclassified
Relationships: They speak a variety of Hindi [hin] (Singh and Manoharan 1993).
Language_Contact: Many also use English [eng].

Alternate_Names: Basturia, Bhatra, Bhattra, Bhattri, Bhottada, Bhottara, Deshia, aisi jaisi got
Location: Chhattisgarh state: Bastar district, Jagdalpur sub-district; Maharashtra state; Odisha state: Koraput district, Kotpad sub-district.
LWC_Support: Came to the Bastar district from Warangal; became widespread under British rule in 1858. Used in trade (opium), daily communication between ethnic groups, and agriculture.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Outer Languages, Eastern, Oriya
Relationships: Intelligibility between dialects at 88% or more. Reportedly similar to Halbi [hlb]. Lexical similarity: 70%–90% between dialects, 58% with Adivasi Oriya [ort].
Language_Use: Vigorous. Home, religion. Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Some also use Hindi [hin], in Madhya Pradesh. Also use Halbi [hlb]. Also use Odia [ory], in Odisha.
Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Duruwa [pci], Halbi [hlb].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 38% in Chhattisgarh [hne] (2001 census).

Location: Himachal Pradesh state: Chamba district, Bhattiyat and Sihunta sub-districts; Jammu and Kashmir state; Punjab state.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Intermediate Divisions, Western, Pahari, Western Pahari
Typology: SOV.
Language_Use: Used by all.
Language_Contact: Also use Eastern Punjabi [pan]. Also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin]. Also use Urdu [urd].

Location: Karnataka state; Madhya Pradesh state: Barwani (Rajpur), southern Dhar, southern Jhabua, and Khargone (Segaon) districts; Maharashtra state: Dhule district; Rajasthan state; a few in Gujarat state.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Intermediate Divisions, Western, Bhil
Language_Contact: Many also use English [eng].

Alternate_Names: Bhagoria, Bhil, Bhilbari, Bhilboli, Bhilla, Bhilodi, Lengotia, Vil
L1_Full: 3,290,000 (2011 census). 10,400,000 for all Bhil languages (2011 census).
Location: Gujarat state: Dohad, Panch Mahals, and Sabarkantha districts; Madhya Pradesh state: Dhar, Indore, Jhabua, Khargone, and Ratlam districts; Rajasthan state: Banswara, Dungapur, and Udaipur districts.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Intermediate Divisions, Western, Bhil
Dialect_Names: Ahiri, Anarya (Pahadi), Bhilodi, Bhim, Charani, Habura, Konkani, Kotali (Kotvali, Kotwalia), Magra Ki Boli, Nahari (Baglani), Naikdi, Panchali, Patelia, Ranawat, Rani Bhil, Siyalgir, Valvi, Labani
Relationships: Bhili of Ratlam District in Madhya Pradesh is inherently intelligible with Wagdi [wbr] and a connecting link between Gujarati [guj] and Rajasthani (Marwari) [mve].
Language_Use: Spoken as L1 by the Patelia in Madhya Pradesh.
Language_Contact: Many also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L1: 1%–5%. Literacy rate in L2: 10%.
General_Remarks: ‘Bhil’ is an ethnic designation (caste or tribe). Bhili is a Scheduled Tribe in Rajasthan, Gujarat, Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, and Tripura; Kotwalia is a Scheduled Tribe in Gujarat and Maharashtra. Dewali (Dehawali) is a cover term for Vasavi and Kotali, among others.

Location: Assam state; Bihar state: Champaran, Saran, and Shahabad districts; Delhi; Jharkhand state: Palamau and Ranchi districts; Madhya Pradesh state; Uttar Pradesh state: Azamgarh, Ballia, Basti, Deoria, Ghazipur, Gorakhpur, Mirzapur, and Varanasi districts; West Bengal state.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Outer Languages, Eastern, Bihari
Dialect_Names: Northern Standard Bhojpuri (Basti, Gorakhpuri, Sarawaria), Western Standard Bhojpuri (Benarsi, Purbi), Southern Standard Bhojpuri (Kharwari), Bhojpuri Tharu, Madhesi, Domra, Musahari
Relationships: May be more than 1 language. Extent of dialect variation in India and Nepal not yet determined. The cover term “Bihari” (a pejorative alternate name for Bhojpuri) is also used for Maithili [mai], and Magahi [mag]. Bhojpuri Tharu dialect is spoken by Tharu caste in Nepal and India. Distinct from other Tharu languages.
Typology: SOV; postpositions; noun head final; gender (masculine/feminine for animate nouns); content q-word in situ; clause constituents indicated by both case-marking (3 cases) and word order; verbal affixation marks person, number and genders of subject and object; no ergativity; tense and aspect; non-tonal; 34 consonant and 6 vowel phonemes, about 4 diphthongs; stress on penultimate syllable.
Language_Contact: Many also use English [eng].
Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Bajjika [vjk], Maithili [mai], Urdu [urd].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L1: 5%–30%. Literacy rate in L2: 50%–75%.
Literature: Literature. Newspapers. Periodicals. Radio. TV. Videos. Grammar. Texts. NT: 1998–2006.

Location: Chhattisgarh state: Raipur district; Madhya Pradesh state: Hoshangabad district; Maharashtra state; Odisha state: Balasore (Baleshwar), Dhenkanal, Kalahandi, Keonjhar, Koraput, and Sambalpur districts, Sunabera Plateau area.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Outer Languages, Eastern, Oriya
Relationships: A more divergent dialect of Halbi [hlb]. Lexical similarity: 68%–72% with Kamar [keq].
Language_Contact: Also use Chhattisgarhi [hne]. Also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 24% in Odisha (2001 census).

Alternate_Names: Baite, Bedesa, Beite, Bete, Beteh, Biete, Hadem
Location: Assam state: North Cachar Hills district; Manipur state; Meghalaya state: Jaintia hills district; Mizoram state: Aizawl district, Darlawn, New Vervek, and Ratu villages.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Kuki-Chin, Central, Mizo
Relationships: Reportedly similar to Hrangkhol [hra], and similar enough to Mizo [lus] and Hmar [hmr] that they can be read with comprehension.
Language_Use: Home, village, church.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin], especially in Assam. Also use Khasi [kha], in Meghalaya. Also use Mizo [lus]. Also use War-Jaintia [aml], in Meghalaya.
Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Sakachep [sch].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L1: 56%.
General_Remarks: An ethnic subgroup of the Mizo. Not the same as the Biate dialect of Chin Thado [tcz] (Breton 1997).

Location: Jharkhand state: Cowerdaga and Ranchi districts; Madhya Pradesh and Odisha states; West Bengal state: Darjeeling and Jalpaiguri districts.
Classification: Austro-Asiatic, Munda, North Munda, Kherwari
Language_Use: Home. Some young people, all adults.
Language_Contact: Most also use Hindi [hin] (Bhattacharya 2016). Most also use Sadri [sck] (Bhattacharya 2016). Also use English [eng].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 10% in Hindi [hin].
General_Remarks: A Scheduled Tribe. Ethnic group called Birjia.

Alternate_Names: Bilaspuri Pahari, Himachali, Kahluri, Kehloori Pahari, Kehluri, Pacchmi, Pahari
Location: Himachal Pradesh state: Bilaspur district; Punjab state: Rupnagar district.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Intermediate Divisions, Western, Pahari, Western Pahari
Relationships: 95% intelligibility of Mandeali [mjl], 94% of Kangri [xnr]. Lexical similarity: 90% with Kangri of Palampur, 86% with Mandeali, 84% with Chambeali [cdh].
Typology: SOV.
Language_Use: Home, community, agriculture, religion. Used by all.
Language_Contact: Also use Eastern Punjabi [pan]. Also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin], especially for instruction in school and politics, but middle-aged and older women have limited comprehension of it. Also use Urdu [urd], especially by middle-aged and older educated people.
General_Remarks: ‘Kahluri’ is based on the old name for the princely state.

Alternate_Names: Bihor, Birhar, Birhore, Birhul, Mankidi, Mankidia, Mankiria
L1_Full: 2,000 (Van Driem 2007). Nomadic habits make assessment difficult. Some estimates as low as 1,000 (Parkin 1991).
Location: Chhattisgarh state: Raigarh district; Jharkhand state: southern Hazaribag, southern Palamau, Ranchi, and Singhbhum districts; Maharashtra state; Odisha state: Kalahandi, Keonjhar, Mayurbhanj, Sambalpur, and Sundargarh districts; West Bengal state: Puruliya district.
Classification: Austro-Asiatic, Munda, North Munda, Kherwari, Mundari
Relationships: Lexical similarity: 55%–72% with Santhali [sat], Ho [hoc], Mundari [unr], and Munda [unx].
Language_Use: Vigorous. No indication of language shift. Most domains. Used by all. Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng], especially the school children. Also use Hindi [hin]. Also use Ho [hoc]. Also use Munda [unx]. Also use Mundari [unr]. Also use Odia [ory]. Also use Sadri [sck]. Also use Santhali [sat].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 10% in Hindi [hin].
General_Remarks: Traditionally nomadic.

Alternate_Names: Bishnupria Manipuri, Bishnupriya, Bishnupriya Manipuri, Bisna Puriya
Location: Assam state: Cachar, Hailakandi, and Karimganj districts; north Tripura state.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Outer Languages, Eastern, Bengali-Assamese
Relationships: Though once regarded as a Bengali-Meitei creole, it retains pre-Bengali features (Masica 1991). Lexical similarity: 81%–85% between dialects in Bangladesh, 41%–45% with Bengali [ben].
Typology: SOV; postpositions, articles before noun heads, question word before the verb, affixes indicate case of noun phrase; CV, CVC, CVV, CCV, VC, VCV; nontonal.
Language_Contact: Also use Bengali [ben]. Also use English [eng].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 80%.
Literature: Literature. Radio. Videos. Grammar. Bible portions: 1995–2011.
General_Remarks: Reported to also live in three villages in Myanmar but these villages cannot be identified.

Alternate_Names: Bodo Paraja, Harja, Jhaliya, Jharia, Jhodia Parja, Parajhi, Parja, Parjhi, Parji, Paroja, Poroja, Sodia Parja
Location: Andhra Pradesh state; Odisha state: Koraput district.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Outer Languages, Eastern, Oriya
Relationships: Phonology and grammar show Indo-European relationship, not related to Dravidian Duruwa Parji. 86%–96% intelligibility between Bodo and Jhodia caste varieties. Lexical similarity: 76%–86% with Bodo and Jhodia caste varieties, 70%–89% with Desia.
Language_Contact: Most also use Adivasi Oriya [ort], in the market. Also use English [eng], especially the youth.
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 15% (2001 census).
General_Remarks: The name Paroja comes from Sanskrit [san] subjects. It is used for a variety of ethnic groups from different language families.

Alternate_Names: Bhonda Bhasha, Bonda, Bondo-Poraja, Nanqa Poroja, Poraja Katha, Remo, Remosum
L1_Full: 9,000 (2002 SIL). 5,570 Upper Bondo and 3,500 Lower Bondo.
Location: Odisha state: Malkangiri district, Khoirput sub-district, Bondo Hills.
Classification: Austro-Asiatic, Munda, South Munda, Koraput Munda, Gutob-Remo-Geta’, Gutob-Remo
Relationships: Lexical similarity: 70%–94% with other Bondo varieties, 45%–51% with Gutob Gadaba [gbj], 22%–32% with Upper Gata’ [gaq] (Didayi).
Language_Use: Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Many also use Adivasi Oriya [ort], for trade and interactions with surrounding communities. Few Upper Bondo are bilingual. Also use English [eng], limited use with the youth.
Literacy: Literacy rate in L1: 1%. Literacy rate in L2: 12% (2001 census).

Alternate_Names: Bara, Bodi, Bodo, Boroni, Kachari, Mech, Meche, Mechi, Meci
L1_Full: 1,470,000 in India (2011 census). 1,460,000 Boro, 11,500 Mech (2011 census).
Location: Assam state: mainly Darrang, Goalpara, Kamrup, Lakhimpur, Nagaon, and Sibsagar districts; Manipur state: Chandel (Tengnoupal) district; Meghalaya state: West Garo Hills district, Tikrikilla sub-district, 7 villages; East Khasi Hills district; West Bengal state: Cooch-Behar, Darjeeling, and Jalpaiguri districts.
Official_Recognition: Statutory language of provincial identity in Assam (1950, Constitution, Schedule VIII), amended 2003.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Sal, Boro-Garo, Boro-Tiwa, Boro
Relationships: West Bengal dialect reportedly different from Assam.
Language_Use: Vigorous Bodo language and culture. Assamese [asm] is L1 for most Bodo Mech dialect speakers in Assam (Breton 1997:24).
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng], especially the youth.
Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Koch [kdq].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 61% Assam (2001 census).
Education: Taught as subject in primary and secondary schools through grade 9 in tribal areas of Assam.
Literature: Literature. Periodicals. Radio. Dictionary. Grammar. Bible: 1981.
Scripts: Bengali (Bangla) script [Beng]. Devanagari script [Deva], primary usage. Latin script [Latn].

Alternate_Names: Bijbhasha, Braj, Braj Bhakha, Bri, Brij Bhasha, Briju, Bruj, Daihaati Zabaan, Dehaati Zabaan
Location: Bihar state; Delhi; Haryana state: Gurgaon district; Madhya Pradesh state: Bhind, Gwalior, and Morena districts; Rajasthan state: Bharatpur and Sawai Madhopur districts; Uttar Pradesh state: Agra region.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Western Hindi, Unclassified
Dialect_Names: Braj Bhasha, Antarbedi (Antarvedi), Bhuksa, Sikarwari, Jadobafi, Dangi, Bhadauri (Towargarhi)
Relationships: Bhuksa is sometimes mentioned as a dialect of Kanauji [bjj]. Braj Bhasha is usually considered a dialect of Hindi [hin], and was the predominant literary language before the switch to Hindi in the 19th century. Chhatapur dialect is widely understood. Other dialects are standard Braj of Mathura, Aligarh, western Agra; standard Braj of Bulandshahr; standard Braj of eastern Agra, southern Morena, southern Bharatpur; Braj merging into Kanauji in Etah, Mainpuri, Budaun, and Bareilly; Braj merging into the Bhadauri subdialect in northern Morena; Braj merging into Jaipuri (Rajasthani) in northern Bharatpur and Sawai Uradhopur; Bhuksa in southern Nainital (Grierson and Konow 1903–1928).
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng].

Alternate_Names: Brok-skad, Brokpa, Brokpa of Dah-Hanu, Dokskat, Kyango, Minaro
Location: Jammu and Kashmir state: Kargil and Ladakh districts along Indus river; Garkhon area, including Batalik, Chulichan, Dah, Darchiks, and Gurgurdo villages.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Outer Languages, Northwestern, Dardic, Shina
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Ladakhi [lbj].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 56% (2001 census).
General_Remarks: A very divergent variety of Shina [scl]. It is the oldest surviving member of the ancient Dardic language.

Location: Arunachal Pradesh state: West Kameng district, Nafra and Singchung sub-districts, Bichom, Diching, Dikiang, Lichini, Mangopom, Namphri, New Kaspi, Ramu, Sachita, Singchung, Situ, and Wangho villages; in mountains on both sides of Rupa river, interspersed among the Aka.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Central Tibeto-Burman, Kho-Bwa
Dialect_Names: Dikhyang, Singchung, Wangho, Bichom, Kaspi, Namphri
Relationships: May be mutually intelligible with Puroik [suv] (Chowdhury 1996); Burling (2003) groups it with Puroik and Sherdukpen [sdp] and possibly also with Lish [lsh] and Sartang [onp]. Lexical similarity: low with all neighboring languages.
Language_Use: Home, village, religion.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin]. Younger people use more Hindi. Also use Hruso [hru]. Also use Kalaktang Monpa [kkf]. Also use Nefamese [nef]. Also use Sherdukpen [sdp]. Older people use more Sherdukpen.
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 24% (1981 census), 35% for men, 12% for women.
General_Remarks: Spoken by the Khoa (Khowa) ethnic group. They are culturally like the Hruso, but speak a different language.

Location: Uttar Pradesh state; Uttarakhand state: southwest Nainital district, Kichha and Kashipur sub-districts, 130 villages, from Keneshpur to Ramnagar; some in Bijnor and Garhwal districts.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Outer Languages, Eastern, Unclassified
Relationships: 95% intelligibility with Rana Tharu [thr]. Lexical similarity: 58%–79% with western Tharu varieties, 58% with Central Tharu [the], 83% with Hindi [hin].
Language_Use: Used by all.
Language_Contact: Some also use Hindi [hin], especially those who are educated, go on to higher studies or jobs in other areas. Also use English [eng].

L1_Full: 5,630,000 (2011 census). Population estimates range up to 20,000,000.
Location: Madhya Pradesh state: Chhatarpur, Chhindwara, Datia, Narsinghpur, Panna, Sagar, Satna, Seoni, Shivpuri and Tikamgarh districts; Maharashtra state: Bhandara and Nagpur districts; Rajasthan state; Uttar Pradesh state: Banda, Hamirpur, Jalaun, Jhansi, and Lalitpur districts.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Western Hindi, Bundeli
Dialect_Names: Standard Bundeli, Lodhanti (Rathora), Chhatapur (Khatola), Banaphari, Kundri, Nibhatta, Tirhari, Gaoli, Kirari, Raghobansi, Nagpuri Hindi, Chhindwara Bundeli
Relationships: Lexical similarity: 41% with Nagpuri Hindi [hin].
Language_Use: Home. Positive attitudes, especially toward Chhatapur dialect.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin], but uneducated speakers have low proficiency.

Autonym: မြန်မာ‎ (Mranmar), မြန်မာစကား‎ (Mranmar sakar), မြန်မာဘာသာ‎ (Mranma bhasa)
L1_Full: 17,000 in India (2024 Joshua Project), based on ethnicity.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Ngwi-Burmese, Burmish, Southern
Typology: SOV; noun head final; tense and aspect; 31 consonants, 8 vowels, 4 diphthongs; tonal (3 tones).
Scripts: Braille script [Brai]. Myanmar (Burmese) script [Mymr], primary usage.

Location: Jammu and Kashmir state: Kargil and Leh districts, especially Ladakh area; group in Srinagar.
Classification: Language isolate
Typology: SOV.
Language_Contact: Also use Kashmiri [kas] (Munshi 2019). Also use Urdu [urd] (Munshi 2019).
Scripts: Arabic script, Naskh variant [Arab]. Arabic script, Nastaliq variant [Aran], primary usage. Latin script [Latn].

Alternate_Names: Bhotia, Byangkho Lwo, Byangkhopa, Byanshi, Byansi, Jaba, Rang, Rang Lo, Saukas, Shaukas
Location: Uttarakhand state: Pithoragarh district, Darchula and Munsyari sub-districts, Garbyang, Gunji, Nabi, Napalchyu, and Rongkang villages; in Kuthi Yangti river valley in the Himalayas on Nepal and Tibet borders; Byangs Patti from Budi south to Kuti village north.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Western Tibeto-Burman, Bodish, West Himalayish, Almora
Relationships: Dialects of Byangs, Chaudangs and Darma valleys are unintelligible to each other (Sharma 1994). Those in Kuti (India) and Tinkar (Nepal) are closely related and quite different from those in other Byangsi villages. Tinkar variety differs from Byangsi, Chaudangsi [cdn], and Darmiya [drd] in forms of agreement affixes and basic vocabulary. Minor dialect differences correspond to geographical divisions (Sharma 2001).
Language_Use: Home, community.
Language_Contact: Also use Central Tibetan [bod]. Also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin], with high level of bilingualism and as the medium of instruction in school. Also use Kumaoni [kfy]. Also use Nepali [npi].
General_Remarks: Cultural center seems to be India. Ranglo or Rang often used as a cover term for Byangs, Chaudangs, Darmiya and Rongpo. Some borrowing from Indo-Aryan languages.

Location: Arunachal Pradesh state: Changlang district, Miao sub-district, Lohit district, Chowkham sub-district, Tirap district; Assam state: Anglong, Cachar, Karbi, and North Cachar districts; Mizoram state: southwest along Karnafuli river; Tripura state: North Tripura district, Kailashahar sub-district; South Tripura district; Manipur and West Bengal states.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Outer Languages, Eastern, Bengali-Assamese
Language_Contact: Also use Bengali [ben]. Also use English [eng]. Also use Mizo [lus].
Education: Taught as subject in primary schools.
Scripts: Bengali (Bangla) script [Beng]. Chakma script [Cakm]. Latin script [Latn].
General_Remarks: Distinct from Chak [ckh].

Alternate_Names: Cameali, Chamĕāḷī, Chamaya, Chambiali, Chambiyali, Chamiyali Pahari, Chamrali, Chamya
Location: Himachal Pradesh state: Chamba district, Chamba sub-district; Jammu and Kashmir state.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Intermediate Divisions, Western, Pahari, Western Pahari
Relationships: 91% intelligibility of Mandeali [mjl], 87% of Kangri [xnr]. Lexical similarity: 90% with Palampuri Kangri [xnr], 86% with Bhattiyali [bht], 84% with Bilaspuri [kfs], 83% with Mandeali [mjl], 79% with Gaddi [gbk], 78% with Churahi [cdj].
Typology: SOV.
Language_Use: Used by all.
Language_Contact: Also use Eastern Punjabi [pan]. Also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin]. Also use Urdu [urd].
Scripts: Devanagari script [Deva]. Takri (Tankri, Takari) script [Takr], no longer in use.

Location: Sikkim state: South district; West Bengal state: Darjeeling, Regu and other parts of the state.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Western Tibeto-Burman, Himalayan, Kiranti, Eastern
Typology: SOV; postpositions; noun head final; no noun classes or genders; content q-word in situ; up to 2 prefixes, up to 7 suffixes; clause constituents indicated by case-marking; verbal affixation marks person and number; split and inverse ergativity; mixed tense-aspect; no passives or voice; nontonal; 28 consonant and 5 vowel phonemes.
Literature: Literature. Periodicals. Radio. Videos. Dictionary. Grammar. Texts. NT: 2015.

Alternate_Names: Byangskat, Byanskat, Champas, Changs-Skat, Changtang, Changtang Ladakhi, Rong, Rupshu, Stotpa, Upper Ladakhi
Location: Jammu and Kashmir state: Tibet border area, Changthang region east and southeast of Leh.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Western Tibeto-Burman, Bodish, Central Bodish, Western
Relationships: 58%–85% intelligibility with Leh dialect of Ladakhi [lbj] with high standard deviation indicating some acquired intelligibility; 94%–95% intelligibility with Stod Bhoti [sbu] from Darcha village. Identify more with Leh Ladakhi culture than with Stod Bhoti despite lack of intelligibility. Related to Rangkas [rgk], Darmiya [drd], Byangsi [bee].
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin]. Also use Kashmiri [kas]. Also use Ladakhi [lbj]. Also use Urdu [urd].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 37% (2001 census).

Alternate_Names: Bangba Lo, Bangba-Lwo, Bangbani, Chanpa Lo, Chaudans Lo, Saukas, Shaukas, Tsaudangsi
Location: Uttarakhand state: Pithoragarh district, Darchula and Munsyari sub-districts, Chilla, Gala, Monggong, Panggu, Rimzhim, Rongto, Rung, Sirdang, Sirkha, Song, Sosa, Syang Khola, Tangkul, Waiku, and Zipti villages; Patti Chaudangs, Kali river west bank facing Nepal border along Mahakali valley.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Western Tibeto-Burman, Bodish, West Himalayish, Almora
Relationships: Related to Rangkas [rgk], Darmiya [drd], and Byangsi [bee] (Sharma 1989), unintelligible with Darmiya and Byangsi (Sharma 1994).
Language_Use: Home, community. Some young people, all adults. Negative attitudes.
Language_Contact: Also use Central Tibetan [bod]. Also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin]. Also use Kumaoni [kfy]. Also use Nepali [npi].
Literacy: Hindi [hin] used for written communication.
General_Remarks: Ranglo or Rang often used as a cover term for Byangs, Chaudangs, Darmiya, and Rongpo.

Location: Andaman and Nicobar Islands union territory: Nicobar Islands, Chaura island.
Classification: Austro-Asiatic, Mon-Khmer, Nicobar, Chowra-Teressa
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng].

Location: Karnataka and Odisha states; Telangana state: mostly Kurnool district, Nallamalla hills.
Classification: Dravidian, South-Central, Telugu
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Telugu [tel].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 43% among Scheduled Tribes in Kurnool District; 43% among Chenchu in Odisha (2001 census).

Alternate_Names: Mamundadan Chetty, Mandadan Chetty, Moundan Chetty
Location: Tamil Nadu state: Nilgiris district, Gudalur sub-district, Cherumulli, Devala, Gudalur, Mudumalai, Padanthurai, Nallakottai, and Srimadurai villages; Kerala state: Wayanad district, Sulthan Bathery, Pulpalli.
Classification: Mixed language, Kannada-Malayalam-Tamil
Relationships: Lexical similarity: 57% with Badaga [bfq], 47% with Kannada [kan], 46% with Malayalam [mal], 45% with Tamil [tam], 41% with Wayanadan Chetti [ctt], 32% with Tulu (Kuravar) [tcy], 31% with Kota [kfe], 18% with Telugu [tel], 14% with Toda [tcx], and 3% with Vaagri Booli [vaa].
Language_Use: Home, community, cultural ceremonies. Used by all. Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Most also use Malayalam [mal]. Most also use Tamil [tam].
Scripts: Malayalam script [Mlym], limited usage. Tamil script [Taml], primary usage.

Location: Karnataka state: Bavali; Kerala state: Wayanad district, Appapara, Chekadi, Kattikkulam, Panavalli, Pulpalli, Thirunelli, and Tholpetti villages; Tamil Nadu state: Coimbatore, Nilgiri and Periyar districts.
Classification: Dravidian, Southern, Tamil-Kannada, Unclassified
Relationships: Lexical similarity: 62%–76% with Gowder, 65% with Jennu Kurumba [xuj], 52% with Kannada [kan].
Language_Use: Older adults only.
Language_Contact: Shifted to Malayalam [mal]. Also use English [eng].
General_Remarks: ‘Chetti’, trader, also loosely employed as a caste name (Thurston and Rangachari 1909). 10 groups of Chetti identified in Tamil Nadu.

L1_Full: 16,300,000 (2011 census). 16,250,000 Chhattisgarh, 89,900 Laria, and 15,600 Pando (2011 census).
Location: Chhattisgarh state: north central; Jharkhand state: Simdega; Madhya Pradesh state: Anuppur and Shahdol (Baigani dialect) districts; Maharashtra state: border areas; Odisha state: Sundargarh.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Intermediate Divisions, Eastern, East Central
Dialect_Names: Sadri Korwa, Baigani (Baiga, Bega, Bhumia, Gowro), Binjhwari, Kalanga, Bhulia, Chhattisgarhi Proper, Kavardi, Khairagarhi
Relationships: Sadri Korwa spoken by Korwa people in Jashpur tahsil of Raigarh District; Baigani in Balaghat, Raipur, and Bilaspur districts of Chhattisgarh, and Sambalpur District of Odisha; Binjhwari in Raipur and Raigarh districts of Chhattisgarh; Kalanga and Bhulia dialects are spoken in Patna District of Bihar; Chhattisgarhi Proper in Raipur, Durg, Bilaspur, and other districts of Chhattisgarh. Lexical similarity: 66%–69% with Kamar [keq].
Language_Use: Nearly all domains. Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin], but with low proficiency. Also use Odia [ory].
Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Bhunjia [bhu], Eastern Muria [emu], Far Western Muria [fmu].
Literature: Literature. Newspapers. Radio. TV. Grammar. NT: 2005–2012.

Location: Assam state; Mizoram state: Aizawl, Chhimtuipui, and Lunglei districts; Tripura state.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Kuki-Chin, Central, Lai
Relationships: Linguistically and ethnically a subgroup of the Laizou (Anal) [anm] (Matisoff et al 1996:8).
Typology: SOV.
Language_Use: Some young people, all adults.
Language_Contact: Also use Assamese [asm], with most youth shifting.
Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Pankhu [pkh].
General_Remarks: A Scheduled Tribe.

Alternate_Names: Falam Chin, Fallam, Halam Chin, Hallam, Tipura
Location: Assam state: Karimganj district, a few villages in Cachar and North Hills districts; Mizoram, Tripura, and West Bengal states.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Kuki-Chin, Central, Lai
Dialect_Names: Chorei, Chari Chong, Halam, Kaipeng (Kaipang, Keipang), Kalai (Koloi), Molsom (Mursum), Rupini, Tapong, Bongcher (Bawngcher, Bondcher, Bongshi)
Typology: SOV; negation is marked after the verb.
Literacy: Literacy among Kaipeng in Tripura is low.
Scripts: Bengali (Bangla) script [Beng], used in India. Latin script [Latn], primary usage.
General_Remarks: Ethnically Halam. Many ethnic Halam speak Kok Borok [trp] as L1. Halam is a generic term under which 9 subgroups, each with a distinct dialect, are grouped together: (Sakachep [sch], Chorei, Rupini, Ranglong [rnl], Marcephang (Khochung–dialect of [cfm]), Molsom, Keipang (dialect of [cfm]), Bondcher (dialect of [cfm]), Rangkhol [hra]).

Alternate_Names: Baungshe, Haka Chin, Hakha Lai, Lai, Lai Hawlh, Lai Pawi, “Haka” (pej.)
Location: Assam and Meghalaya states; Mizoram state: Aizawi district, Champhai subdistrict, southernmost tip; Chhimtuipui district, 41 villages.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Kuki-Chin, Central, Lai
Typology: SOV; negation is marked after the verb.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng].
Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Matu Chin [hlt], Zyphe Chin [zyp].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 54% (1981 census). Most young people can read in Hakha.

Alternate_Names: Kami, Khami, Khumi, Khumi Chin, Khuni, Kumi, “Khweymi” (pej.)
Location: Mizoram state.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Kuki-Chin, Peripheral, Southern
Typology: SOV; genitives, articles, adjectives, numerals after noun heads; negation is marked after the verb.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng].
General_Remarks: Called Khami Chin in India.

Alternate_Names: Matu, Matu Chin, Matupi, Nga La
Location: Mizoram state.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Kuki-Chin, Peripheral, Southern, Cho-Asho, Cho
Typology: SOV; negation is marked after the verb.
Language_Contact: Most also use Hakha Chin [cnh]. Also use English [eng].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 70%.

Alternate_Names: Haithe, Paite, Paithe, Parte, Vuite, Zome, Zomi, Zoukam
Location: Assam state; Manipur state: Churachandpur district, Khuga valley, Copur Bazar; Mizoram state: Aizawl district, Champhai sub-district, 20 villages; Tripura state.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Kuki-Chin, Peripheral, Northern, Thado
Dialect_Names: Bukpi (Bukpui), Dapzal (Dapzar), Dim, Dimpi, Lamzang, Lousau, Saizang, Sihzang, Telzang (Teizang), Tuichiap
Typology: SOV.
Language_Contact: Many also use English [eng]. Also use Mizo [lus].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L1: 75% (2005 BI). Literacy rate in L2: 79% (2001 census).
Education: Taught as subject at Manipur University.
General_Remarks: Paites in Mizoram speak Mizo (Go 1996). Most speak Teizang and Dapzal dialects (Singh 1995b). Zomi is a collective ethnic autonym generally used by Tedim Chin [ctd] of Myanmar, Paite, and Vaiphei [vap] of Manipur.

Location: Assam, Manipur (south), and Mizoram (north) states.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Kuki-Chin, Peripheral, Northern, Thado
Typology: SOV; negation is marked after the verb.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng].
Scripts: Latin script [Latn]. Pau Cin Hau alphabet [Pauc], for liturgical purposes only.

Alternate_Names: Kuki, Kuki-Thado, Thaadou, Thaadou Kuki, Thaadow, Thado, Thado-Pao, Thado-Ubiphei, Thadou, Thadow
Location: Assam state; Manipur state: Chandel, Churachandpur, Senapati, and Tamenglong districts; Mizoram state: northeast; Nagaland state: Kohima district; Tripura state.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Kuki-Chin, Peripheral, Northern, Thado
Dialect_Names: Changsen, Jangshen, Kaokeep, Khongzai, Kipgen, Langiung, Saihriem (“Sairang” (pej.)), Thangngen, Hawkip, Shithlou, Singson (Shingsol)
Relationships: Several varieties, but high mutual intelligibility among dialects. Related to Kamhau (Tedim Chin [ctd] dialect), Ralte [ral], Paite Chin [pck], Zou [zom].
Typology: SOV.
Language_Contact: Also use Meitei [mni]. Also use Nepali [npi].
Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Sakachep [sch].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 57% in Manipur (2001 census). Literacy lower among older people and in villages.
Literature: Literature. Periodicals. Radio. Dictionary. Grammar. Bible: 1971–1994.
General_Remarks: Some listed dialects are separate languages.

Location: Mizoram state: Saiha district, Iana and Siata villages.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Kuki-Chin, Maraic
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Hakha Chin [cnh]. Also use Mara [mrh].

Alternate_Names: Chana, Channali, Chinal, Dagi, Harijan, Shipi
Location: Himachal Pradesh state: Lahul and Pattan valleys, and Gushal village.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Unclassified
Relationships: Closely related to Sanskrit [san].
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng].
General_Remarks: Spoken by the Chinal caste. Many are well educated.

L1_Full: 9,900 in India (2024 Joshua Project), based on ethnicity.
Location: Kolkata and Mumbai: scattered Chinese variety speakers in these and other urban areas.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Chinese
Typology: SVO; prepositions; noun head final; 6 full (concrete meaning) word classes; no articles; passives; 24 consonants, 8 vowels, 6 diphthongs; tonal (4 phonemic tones).
Scripts: Bopomofo script [Bopo], used since 1913, revised in 1920 and 1932, mainly used in Taiwan. Braille script [Brai]. Han script, Simplified variant [Hans], used since 1956, official in Mainland China (1956) and Singapore (1969), also used elsewhere. Han script, Traditional variant [Hant], used since mid-19th century, official in Taiwan, also used elsewhere. Latin script [Latn].

Location: Assam state: Cachar district, a village near Jirbom; Manipur state: Bishnupur district; Churachandpur district, Charoi Khullen village; Tamenglong district, Bungte, Dolang, Dolang Khunou, Kangchup, Lamdangmei, Nungshai, Sadu, Senapati, Thangzing, and Uram villages; Thoubal district, Vaithou; Nagaland state. Scattered.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Kuki-Chin, Northwestern
Relationships: Reportedly most similar to Chin Mizo [lus].
Language_Use: Educated youth more interested in developing L1 and preserving culture than elders. Community. Used by all. Mixed attitudes.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Meitei [mni].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 56% in English [eng] and Meitei [mni] (2000 A. Khorong).

Alternate_Names: Bhil, Chaudhari, Chaudri, Chodhari, Choudhara, Choudhary, Chowdhary
L1_Full: 111,000 (2011 census). More speakers in Tapi district.
Location: Gujarat state: Surat and Tapi districts.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Intermediate Divisions, Western, Bhil
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Gujarati [guj].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 63% in Gujarat [guj] (2001 census).

Location: Arunachal Pradesh state: West Kameng district; Chug valley, Jagarbasti, Tsangpa, and Duhum villages and associated hamlets.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Central Tibeto-Burman, Kho-Bwa
Relationships: Reportedly most similar to Lish [lsh]. Lexical similarity: 59%–74% with Lish [lsh].
Language_Use: Currently relatively vigorous but low speaker population and rapid socio-economic developments in the region pose severe threats to the long-term survival of the language (Bodt 2020: 50–51).
Language_Contact: Some also use Brokpake [sgt] (Bodt 2020). A few also use English [eng], mostly younger people (Bodt 2020). Also use Central Tibetan [bod], used by religiously educated people (Bodt 2020). Also use Hindi [hin], mostly younger generation with other speakers (Bodt 2020). Also use Tawang Monpa [twm] (Bodt 2020). Also use Tshangla [tsj], mostly adults over 40 years of age (Bodt 2020).
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 22% for Hindi [hin] for the villages in the Chug valley (Bodt 2020:41), based on 2011 census.
General_Remarks: There is some confusion about ethno-linguistic classification of Monpa (Bodt 2014).

Alternate_Names: Chaurahi, Churahi Pahari, Churai Pahari, Himachali, Pahari
Location: Himachal Pradesh state: Chamba district, Chaurah and Saluni sub-district, Bhalai; Jammu and Kashmir state: Doda and Kathua districts.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Intermediate Divisions, Western, Pahari, Western Pahari
Relationships: 90% intelligibility of Mandeali [mjl], 83% of Kangri [xnr], 85% of Chambeali [cdh]. Lexical similarity: 78% with Chambeali [cdh] (most similar), 70% with Palampuri Kangri [xnr] and Bhattiyali [bht], 67%–69% with Gaddi [gbk], 65% with Mandeali [mjl] and Bilaspuri [kfs], 64% with Pangi.
Typology: SOV; postpositions; genitives after noun heads; adjectives, numerals before noun heads; question word initial; verb suffixes mark person, number, gender of subject.
Language_Use: Used by all.
Language_Contact: Also use Eastern Punjabi [pan]. Also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin]. Also use Urdu [urd].

Alternate_Names: Dangri, Dangs Bhil, Dhanka, Dhanki, Kakachhu-Ki Boli, Tadavi, Tadvi Bhil
Location: Gujarat state: Dangs district; Maharashtra state: Jalgaon district; Karnataka and Rajasthan states.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Intermediate Divisions, Western, Khandesi
Relationships: Similar to Khandesi [khn]. Kukna [kex] speakers consider Dhanki to be a variety of their own language (2020 A. K. Lima).
Language_Contact: Also use Gujarati [guj].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 53% in Gujarat (2001 census).
General_Remarks: Dhanka of Rajasthan reportedly speak Hindi [hin] as L1; Dhanka of Maharashtra use Gujarati [guj] as L1; Tadvi Bhil reportedly use Bhili [bhb] as L1.

Location: Assam state: Cachar district; Tripura state: North Tripura district, Kailashahar and Kamalpur sub-districts.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Unclassified
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 45%.

Alternate_Names: Darimiya, Darma, Darma Lwo, Darma-Lwo, Darmani, Saukas, Shaukas
Location: Uttarakhand state: Pithoragarh district, Darchula and Munsyari sub-district, Baling, Baun, Bongling, Dar, Datu, Dhakar, Dugtu, Gwo, Marchha, Nanglin, Philam, Saung, Selachal, Sipoo, and Sobla villages; in Dhauli valley, from Tawaghat near Dharchula south to Sipoo north along Dhauli river.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Western Tibeto-Burman, Bodish, West Himalayish, Almora
Relationships: Related to Rangkas [rgk], Chaudangsi [cdn] and Byangsi [bee].
Language_Use: Learn Kumaoni [kfy] and Hindi [hin] simultaneously with their mother tongue. Code switching and code mixing very common. Uncertain whether stable bilingualism will continue or whether Kumaoni or Hindi will replace Darmiya. Home, community. Some young people, all adults.
Language_Contact: Also use Central Tibetan [bod]. Also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin], with high rates of bilingualism and as the medium of education at all levels. Also use Kumaoni [kfy]. Also use Nepali [npi].
General_Remarks: Ranglo or Rang often used for Byangs, Chaudangs, Darmiya, and Rongpo.

Alternate_Names: Dakhini, Dakhni, Dakini, Dakkani, Dakkhani, Deccani, Desi
Location: Gujarat state; Madhya Pradesh state: Raisen and Sehore districts; Karnataka state: Belgaum and Vijayapura districts.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Outer Languages, Southern, Unclassified
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng].
Scripts: Arabic script, Naskh variant [Arab]. Arabic script, Nastaliq variant [Aran], primary usage. Devanagari script [Deva].
General_Remarks: May be the same as Dakhini dialect of Urdu [urd].

Alternate_Names: Chutiya, Dari, Deori-Chutiya, Deuri, Dewri, Drori, Jimochaya, Jimosaya
Location: Assam state: Demaji, Lakhimpur, Jorhat, and Tinsukia districts; Arunachal Pradesh state: Lohit district.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Sal, Boro-Garo
Relationships: May constitute its own subgroup under Bodo-Garo. Reportedly not similar to other languages. Dialect of Lakhimpur District is regarded as purest. Lexical similarity: 77%–93% with Deori varieties, 11%–16% with Bodo [brx].
Language_Use: Vigorous among the Dibongya, the only subgroup that has retained the language. Home, village, religion, work. Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Many also use Assamese [asm], but women, older adults and uneducated have less proficiency. Also use English [eng].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 71%.
General_Remarks: ‘Deori’, the temple guard. Deori Chutiya is 1 of 4 Chutiya subgroups. Do not call themselves Chutiya.

Alternate_Names: Deshia, Desia, Desiya Oriya, Koraput Oriya
Location: Chhattisgarh state: Bastar district; Odisha state: Koraput district, Lamtaput sub-district; Nabarangapur district.
LWC_Support: Native to India; became dominant around the second half of the 19th century under British rule. Used in literature, poetry, music, song, trade, and interethnic communication.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Outer Languages, Eastern, Oriya
Relationships: Intelligible with Adivasi Oriya [ort] but uses different scripts. Lexical similarity: 80%–85% with Adivasi Oriya [ort] dialects in Andhra Pradesh.
Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Bodo Gadaba [gbj], Gata’ [gaq], Mirgan [zrg], Pottangi Ollar Gadaba [gdb].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 6%.

Location: Rajasthan state: west.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Intermediate Divisions, Western, Rajasthani, Marwari
General_Remarks: A Scheduled Tribe.

Location: Jharkhand state: Bokaro district; West Bengal state: Puruliya district, 16 villages.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Sal, Dhimalish
Typology: SOV; postpositions; noun head final; no noun classes or genders; content q-word in situ; genitives, demonstratives, relatives before noun heads; 1 prefix, up to 3 suffixes; clause constituents indicated by case-marking; verbal affixation marks person; non-ergative; tense and aspect; passives and voice; nontonal; 31 consonant and 16 vowel phonemes (includes 5 basic vowels, 5 long vowels and 5 nasalized vowels); honorificity is marked for first person when speaking with in-laws.
Literature: Literature. Periodicals. Radio. Dictionary. Grammar. Texts. NT: 2017.

Location: Gujarat state: Surat and Valsad districts, Dadra, Daman and Diu union territory, and Nagar Haveli; Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, and Rajasthan states.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Intermediate Divisions, Western, Bhil
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Gujarati [guj].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 76% in Gujarat (2001 census).

Alternate_Names: Dhundari-Marwari, Dhundhari, Jaipuri, Jhar-sahi boli, Kai kui ki boli, Marwari
Location: Rajasthan state: Dausa, Jaipur, and Tonk districts; possibly in Ajmer, Bundi, Jhalawar, northern Karauli, Kishangarh, Kota, and Sawai Madhopur districts.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Intermediate Divisions, Western, Rajasthani, Marwari
Relationships: 54% intelligibility of Marwari [rwr]; 86% of Shekhawati [swv]. Lexical similarity: 75%–89% with dialects; 62%–70% with Merwari [wry], 65%–81% with Shekhawati [swv], 46%–66% with Godwari [gdx], 56%–64% with Mewari [mtr], 64%–73% with Haroti [hoj], 62%–67% with Mewati [wtm], 59% with Hindi [hin].
Typology: SOV.
Language_Use: Vigorous. Home, village, market, religion. Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin], but the educated are more fluent.

Alternate_Names: Digaro, Digaro Mishmi, Digaru, Mishmi, Taaon, Taraon, Tawra, Taying
Location: Arunachal Pradesh state: Lohit district, Changlagam, Goiliang, and Hayuliang circles, Dibang Valley district; Assam state.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Central Tibeto-Burman, Digarish
Relationships: May not be in the Tani group, but is related. Lexical similarity: 25% with Idu-Mishmi [clk], 10% with Miju-Mishmi [mxj].
Typology: SOV; 4 tones which are reported to vary considerably among speakers.
Language_Contact: Also use Assamese [asm]. Also use English [eng].
Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Miju-Mishmi [mxj].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 40% for Mishmi (2001 census).

Alternate_Names: Dimasa Kachari, Grau Dima, Hills Kachari, Magrau
Location: Assam state: north Cachar district and Cachar hills; Karbi Anglong and Nagaon districts; Nagaland state: Haflong district; Meghalaya and Mizoram states.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Sal, Boro-Garo, Dimasa-Kokborok
Dialect_Names: Hasao, Hawar, Dembra, Dijuwa, Humri, Semsa, Walgong
Relationships: Related to Kachari [xac].
Typology: SOV; agglutinative; tonal; honorific.
Language_Use: Largely assimilated into Bengali [ben] and Assamese [asm] communities (Van Driem 2007).
Language_Contact: Some also use Assamese [asm], especially in Karbi Anglong and Nagaon districts (Longmailai 2012). Some also use Bengali [ben], especially in Cachar plains (Longmailai 2012). Some also use Nagamese [nag], especially in Nagaland with speakers of other languages (Longmailai 2012). Also use English [eng].
Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Sakachep [sch].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 60% in Assam (2001 census).
General_Remarks: Some ethnic Dimasa speak other languages as L1: Mikir Karbi [mjw], Bengali [ben], and Assamese [asm].

Alternate_Names: Dhogaryali, Dogari, Dogri Jammu, Dogri Pahari, Dogri-Kangri, Dongari, Hindi Dogri, Tokkaru
Location: Jammu and Kashmir state: Kathua, Poonch, Reasi, and Udhampur districts; Himachal Pradesh state: Chamba and Kangra districts; Punjab state: Gurdaspur district.
Official_Recognition: Statutory language of provincial identity in Jammu and Kashmir (1950, Constitution, Schedule VIII), amended 2003.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Intermediate Divisions, Western, Pahari, Western Pahari
Relationships: Dogri speakers understand each other well. Some reported difficulty understanding Kangri [xnr]. Department of Dogri at Jammu University designated Samba as the standard dialect and published textbooks based on this variety. Lexical similarity: 78% between dialects; excluding the most divergent site, others more than 86%.
Typology: SOV.
Language_Use: Taught in government schools and as a subject in university. All domains. Used by all. Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Also use Eastern Punjabi [pan], in shops. Also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin], in school and shops; many have only rudimentary knowledge of it. Also use Urdu [urd], especially middle-aged and older speakers.
Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Gujari [gju], Khah [hkh].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 18%–19%. Young people are becoming literate in Dogri.
Education: Taught in primary and secondary schools through grade 5 and as subject thereafter in Jammu and Kashmir state.
Scripts: Arabic script, Nastaliq variant [Aran], no longer in use. Devanagari script [Deva]. Dogra script [Dogr], no longer in use. Takri (Tankri, Takari) script [Takr], no longer in use.
General_Remarks: Dogri formerly considered a Punjabi dialect, but now promoted as a written language in India. Dhogri is a Scheduled Caste in Himachal Pradesh and Punjab who speak Chambeali [cdh] in Himachal and Dogri in Punjab (Singh 1995b).

Location: Maharashtra, Uttar Pradesh, and Uttarakhand states.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Intermediate Divisions, Eastern, Eastern Pahari
Literature: Literature. Periodicals. Radio. TV. Dictionary. Grammar. NT: 2017.

Ethnic: 791,000 (2007). Over half the ethnic group uses Gujarati [guj] (2007).
Location: Gujarat state: Bharuch (Broach), Surat, Vadodara, and Valsad districts; Maharashtra state: Thane district, Dahanu and Talasari cities’ areas, Dadra and Nagar Haveli, Daman and Diu enclaves; Karnataka and Rajasthan states.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Intermediate Divisions, Western, Bhil
Relationships: Dubli of Bharuch district is intelligible with Dungri dialect of Vasavi [vas].
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 48% in Gujarat (2001 census).

Alternate_Names: Bhilori, Dongre Bhil, Dungra Bhili, Dungri Bhil
Location: Gujarat state: Vadodara district, Chotaudeyapur and Naswadi sub-districts; Madhya Pradesh state: Jhabua district, Alirajpur sub-district; Maharashtra state: Dedgam sub-district; slopes of Vindhya Satpura mountains. 200 villages.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Intermediate Divisions, Western, Bhil
Relationships: 84%–89% intelligibility with Bhilori [noi] of Maharashtra. Lexical similarity: 75%–85% between subgroups, 71%–87% with Bhilori and Noiri Bhili, less than 53% with Garasia [gas].
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 3%–5%.
General_Remarks: A Bhil subgroup. Dungra Bhil sometimes used as alternate name for Adivasi Garasia [gas] and Rajput Garasia [gra] but probably refers to more than 1 group living in the hills. ‘Dungra’, hill.

Alternate_Names: Dhruva, Dhurwa, Durva, Paraja, Parajhi, Parjhi, Parji, Tagara, Thakara, Tugara
Location: Chhattisgarh state: Bastar district, southeast Jagdalpur sub-district; Odisha state: Koraput district.
Classification: Dravidian, Central, Parji-Gadaba
Relationships: Nethanar dialect is central. Lexical similarity: 90%–96% with dialects.
Language_Use: Madiya [mrr] speak Duruwa to communicate with the Dhurwa people. Some young people, all adults.
Language_Contact: Also use Bhatri [bgw], especially the younger generation. Also use English [eng]. Also use Halbi [hlb], especially the younger generation. Also use Hindi [hin], especially the younger generation. Also use Odia [ory], especially the younger generation.
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 15%–25%.

Location: West Bengal state: Darjeeling and Kalimpong, just inside the Indo-Bhutan border; Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Manipur, Meghalaya, Nagaland, and Sikkim states.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Western Tibeto-Burman, Bodish, Central Bodish, Central, Southern
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng].
Scripts: Braille script [Brai]. Tibetan script [Tibt], official usage.

Official_Recognition: Statutory national working language (1950, Constitution, Articles 343 and 348(1)).
Classification: Indo-European, Germanic, West, English
Typology: SVO; prepositions; genitives after noun heads; articles, adjectives, numerals before noun heads; question word initial; word order distinguishes subject, object, indirect objects, given and new information, topic and comment; active and passive; causative; comparative; consonant and vowel clusters; 24 consonants, 13 vowels, 8 diphthongs; non-tonal; free stress; phrasal verbs.
Education: Taught in some primary and secondary schools, more in southern India than in northern India; taught as subject in all other schools. Taught in most tertiary schools.
Scripts: Braille script [Brai]. Deseret Alphabet [Dsrt], limited usage only in the United States between 1854–1877. Duployan shorthand [Dupl]. Latin script [Latn], primary usage. Shavian (Shaw) script [Shaw], no longer in use.
General_Remarks: Neither British nor American English but a distinct Indian dialect with its own unique vocabulary and style.

Ethnic: 5,440 (2001 census). 3,890 in Kerala and 1,560 in Tamil Nadu.
Location: Kerala state: Palakkad district, Chittoor sub-district; Tamil Nadu state: Coimbatore district.
Classification: Dravidian, Southern, Tamil-Kannada, Tamil-Kodagu, Tamil-Malayalam, Tamil
Relationships: Lexical similarity: 91% between Eravallan of Coimbatore and of Palakkad, 70%–74% with Tamil [tam], 59%–77% with Irula [iru], 77%–86% with Malasar [ymr].
Language_Use: Shifting to Tamil [tam]. Most children learn Tamil first. Some young people, all adults.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Tamil [tam].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 42% in Tamil [tam]. Resistant toward literacy in Eravallan.

Location: Puducherry Union Territory.
Official_Recognition: Statutory language of provincial identity in Puducherry Union Territory (1950, Constitution, Articles 345–347 inclusive), unscheduled language.
Classification: Indo-European, Italic, Romance, Italo-Western, Western, Gallo-Iberian, Gallo-Romance, Gallo-Rhaetian, Oïl, French
Typology: SVO; prepositions; noun head final for common adjectives, numbers, possessives, but most attributive adjectives come after the noun; gender (masculine/feminine); definite and indefinite articles; verb affixes mark person, number; passives; tense; comparatives; 20 consonant and 14 vowel phonemes; non-tonal; syllable-timed stress.
Education: Taught in primary and secondary schools through grade 5 and as subject thereafter in Puducherry Union Territory.
Scripts: Braille script [Brai]. Duployan shorthand [Dupl]. Latin script [Latn], primary usage.

Alternate_Names: Boi Gadaba, Gadba, Gadwa, Godwa, Gudwa, Gutab, Gutob, Gutob-Gadaba, Gutop
Location: Andhra Pradesh state: Visakhapatnam district; Odisha state: Koraput district, Lamtaput sub-district, 40 villages; Malkangiri district, Khoirput sub-district.
Classification: Austro-Asiatic, Munda, South Munda, Koraput Munda, Gutob-Remo-Geta’, Gutob-Remo
Dialect_Names: Birong Raji, Kinda Raji, Lamtaput, Koraput
Relationships: Dialects mutually intelligible. Speakers in Lamtaput block have 89%–94% intelligibility in Tikrapada and Audipoda villages. Intelligibility of the Hanumal village variety is less. Lexical similarity: 69%–89% among 7 varieties in Odisha, 90% between listed dialects.
Language_Use: Many speak and are shifting to Desiya [dso] in home and religious domains. Some young people, all adults. Mixed attitudes.
Language_Contact: A few also use Odia [ory], in Odisha. Also use Desiya [dso]. Also use English [eng]. Also use Telugu [tel], in Andhra Pradesh.
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 9% (2000 H. Rajan). Literacy classes in progress.
General_Remarks: Some ethnic Gadaba in Madhya Pradesh speak Bhatri [bgw] as L1. Different from Dravidian Mudhili Gadaba [gau] and Pottangi Ollar Gadaba [gdb].

Alternate_Names: Gadaba, Gol Gadaba, Kondekar, Kondko, Konekor Gadaba
Location: Andhra Pradesh state: Vizianagaram district, Salur and Pachipenta sub-districts; Srikakulam and Vishakhapatnam districts.
Classification: Dravidian, Central, Parji-Gadaba
Relationships: 93%–98% intelligibility among dialects. Lexical similarity: 84%–94% between dialects. Different from Dravidian Mudhili Gadaba [gau] and Pottangi Ollar Gadaba [gdb].
Language_Use: All domains. Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Also use Telugu [tel], but with low proficiency.
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 34%–42% (2001 census).

Alternate_Names: Allar, Gadaba, Gadba, Hallari, Hollar Gadbas, Konekor, Konekor Gadaba, Mundli, Ollar Gadaba, Ollari, Ollaro, San Gadaba, Sano
Location: Odisha state: Koraput district, Nandapur and Pottangi sub-districts.
Classification: Dravidian, Central, Parji-Gadaba
Relationships: Lexical similarity: 69%–80% with 4 varieties in Odisha; 42%–47% with 1 variety in Andhra Pradesh; 52%–62% with Mudhili Gadaba [gau] in Andhra Pradesh.
Language_Use: Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Also use Desiya [dso], as main L2. Also use Telugu [tel], but with low proficiency.
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 7%.
Scripts: Oriya (Odia) script [Orya], used in Odisha. Telugu script [Telu], used in Andhra Pradesh.
General_Remarks: Different from Gadaba [gbj] in Munda family, also spoken in Koraput.

Alternate_Names: Bharmauri Bhadi, Gaddyali, Gadi, Gadiali, Pahari Bharmauri, Panchi Brahmauri Rajput
Location: Himachal Pradesh state: Chamba district, Brahmaur sub-district; Jammu and Kashmir, Madhya Pradesh, Punjab, and Uttar Pradesh states; Delhi.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Intermediate Divisions, Western, Pahari, Western Pahari
Relationships: 93% intelligibility of Mandeali [mjl], 97% of Kangri [xnr], 83% of Chambeali [cdh]. Lexical similarity: 74%–80% with Palamuri Kangri [xnr], 79% with Chambeali [cdh], 67%–73% with Mandeali [mjl].
Typology: SOV.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin], in shops, cities, and as language of instruction in schools.
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 37% for Jammu and Kashmir (2001 census).
Scripts: Devanagari script [Deva]. Takri (Tankri, Takari) script [Takr], no longer in use.
General_Remarks: Gaddi is generic for all indigenous populations of Bharmaur area of Chamba District.

Alternate_Names: Boonan, Bunan, Erankad, Ghara, Keylong Boli, Lahuli, Lahuli of Bunan, Poonan, Punan
Location: Himachal Pradesh state: Barbog, Biling, Gumrang, Guskyar, Kardang, Kyelang, Paspara, Pyukar, and Styering, and Yurnad villages; Gahr Valley along Bhaga river from confluence with the Chandra and upstream.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Western Tibeto-Burman, Bodish, West Himalayish, Kinauri
Relationships: Lexical similarity: 39% with Sunam [ssk], 26%–39% with varieties of Chamba Lahuli (Pattani) [lae], 37% with Tinani [lbf], 26%–34% with some varieties of Central Tibetan [bod], 34% with Jangshung [jna] and Shumcho [scu], 31% with Kinnaur Bhoti [nes], 30% with Chitkuli [cik] and Chhoyul Kinnauri [tpq], 24% with Lhasa dialect of Central Tibetan [bod], 23% with Kanauri [kfk].
Typology: Only singular and plural number; no gender indicated in verbs or pronouns.
Language_Use: All domains. Some young people, all adults.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng].
Scripts: Takri (Tankri, Takari) script [Takr], no longer in use. Tibetan script [Tibt].
General_Remarks: Bodh caste, but speak a different language from Bodhs of Mayar, Khoksar, and Stod valleys. They consider themselves different from Bodhs of the north, whom they call Tibetans.

Alternate_Names: Gamati, Gameti, Gamith, Gamta, Gamti, Gavit
Location: Gujarat state: Surat district; some in Bharuch, Dangs, and Valsad districts; Maharashtra state: Nandurbar district; some in Dhule district.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Intermediate Divisions, Western, Bhil
Relationships: Reportedly similar to Mawchi [mke].
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 53% (2001 census). Most have high school or college education.

Location: Manipur state: south Churachandpur district, 37 villages; Assam and Meghalaya states.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Kuki-Chin, Peripheral, Northern, Sizang
Relationships: Related to Thado Chin [tcz]. Differs little from Vaiphei [vap], Paite [pck], or Zou [zom].
Language_Use: Under pressure from Meitei [mni] (Van Driem 2007).
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Meitei [mni].
Literacy: Literacy high among young people and lower among older people.

Alternate_Names: Adiwasi Girasia, Adiwasi Gujarati, Garasia, Girasia
