Location: Gujarat state: Banaskantha district, Danta sub-district; Sabarkantha district, Poshina sub-district; Rajasthan state: Jalor district.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Intermediate Divisions, Western, Bhil
Relationships: Understand Rajput Garasia [gra] well. Lexical similarity: 89%–96% between dialects, 75%–93% with dialects of Rajput Garasia; 79%–92% with dialects of Patelia [bhb]; 79%–93% with Wagdi [wbr]; 76%–87% with Marwari [rwr] dialects.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Gujarati [guj], but with low proficiency.
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 15%–25%.
General_Remarks: Speakers are Bhils. Dungra Bhil is sometimes used as an alternate name for Adiwasi Garasia and Rajput Garasia [gra] but probably refers to more than 1 group living in the hills (Dungra means hill).

Alternate_Names: Dhungri Garasia, Dungari Garasia, Dungri Grasia, Girasia, Grasia, Nyar
Location: Gujarat state: Banaskantha district; Rajasthan state: Pali, Sirchi, and Udaipur districts.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Intermediate Divisions, Western, Bhil
Relationships: Rajput Garasia do not understand Adiwasi Garasia [gas] but intelligibility is high the other way. Lexical similarity: 94%–99% with Gujarati [guj] and Rajasthani [mve] dialects, 75%–93% with Adiwasi Garasia [gas] dialects; 76%–84% with Patelia [bhb] dialects; 79%–86% with Wagdi [wbr]; 67%–84% with Marwari [rwr] dialects.
Language_Use: Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Also use Gujarati [guj]. Also use Hindi [hin].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 15%–25%.
General_Remarks: Warrior Caste. Distinct from Dungra Bhil [duh], which is sometimes used as an alternate name for Adiwasi Garasia [gas] and Rajput Garasia but probably refers to more than 1 group living in the hills (Dungra means hill).

Alternate_Names: Gadhavali, Gadhawala, Gadwahi, Gashwali, Girwali, Godauli, Gorwali, Gurvali, Pahari Garhwali
Location: Himachal Pradesh state; Uttarakhand state: Chamoli, Dehra Dun, Pauri Garhwal, Rudraprayag, Tehri Garhwal, and Uttarkashi districts.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Intermediate Divisions, Western, Pahari, Garhwali
Dialect_Names: Srinagari, Tehri (Gangapariya), Badhani, Dessaulya, Lohbya, Majh-Kumaiya, Bhattiani, Nagpuriya, Rathi, Salani (Pauri), Ravai, Parvati, Jaunpuri, Gangadi (Uttarkashi), Chandpuri
Relationships: Jaunsari [jns] is sometimes referred to as a dialect of Garhwali, but most say they cannot understand it. Parvati dialect also reportedly not mutually intelligible; Srinagari is literary standard; Pauri generally regarded as the sweetest; Srinagari and Pauri are very similar. Lexical similarity: 53%–84% among dialects; 54%–69% with Hindi [hin], 55%–66% with Kumaoni [kfy]. The divergent dialect varieties of Bangani, Parvati, and Ravai are no more similar to Western Pahari varieties than to Garhwali.
Typology: SOV.
Language_Use: Vigorous. Home, village. Used by all. Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin], in the market, and with more fluency among men, the educated, and youth.
Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Gujari [gju], Jad [jda], Rongpo [rnp].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 72% for Uttarakhand (2001 census). Older women lack literacy.
General_Remarks: Jaunpuri and Ravai dialects are culturally similar to Jaunsari and distinct from Garhwali. Castes are Brahmin, Rajput, Harijan.

Location: Assam state: Goalpara, Kamrup, and Karbi Anglong districts; Meghalaya state: Garo Hills district; Nagaland state: Kohima district; Tripura state: south Tripura district, Udaipur sub-district; north Tripura district, Kailasahar and Kamalpur sub-districts; west Tripura district, Sadar sub-district; West Bengal state: Jalpaiguri and Koch Bihar districts.
Official_Recognition: Statutory provincial language in Meghalaya State (1950, Constitution, Articles 347), unscheduled language.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Sal, Boro-Garo
Dialect_Names: A’beng (A’bengya, Am’beng), A’chick (A’chik, A’we, Chisak, Dual, Matchi), Dacca, Ganching, Kamrup
Relationships: A’chick is the standardized dialect in India. A’beng dialect used in Bangladesh, but is not mutually intelligible. Reportedly most similar to Koch [kdq].
Typology: SOV; postpositions; case-marking (9 cases); numeral classifiers; tense markers; 16 consonant and 5 vowels; non-tonal.
Language_Use: Awe dialect, spoken in Assam, has few remaining speakers. Most use standard Garo.
Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Atong [aot], Hajong [haj], Koch [kdq], Lyngngam [lyg], Rabha [rah], Ruga [ruh].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 55% for Meghalaya (2001 census). General level of education is low compared to Khasi [kha].
Education: Taught in primary and secondary schools in Meghalaya state. Taught as subject at North-Eastern Hill University.
Literature: Literature. Radio. Videos. Dictionary. Grammar. Bible: 1924–1994.
Scripts: Bengali (Bangla) script [Beng]. Braille script [Brai], used since 1998. Latin script [Latn].

Alternate_Names: Didayi, Didei, Dire, Gataq, Geta’, Getaq, Gta Asa, Gta’
Location: Andhra Pradesh state: east Godavari district; Odisha state: Koraput and Malkangiri districts, Kudumulgumma and Chitrakonda sub-districts south of Bondo Hills; some in Khairput sub-district. 47 villages.
Classification: Austro-Asiatic, Munda, South Munda, Koraput Munda, Gutob-Remo-Geta’, Geta’
Relationships: Ruhlen treats Plains Geta’ and Hill Geta’ as separate languages. Lexical similarity: 68%–93% among dialects, 27%–37% with Bondo [bfw] varieties, 22%–28% with Gadaba Gutob [gbj] dialect.
Language_Use: Some young people, all adults.
Language_Contact: Also use Desiya [dso]. Also use English [eng]. Also use Odia [ory].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 10% in Odisha (2001 census).

Location: Gujarat state: Banas Kantha and north Sabar Kantha; Rajasthan state: Jhalor, Pali, and Sirohi districts.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Intermediate Divisions, Western, Rajasthani, Marwari
Relationships: 88%–92% intelligibility of Marwari [rwr]. Lexical similarity: 70% between dialects; 62%–75% with Merwari [wry], 45%–69% with Shekhawati [swv], 51%–73% with Mewari [mtr], 46%–66% with Dhundari [dhd], 44%–67% with Haroti [hoj], 62%–74% with Marwari [rwr].
Language_Use: Home, village, market, religion. Some of all ages. Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin], with very good proficiency among the educated.

Alternate_Names: Gunjala Gondi, Koyang, Nirmal, Raj Gond, Telugu Gondi
L1_Full: 300,000 (2015 M. Penny). All Gondi speakers: 2,910,000 (2011 census).
Location: Maharashtra state: south Chandrapur, Nanded, and Yavatmal districts; Telangana state: Adilabad, north Karimnagar, and Warrangal districts.
Classification: Dravidian, South-Central, Gondi-Kui, Gondi
Relationships: Intelligibility of Northern Gondi [gno] 49%–58%.
Language_Use: All domains. Used by all.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 25%–50%.
Education: Taught in primary schools in early grades only. The State Education Department has recognized this language and has been active in promoting it for primary education (2015 M. Penny).

L1_Full: 150,000 (2015 B. Kurian). All Gondi speakers: 2,910,000 (2011 census).
Location: Maharashtra state: Gadchiroli district; Telangana state: Adilabad district.
Classification: Dravidian, South-Central, Gondi-Kui, Gondi
Relationships: Sironcha dialect understood best by the others, with 73%–98% intelligibility. 49%–58% intelligibility of Northern Gondi [gno]. Lexical similarity: 34%–43% with Adilabad Gondi [wsg].
Language_Use: Used by all.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 25%–50%.

Alternate_Names: Gaudi, Ghond, Godi, Gondi, Gondiva, Gondu, Gondwadi, Goondile, Goudi, Goudwal
L1_Full: 1,950,000 (1997 Bible Society of India). All Gondi speakers: 2,910,000 (2011 census).
Location: Madhya Pradesh state: Balaghat, Betul, Chhindwara, Mandla, and Seoni districts; Maharashtra state: Amravati, Bhandara, Nagpur, Wardha, and Yavatmal districts.
Classification: Dravidian, South-Central, Gondi-Kui, Gondi
Dialect_Names: Betul, Chhindwara, Mandla, Seoni, Amravati, Bhandara, Nagpur, Yavatmal
Relationships: Inherent intelligibility between dialects 94%–97%. Speakers tested in other dialects understood Amravati 94%–97%; Betul 83%–96%, and Seoni 82%–97%. 58%–78% intelligibility of Adilabad Gondi [wsg] and Aheri Gondi [esg]. Different from Muria [hlb], Maria [mrr] of Garhchiroli, Dandami Maria [daq], and Koya [kff]. Lexical similarity: 58%–90% among dialects.
Language_Use: Used by all. Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin], especially in Madhya Pradesh, but with low proficiency. Also use Marathi [mar], especially in Maharashtra, but with low proficiency.
Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Nagarchal [nbg], Northwestern Kolami [kfb].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L1: 1%–5%. Literacy rate in L2: 25%–50%.

Location: Madhya Pradesh state: Hoshangabad district; Maharashtra state: Amravati district, and among Korku [kfq] people; some in north Karnataka state.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Outer Languages, Southern, Unclassified
Relationships: Dialects in Maharashtra and Karnataka reportedly different. May be more similar to Hindi [hin] (Central zone) than to Marathi [mar] (Southern zone).
Language_Use: Home. Mixed attitudes. Positive attitudes toward Gowlan and Hindi [hin]. Only some want their children to learn Marathi [mar].
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin], but with low bilingualism in Chikli area.
General_Remarks: Surrounded by Korku. Belong to Gowli caste.

Location: Madhya Pradesh state; Maharashtra state: Amravati district.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Western Hindi, Unclassified
Relationships: Nand subdialects have 93% or higher intelligibility with Khamla dialect. Dialect used in Madhya Pradesh appears more similar to Marathi [mar] (Southern zone) than to Hindi [hin] (Central zone). Lexical similarity: 84%–92% between the Ranya and Nand dialects.
Language_Use: Home.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin]. Also use Marathi [mar].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 5%–15%.
General_Remarks: Speakers belong to Gowli caste. 1 and a half subgroups; Nand Gowli the highest, Musalman (the half tribe) the lowest. Surrounded by Korku [kfq].

L1_Full: No known L1 speakers. The last fluent speaker, Nao, died in 2009 (2009 A. Abbi).
Location: Andaman and Nicobar Islands union territory: Strait island, about 100 km northeast of Port Blair.
Classification: Andamanese, Great Andamanese
Typology: The linguistic system of Mixed Great Andamanese appears to be close to Koineization. It is a mixture of three to four languages spoken once on the island, including Jeru, Khora, Sare and Bo.
Language_Contact: Shifted to Andaman Hindi Creole [hca].
Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Aka-Jeru [akj].
General_Remarks: Only one other language in the Central Andamanese group, Aka-Jeru [akj], has any remaining speakers.

Location: Sikkim state: North Sikkim district, Chumbi valley.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Western Tibeto-Burman, Bodish, Central Bodish, Central, Southern
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng].

Location: Gujarat state: both shores of Gulf of Khambhat; Maharashtra state: Nandubar and Nashil districts; Rajasthan state: Jalor and Sirohi districts; Daman and Diu Union Territory.
Official_Recognition: Statutory provincial language in Gujarat State; Dadra and Nagar Haveli, Daman and Diu union territories (1950, Constitution, Schedule VIII).
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Intermediate Divisions, Western, Gujarati
Dialect_Names: Standard Gujarati (Mumbai Gujarati, Nagari, Patnuli, Saurashtra Standard), Gamadia (Ahmedabad Gamadia, Anawla, Brathela, Charotari, Eastern Broach Gujarati, Gramya, Patani, Patidari, Surati, Vadodari), Parsi (Parsee), Kathiyawadi (Bhawnagari, Gohilwadi, Holadi, Jhalawadi, Sorathi), Kharwa, Kakari, Tarimuki (Ghisadi)
Relationships: The Parsi dialect has less than 55,000 speakers, with only a very few knowing how to read or write it (2017 R. Doctor). Parsi is not inherently intelligible with Parsi-Dari [prd], from whom they separated 600–700 years ago. Other reports say they came to India 1,300 years ago.
Typology: SOV; postpositions; noun head final; gender (masculine/feminine/neuter); no articles; case-marking (6 cases); verb affixes mark person, number, gender of subject; split ergativity; passives; tense and aspect; comparatives; 31 consonants, 8 vowels, 2 diphthongs; non-tonal; stress on penultimate syllable.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng].
Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Adiwasi Garasia [gas], Chodri [cdi], Dangi [dhn], Dhodia [dho], Indo-Portuguese [idb], Kacchi [kfr], Rajput Garasia [gra], Sansi [ssi], Varli [vav].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L1: 70% for Gujarat state (2001 census).
Education: Taught in primary and secondary schools through grade 5 and as subject thereafter in Gujarat State; Dadra and Nagar Haveli, Daman and Diu union territories.
Scripts: Braille script [Brai]. Gujarati script [Gujr], primary usage. Khojki script [Khoj].

Alternate_Names: Gogri, Gojari, Gojri, Gujar, Gujer, Gujjari, Gujuri, Gurjar, Hindki, Kashmir Gujuri, Parimu, Rajasthani Gujuri
Ethnic: 1,600,000 (2002). In Uttar Pradesh, Haryana, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, Maharashtra, Gujarat, Punjab, Delhi.
Location: Jammu and Kashmir state: Anantnag district, Doru, Kukernag, and Pahalgam sub-districts; Baramulla district, Uri sub-district; Ganderbal district, Kangan sub-district; Kulgam district; Kupwara district, Handwara, Karnah, and Kupwara sub-districts; Pulwama district, Tral sub-district; Shopian district.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Intermediate Divisions, Western, Rajasthani
Relationships: Poonchi [phr] may be understood by others and form the basis for a standard dialect. In Pakistan, Eastern Gujari appears more similar to Northern Hindko [hno] or Pahari-Potwari [phr]. Western Gujari appear to understand the Eastern dialect better than vice versa. Comparison with India varieties is needed. Lexical similarity: 60% between Uttar Pradesh and Pakistan, 76% with Poonchi.
Language_Use: In general, Hindu agriculturalists have not retained Gujari language and culture, whereas Muslim Gujari have. Gujars outside Jammu-Kashmir and Himachal Pradesh do not speak Gujari, but regional languages. All domains. Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Also use Dogri [dgo]. Also use English [eng]. Also use Garhwali [gbm]. Also use Hindi [hin]. Also use Jaunsari [jns]. Also use Kashmiri [kas]. Also use Kullu Pahari [kfx]. Also use Kumaoni [kfy]. Also use Urdu [urd].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 5%–15%.
Literature: Literature. Periodicals. Radio. TV. Dictionary. Grammar. Texts.
Scripts: Arabic script, Naskh variant [Arab]. Arabic script, Nastaliq variant [Aran], primary usage. Devanagari script [Deva], plans for future development using this script.

Alternate_Names: Gurung Kura, Tamu Kyi, Western Gurung
Location: Sikkim state: South district; West Bengal state: Darjeeling district.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Western Tibeto-Burman, Bodish, West Bodish, Gurung-Tamang, Gurungic
Typology: SOV; postpositions; genitives, adjectives, relative clauses precede noun heads; numerals after noun heads; noun head final; no noun classes or genders; content q-word in situ; rising intonation marks bipolar questions; one negative prefix on verbs; up to 2 suffixes; clause constituents indicated by case-marking; case of noun phrases is indicated by postpositions; no subject or object referencing in verbs; split ergative system according to tense; causatives; benefactives; aspect; no passives or voice; 24 consonant and 5 vowel phonemes; CV, CCV, CCCV; tonal: voice quality or register is part of the tone system.
Language_Contact: All also use Nepali [npi].
Literature: Literature. Newspapers. Periodicals. Radio. TV. Videos. Dictionary. Grammar. Texts. NT: 1982–2020.

Location: Assam state: Goalpara, and Nagaon districts; Meghalaya state: West Garo Hills district, west side; West and East Khasi hills districts; Arunachal Pradesh and West Bengal states.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Outer Languages, Eastern, Bengali-Assamese
Relationships: No prestige or standard dialect recognized. Intelligible with Hajong of Bangladesh. Lexical similarity: 82%–91% between Banai dialect of Koch [kdq] and mainstream Hajong varieties, 74%–77% between Dalu dialect and mainstream Hajong varieties, 79% between Banai dialect of Koch [kdq] and Dalu, 54%–64% with Assamese [asm], 63%–67% with Bengali [ben], 74%–85% with Hajong of Bangladesh.
Language_Use: Vigorous. All domains. Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Also use Assamese [asm]. Educated have high fluency in Assamese. Also use Bengali [ben]. Also use English [eng]. Also use Garo [grt].
Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Koch [kdq].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 20%–25%; 48% for Meghalaya (2001 census).
Scripts: Bengali (Bangla) script [Beng], used in Bangladesh and India. Latin script [Latn], used in India.
General_Remarks: Jharua may be an alternate name. Though linguistically different, the Banai affiliate themselves with the Koch.

Alternate_Names: Halabi, Halba, Halvas, Halvi, Holva, aia jaia got
Location: Andhra Pradesh state; Chhattisgarh state: Bastar district plains; Madhya Pradesh state: Balaghat district; Maharashtra state: Gondia district; Odisha state: Koraput district.
LWC_Support: Became dominant in the 19th century under British rule. Main means of communication for various groups across the central part of India. Used in trade, music, and communication among the less educated.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Outer Languages, Eastern, Bengali-Assamese
Dialect_Names: Adkuri, Bastari, Bhunjia, Chandari, Gachikolo, Govari of Balaghat, Kawari, Kunbi, Mahari (Mahara, Mehara, Mehari), Muri (Muria), Sundi
Relationships: Bhunjia and Kawari dialects considered more divergent dialects. Reportedly a creole language. Grierson and Konow called it a dialect of Marathi [mar] for convenience, but noted similarities to Bhatri [bgw], a dialect of Odia [ory] (Grierson and Konow 1903–1928).
Typology: SOV; postpositions; genitives, articles, adjectives, numerals before noun heads; 2 or 3 affixes per word; word order distinguishes given and new information; noun affixes indicate case; verb affixes mark person, number, gender of subject; passives; causatives; comparatives; CV, CVC, CVV; nontonal.
Language_Contact: Also use Bhatri [bgw]. Also use Hindi [hin], especially educated men, for trading and common topics.
Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Bhatri [bgw], Duruwa [pci], Eastern Muria [emu], Maria [mrr], Mirgan [zrg].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 74% for Chhattisgarh plains (2001 census). Government literacy program uses Hindi [hin] primers.

Location: Madhya Pradesh state: Neemuch district, 3 other border areas; Rajasthan state: Baran, Bundi, Jhalawar, and Kota districts.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Intermediate Divisions, Western, Rajasthani, Unclassified
Relationships: 45% intelligibility with standard Marwari [rwr], 57%–67% with Merwari [wry], 58%–66% with Shekhawati [swv], 44%–67% with Godwari [gdx], 61%–71% with Mewari [mtr], 64%–73% with Dhundari [dhd], 52%–70% with Mewati [wtm], 55%–62% with Bagri [bgq], 63%–77% with Hindi [hin].
Typology: SOV.
Language_Use: Vigorous. Home, village; market, religion. Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin], with widespread bilingualism. 40% have very good proficiency, with greater proficiency among the educated.
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 75% in Kota District (2001 census).

Alternate_Names: Bangaru, Banger, Bangri, Bangru, Chamarwa, Desari, Hariani, Hariyani, Haryani, Jatu
Location: Haryana, Himachal Pradesh, Karnataka, Punjab, Rajasthan, and Uttar Pradesh states; Delhi.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Western Hindi, Unclassified
Relationships: Good intelligibility among dialects, but Haryanvi is not intelligible with Hindi [hin]. Reportedly most similar to Braj Bhasha [bra]. Lexical similarity: 92% among dialects.
Language_Use: Home, religion. Used by all. Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin], with proficiency higher among the educated.
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 55% in Hindi [hin].
General_Remarks: Khadar used by speakers in Jind to refer to the speech of Rohtak and Sonipat.

Location: Widespread in north India: northern Bihar, Himachal Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Punjab, Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh, and Uttarakhand states; Delhi.
Official_Recognition: Statutory national language (1950, Constitution, Article 343), also statutory provincial language in Bihar State and 12 other jurisdictions.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Western Hindi, Hindustani
Dialect_Names: Khari Boli (Dehlavi, Kauravi, Khadi Boli, Khari, Khariboli, Vernacular Hindustani)
Relationships: Formal vocabulary borrowed from Sanskrit, de-Persianized, de-Arabicized. Literary Hindi, or Hindi-Urdu, has 4 varieties: Hindi (High Hindi, Nagari Hindi, Literary Hindi, standard Hindi); Urdu [urd]; Dakhini; Rekhta. Hindustani, though not listed separately in India, refers here to the unofficial lingua franca of northwest India. Has a lexical mixture in varying proportions of Hindi (vocabulary derived from Sanskrit) and Urdu (vocabulary derived from Persian or Arabic).
Typology: SOV; postpositions; noun head final; content q-word in situ; gender (masculine/feminine); no articles; clause constituents partially indicated by case-marking (direct, oblique), postpositions, and word order; verbal affixation marks person, number, gender, and honorificity of subject; split ergativity; both tense and aspect; passives and voice; causatives; non-tonal; 30 consonants, 10 vowels, 2 diphthongs; stress linked to syllable weight.
Education: Taught in all primary and secondary schools, more in northern India than in southern India. Taught in tertiary schools.
Scripts: Braille script [Brai]. Devanagari script [Deva], primary usage. Latin script [Latn], recent informal usage, especially online on social media. Mahajani script [Mahj], no longer in use, historic usage. Newa script [Newa], no longer in use, historic usage.
General_Remarks: Hindi, Hindustani, Urdu could be considered co-dialects, but have important sociolinguistic differences.

Location: Himachal Pradesh state: Solan district, Nalagarh, Ramshahr, and surrounding villages.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Intermediate Divisions, Western, Pahari, Western Pahari
Relationships: Reportedly most similar to Bilaspuri [kfs]. Lexical similarity: 67% with Baghliani dialect of Mahasu Pahari [bfz] spoken in Arki, 60% with Lower Mahasui dialect of Pahari [bfz], 56% with Upper Mahasui dialect of Pahari [bfz] and Sirmauri [srx], 64% with Hindi.
Language_Use: Home, village. Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin].

Location: Assam state: Cachar district; Manipur state: south, Churachandpur, Tipaimukh, 35 villages; Mizoram state: Aizawl district; Tripura state.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Kuki-Chin, Central, Mizo
Relationships: Reportedly similar to Zou [zom].
Language_Contact: Also use Assamese [asm]. Also use English [eng]. Also use Meitei [mni]. Also use Mizo [lus].
Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Sakachep [sch].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 90%.
Education: Taught in primary schools in Assam, Manipur and Mizoram states.
General_Remarks: Ethnic Hmar living in Mizoram speak Mizo [lus] as L1.

Autonym: Ho jagar, Ho kaji, Ho̅, हो जगर‎ (Ho jagar), ହୋ ଜାଗାର‎ (Ho jagaara), 𑢹𑣉𑣉 𑣎𑣋𑣜‎ (Ho jagar)
Alternate_Names: Bihar Ho, Hōō jagara, Ho haram, Ho: basa, Lanka Kol
Location: Bihar state; Jharkhand state: Purbi Singhbhum district, Kolhan, Seraikella; East Singhbhum district, Dhalbhum sub-district; Odisha state: Koenjhar and Mayurbhanj districts; West Bengal state.
Classification: Austro-Asiatic, Munda, North Munda, Kherwari, Mundari
Relationships: Most understand Chaibasa and Thakurmunda dialects well; 90%–92% comprehend narrative discourse. Kherwari (Khanwar, Kharar, Kharoali, Kharwari) is group name for Ho, Mundari [unr], Munda [unx], and Santhali [sat], closely related languages, and other smaller languages or dialects. Lexical similarity: 85% between most dialects, except for 3 on Ho area east and south edges.
Language_Use: Vigorous. Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin]. Also use Odia [ory]. Also use Sadri [sck]. Also use Santhali [sat].
Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Birhor [biy].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L1: 1%–5%. Literacy rate in L2: 25%–50%. Literacy program in progress.
Scripts: Devanagari script [Deva], used in Bihar. Latin script [Latn]. Oriya (Odia) script [Orya], used in Odisha. Telugu script [Telu]. Warang Citi script [Wara].
General_Remarks: Different from Ho (Hani [hni]) of Myanmar, China, Vietnam, Laos.

Alternate_Names: Gohllaru, Golari-Kannada, Holar, Holari, Hole, Holian, Holu
Location: Madhya Pradesh state: Balaghat and Seoni districts; Karnataka and Maharashtra states.
Classification: Dravidian, Southern, Tamil-Kannada, Kannada
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Kannada [kan].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 5% in Kannada [kan].
General_Remarks: A Scheduled Caste in Madhya Pradesh.

Location: Assam, Manipur, Mizoram, and Tripura states.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Kuki-Chin, Central, Mizo
Relationships: Reportedly most similar to Biate [biu].
Typology: SOV.
Language_Use: Use declining in Mizoram, Manipur and even Assam; shifting to Assamese [asm] or Bengali [ben] (Van Driem 2007). Home, village. Some of all ages.
Language_Contact: Some also use English [eng]. Also use Assamese [asm]. Also use Hindi [hin]. Also use Mizo [lus].
Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Sakachep [sch].
Literacy: Literature committee since 1960.

Alternate_Names: Aka, Angka, Angkae, Gusso, Hrusso, Tenae
Location: Arunachal Pradesh state: West Kameng district, Thrizino sub-district, Balipho, Bhalukpong, Buragaon, Dijungonia, Gijiri, Gohainthan, Husigaon, Jamiri, Karangonia, Khuppi, Palizi, Polatari, Raghupam, Raindogonia, Tania, Tulu, and Yayom villages; East Kameng district, Seppa sub-district, Pisang village.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Central Tibeto-Burman, Hrusish
Relationships: No apparent wider affiliation within Tibeto-Burman. Varieties sometimes grouped under Tibeto-Burman as Hruish. Levai is similar to Miji [sjl] and may be a distinct language. Lexical similarity: 9% between Koro [jkr] and the Hruso dialect [hru]. Both are highly dissimilar to neighboring languages.
Typology: SOV.
Language_Use: Steady shift away from Hruso, especially among youth educated outside the area. Some young people, all adults.
Language_Contact: Also use Assamese [asm]. Also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin]. Also use Miji [sjl].
Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Bugun [bgg], Miji [sjl].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 48%: males 58%, females 39% (2001 census).
General_Remarks: ’Aka’, painted. Has 2 ethnic groups (Kavatsun and Kutsun) and an additional subdivision called Miri-Akas on the other side of Kaya River (known as Khrome) who speak Mising [mrg], not Hruso. Probably not the same as Plains Miri or Hill Miri (Mising) [mrg] (Sinha 1962). Aka in East Kameng District are called Koro Aka [jkr], distinct from Hruso Aka in West Kameng.

Location: Arunachal Pradesh state: Dibang Valley district, Dibong Valley and Lower Dibong Valley districts; Assam state.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Central Tibeto-Burman, Digarish
Relationships: Reportedly most similar to Digaro-Mishmi [mhu]. Different from Adi [adi]. Lexical similarity: 7% with the Miju-Mishmi dialect of Miju-Mishmi [mxj], 25% with Digaro-Mishmi [mhu].
Typology: SOV; postpositions; genitives before noun heads; numerals after noun heads, adjective and relatives before noun head; affixes indicate case of noun phrase; comparatives; nasal vowels; tonal (3 level tones: high, mid, low).
Language_Use: Home, community, religion. Some young people, all adults. Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Also use Assamese [asm], especially older people. Also use English [eng], especially educated individuals. Also use Hindi [hin], especially younger people.
Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Khamba [kbg].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 55% (2001 census).
General_Remarks: May not be in the Tani group, but is related.

Alternate_Names: IPSL, ISL, Indo-Pakistani Sign Language, Urban Indian Sign Language
L1_Full: 6,000,000 in India (2021 SIL). Estimated 4–8 million deaf signers, based on 0.3%–0.6% of the general population. Other estimates vary: 1.5 million (2008 S. Panda); 5.9 million profoundly deaf in India (2014 IMB); 8 million deaf signers (2017 Indian Sign Language Research and Training Centre).
Location: Scattered.
Classification: Sign language, Deaf community sign language
Dialect_Names: Mumbai-Delhi, Kerala, Hyderabad (Andhra Pradesh), Bangalore (Karnataka), Chennai (Tamil Nadu)
Relationships: Most sign language varieties in south Asia appear to be related, but there is considerable variation, which has only been partially assessed. Some scholars regard most varieties in India, Pakistan, Bangladesh and possibly Nepal as dialects of one language called Indo-Pakistani Sign Language (IPSL), while others feel at least some varieties should be recognized as separate languages. The ISO standard currently (as of 2020) distinguishes ISL from Pakistan Sign Language [pks], West Bengal Sign Language (Kolkata Sign Language) [wbs], and Nepalese Sign Language [nsp]. The variety that originated in Delhi is the most widely-recognized and promoted; Mumbai is very similar. Varieties in the southern Indian states of Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, Kerala, and Tamil Nadu are quite divergent from the Delhi variety and may need to be recognized as a distinct language (2020 D. Eberle). Some villages, such as Alipur, Karnataka have an indigenous sign language unrelated to ISL (Panda 2012). Some influence from British Sign Language [bfi] in the fingerspelling system and a few other signs developed indigenously in India.
Language_Use: Vigorous. Used by all.
Language_Contact: Many also use American Sign Language [ase], especially in Bangalore (Panda 2012).
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: Below 2%. Male literacy rate in L2 is higher than female as boys are more likely to attend school.
Literature: TV. Videos. Dictionary. Grammar. Bible portions: 2023–2024.
Language_Planning_Org: Indian Sign Language Research and Training Centre at Indira Gandhi National Open University.
General_Remarks: Only about 550–700 schools use ISL (2008 S. Panda, 2017 BBC). 2% or less of deaf children attend deaf schools, with a high drop-out rate. Vocational programs use ISL more often. Nearly all educated deaf are bilingual in a written language of wider communication to some degree, and ISL serves as a signed language of wider communication among deaf in India, especially in cities. The government and educational institutions promote the Delhi variety for use in the entire country. Starting 2001, interpreter training in Mumbai by the Ali Yavar Jung National Institute for Hearing Handicapped.

Monolingual: Relatively few monolinguals, even in Korlai (Cardoso 2006).
Location: Kerala state: Kannur; Maharashtra state: Korlai near Mumbai; Daman and Diu Union Territory.
Classification: Creole, Portuguese based
Language_Use: It is mostly, if not entirely, spoken by multilingual speakers (Cardoso 2006). Some communities in India have no remaining speakers. Few remaining speakers in Cannanore; last speaker in Cochin, Mr. William Rozario, died on Vypeen Island (2010). Some young people, all adults.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Gujarati [guj]. Also use Hindi [hin]. Also use Marathi [mar]. Also use Portuguese [por], extensively (Cardoso 2006).
General_Remarks: The term Indo-Portuguese does not stand for 1 language but rather a number of Portuguese-lexified creoles scattered across South Asia (Cardoso 2006).

Alternate_Names: Erukala, Irava, Irulan, Irular, Irular Mozhi, Irulavan, Iruliga, Iruligar, Kad Chensu, Korava
Location: Kerala state: Palakkad district, Attapady and Walayar sub-districts; Tamil Nadu state: Coimbatore, Nilgiri, Periyar districts; Andhra Pradesh and Karnataka states.
Classification: Dravidian, Southern, Tamil-Kannada, Tamil-Kodagu, Tamil-Malayalam, Tamil
Dialect_Names: Mele Nadu Irula (Malanadu, Southern Irula), Northern Irula (Kasaba, Kasava, Kasuba), Vette Kada Irula (Irula Pallar, Vettakada), Irula Urali, Attapady Irula, Walayar Irula (Urali Irula)
Relationships: Dialects: Vette Kada 73% intelligibility of Mele Nadu; Northern Irula 83% of Mele Nadu; no intelligibility of Tamil [tam] (1993 Irula survey); Vette Kada 94% of Attapady; Walayar 84% of Attapady. (2004 Palakkad survey). Lexical similarity: 78%–86% between Mele Nadu dialect varieties, 67%–70% with Northern Irula, 64%–66% with Vette Kada, 47%–50% with Tamil [tam]. Attapady has 73%–75% with Mele Nadu and 85%–89% with Vette Kada. Walayar has 74%–79% with Attapady, 76% with Vette Kada, and 69% with Mele Nadu.
Typology: SOV; postpositions; nontonal.
Language_Use: All domains. Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Many shifting to Kannada [kan]. Many shifting to Tamil [tam]. Also use Badaga [bfq]. Also use English [eng]. Also use Malayalam [mal].
Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Attapady Kurumba [pkr].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 20% among adults, 50% among younger generation.
Scripts: Malayalam script [Mlym], used in Kerala. Tamil script [Taml], used in Tamil Nadu.
General_Remarks: Some people called Irula speak Tamil [tam] as mother tongue. Urali Irula (Periyar) is separate from both Betta Kurumba Urali [xub] and Urali [url] in Idukki District, Kerala. Two Urali Irula dialects in Periyar and Palakkad.

Location: Himachal Pradesh state: Kinnaur district; Uttarakhand state: Uttarkashi district, Harsil subdistrict, Jadang and Nilang villages in Jad Ganga gorges.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Western Tibeto-Burman, Bodish, Central Bodish, Central, Western
Relationships: Reportedly similar to Spiti Bhoti [spt].
Typology: Does not have pronominalization found in other languages of the area.
Language_Use: Garhwali [gbm] learned together with Jad. Code switching and code mixing common. Uncertain whether stable bilingualism will continue or whether Jad will be replaced by Garhwali [gbm] or Hindi [hin]. Home, community. Used by all. Negative attitudes.
Language_Contact: Also use Central Tibetan [bod]. Also use English [eng]. Also use Garhwali [gbm]. Also use Hindi [hin].
Literacy: Hindi used for all written communication.
General_Remarks: Some borrowing of vocabulary from Hindi [hin] and Garhwali [gbm].

Alternate_Names: Central Kinnauri, Jangiam, Jangrami, Thebarskad, Thebor, Thebör Skadd, Zangram, Zhang-Zhung
Location: Himachal Pradesh state: Kinnaur district, Morang sub-district, Asrang, Jangi, and Lippa villages.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Western Tibeto-Burman, Bodish, West Himalayish, Kinauri
Relationships: Lexical similarity: 70% with Shumcho [scu], 65% with Sunam [ssk], 51% with Chitkuli Kinnauri [cik], 49% with Pahari Kinnauri [kjo].
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng].

L1_Full: 8,200 in India (2023 census), based on nationality.
Classification: Japonic
Typology: SOV; agglutinative language; postpositions; demonstrative, numeral, adjective, possessive, relative clause, proper noun precedes noun head; adverb precedes verb; sentence final question particle; no articles; passives; tense and aspect; causatives; 15 consonants, 5 vowels, 3 diphthongs; non-tonal; pitch-accentuation pattern.
Scripts: Braille script [Brai]. Han, Hiragana, and Katakana scripts [Jpan], primary usage. Latin script [Latn].

Monolingual: 340 monolinguals (Kumar 2012). Monolingual group, with some language contact with Hindi [hin] (Kumar 2012).
Location: Andaman and Nicobar Islands Union Territory: interior and south central Rutland Island; central and south interiors of South Andaman Island; Middle Andaman Island, west coast, 70 square km reserve.
Classification: Andamanese, South Andamanese
Relationships: Different from Önge [oon] and Sentinel [std].
Language_Use: Used by all.
General_Remarks: Seminomadic, monolingual group starting to use some Hindi [hin] words (Kumar 2012).

Location: Himachal Pradesh state: Shimla district; Uttar Pradesh state: Saharanpur district; Uttarakhand state: Dehra Dun district, Kalsi, Tiuni, and Chakrata sub-district, Jaunsar-Bawar area.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Intermediate Divisions, Western, Pahari, Western Pahari
Relationships: 97% intelligibility between dialects. Perceived by some as a Garhwali [gbm] dialect; but users perceive Garhwali as distinct and report lack of intelligibility. Lexical similarity: 70%–77% between dialects, 63%–70% with Garhwali dialects [gbm], 64% with Kumaoni [kfy], 66% with Hindi [hin], 51%–64% with Sirmauri [srx].
Language_Use: Vigorous. Home, village, private prayer. Used by all. Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Also use Hindi [hin], with proficiency higher among the educated.
Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Gujari [gju].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 26%. Hindi preferred for education.
Scripts: Devanagari script [Deva]. Latin script [Latn], no longer in use. Takri (Tankri, Takari) script [Takr], no longer in use.
General_Remarks: A Scheduled Tribe.

Location: Odisha state: north Angul, east Dhenkanal, south Keonjhar districts.
Classification: Austro-Asiatic, Munda, South Munda, Kharia-Juang
Relationships: Not closely related to other languages. Lexical similarity: 20%–22% with Kharia [khr].
Language_Use: Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Some also use Odia [ory], especially men and educated. Also use English [eng].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 21% (2001 census).

Location: Odisha state.
Classification: Austro-Asiatic, Munda, South Munda, Koraput Munda, Sora-Juray-Gorum, Sora-Juray
Relationships: Reportedly most similar to Sora [srb].
Typology: SOV.
Language_Use: Home, community. Older adults only.
Language_Contact: Many shifted to Odia [ory] (Anderson and Gomango 2016). Many shifted to Sora [srb] (Anderson and Gomango 2016).

Alternate_Names: Cuchi, Cutch, Kachchhi, Kachchi, Kachi, Katch, Katchi, Kautchy, Kutchchi, Kutchie
Location: Gujarat state: Rann of Kutch area; Andhra Pradesh, Assam, Karnataka, Kerala, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Odisha, Tamil Nadu, Uttar Pradesh states.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Outer Languages, Northwestern, Sindhi
Relationships: Reportedly similar to Sindhi [snd].
Language_Contact: Most also use Gujarati [guj]. Also use English [eng].

Location: Assam state: north Cachar district, Cachar hills; Nagaland state: Kohima district; Dimapur district, Dhansiri sub-district. 16 villages.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Sal, Boro-Garo, Boro-Tiwa, Boro
Language_Use: Some ethnic Kachari speak it as L1. Most speak Assamese [asm] as L1. Rapidly assimilating to Bengali [ben] or Assamese [asm] (Van Driem 2007). Some young people, all adults.
Language_Contact: Also use Assamese [asm]. Also use English [eng].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 81% in Assam (2001 census).
General_Remarks: A Scheduled Tribe.

Location: Kerala state: Thrissur district; Palakkad district, Chittoor sub-district; Tamil Nadu state: Coimbatore district.
Classification: Dravidian, Southern, Tamil-Kannada, Tamil-Kodagu, Tamil-Malayalam, Malayalam
Relationships: Phonology related to Tamil [tam] and vocabulary related to Malayalam [mal] (Menon 1996). Lexical similarity: 56%–62% with Tamil [tam], 62%–65% with Malayalam [mal], 67% with Mala Malasar [ima], 61%–63 % with Kanikkaran [kev].
Language_Use: Some language shift to Malayalam [mal] observed in Kerala. Home, village, religious services. Some young people, all adults.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Malayalam [mal]. Also use Tamil [tam].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 51% in Kerala, 56% in Tamil Nadu (2001 census).
General_Remarks: 3 groups named Kadar in Kerala and Tamil Nadu. The Kadar who use the Kadar language live primarily Palakkad and Thrissur hills, and Coimbatore. A second group lives in Wayanad District and use Malayalam [mal]. A third Kadar (Kadir) group is in Tamil Nadu, Triuchirapalli and Tanjavur districts. They have nothing in common with Western Ghats Kadar. Seen as less developed than other tribes of Chittoor.

Location: Madhya Pradesh state: Betul district; Maharashtra state: Amravati district.
Classification: Dravidian, Southern, Tamil-Kannada, Tamil-Kodagu, Tamil-Malayalam, Tamil
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng].
General_Remarks: Nomadic.

Location: Kerala state: Wayanad district, southwest.
Classification: Dravidian, Southern
Relationships: Lexical similarity: 75% with Malayalam [mal], 74% with Paniya [pcg], 72%–75% with Wayanad Kurichiya [kfh], 79%–83% with Mullu Kurumba [kpb], 88% with Pathiya [pty], 81% with Kunduvadi [wku].
Language_Use: Continued vitality doubtful, due to small population, no separate settlements, living with Malayalis, and similarity to Malayalam [mal]. Home.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Malayalam [mal].
Literacy: Younger generation reportedly literate in Malayalam [mal].
General_Remarks: Common cultural origin with Kunduvadiyar and Pathiyar.

Location: Chhattisgarh state: Raipur district; Madhya Pradesh state: Rewa district; Maharashtra state.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Intermediate Divisions, Eastern, East Central
Relationships: Lexical similarity: 68%–72% with Bhunjia [bhu], 66%–69% with Chhattisgarhi [hne], 68% with Oriya [ory], 61% with Hindi [hin], 27% with Telugu [tel].
Language_Use: Chhattisgarhi [hne] used among themselves and Hindi [hin] with others (Singh 1994b).
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng].
General_Remarks: A Scheduled Tribe. No relationship between the Kamar caste of iron workers in Bengal and Chota Nagpur and this ethnic group.

Alternate_Names: Deshi Bhasa, Goalparia, Kamata, Kamta, Koch Rajbanshi, Rajbangsi, Rajbanshi, Rajbansi, Rajbongshi
Location: West Bengal state: Darjeeling, Koch Bihar, Jalpaiguri, and Uttar Dinajpur districts; Assam state: Dhubri and Kokrajhar districts.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Outer Languages, Eastern, Bengali-Assamese
Language_Use: Strong vitality in West Bengal and parts of Assam near Koch Bihar. Vitality weakens east of Dhubri in Assam. Those farthest east in Assam tend to prefer Assamese over their mother tongue. Used by all.
Language_Contact: Also use Assamese [asm]. Bilingual ability increases with education. Also use Bengali [ben]. Also use English [eng].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 15%–20% men, lower for women (2007 Word For All).
Literature: Literature. Radio. Dictionary. Grammar. Bible portions: 2008–2011.
General_Remarks: Strong language movement. Kamtapuri has become a symbol of community political aspirations.

Location: Himachal Pradesh state: Kullu district, Kullu sub-district, Bios valley glen, Malana (Malani) village area.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Western Tibeto-Burman, Bodish, West Himalayish, Kinauri
Relationships: No intelligibility with any Tibeto-Burman languages of Lahul-Spiti and Kinnaur (Chauhan).
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin].
General_Remarks: Surrounded by Indo-Aryan languages. Malana village has the oldest surviving democracy in the world. They practice their own parliamentary form of government.

Alternate_Names: Bhakha, Braj, Braj Kanauji, Dehati, Hindi, Kannauji
Location: Uttar Pradesh state: Auraiya, Etawah, Farrukhabad, Hardoi, Kanpur, Pilibhit, Mainpuri, and Shahjahanpur districts.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Western Hindi, Unclassified
Relationships: Transitional Kanauji dialect is between Kanauji and Awadhi [awa]. Grierson and Konow call it a form of Braj Bhasha [bra]. The variety spoken in Kannauj and Farrukhabad is considered the pure form (Grierson and Konow 1903–1928). Lexical similarity: 84%–97% between all varieties of Kanauji, 72%–76% with Bundeli [bns], 70%–78% with Braj Bhasha [bra], 83%–94% with Hindi [hin].
Language_Use: Shifting to Hindi [hin]. In urban areas, almost replaced by Hindi [hin], while in rural areas, Kanauji is still functional (Dwivedi and Kar 2016). Various domains. Some young people, all adults. Negative attitudes.
Language_Contact: Most also use Hindi [hin], the less-educated having lower proficiency. Also use English [eng].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 60% (2001 census).
General_Remarks: Kanauji may be only a name given by scholars. Language not commonly referred to as Kanauji. Very low identity. Regard their language as a variety of Hindi [hin]. However, a small local group is interested in promoting Kanauji before it dies out.

Location: Himachal Pradesh state: Hamirpur, Kangra, and Una districts; Punjab state: Gurdaspur and Hoshiarpur districts.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Intermediate Divisions, Western, Pahari, Western Pahari
Relationships: Lexical similarity: Palampuri dialect; 90% with Bilaspuri [kfs] and Chambeali [cdh], 89% with Mandeali [mjl], 83% with Bhattiyali [bht], 80% with the MacLeod Ganj dialect of Gaddi [gbk].
Language_Use: Vigorous. Home, work, market. Used by all. Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: A few also use English [eng]. Also use Eastern Punjabi [pan]. Also use Hindi [hin], for communicating with outsiders. Also use Urdu [urd].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 70%. Educators promote Kangri. Acceptability of other Pahari dialects is high.
Scripts: Devanagari script [Deva]. Takri (Tankri, Takari) script [Takr], no longer in use.

Location: Kerala state: Ernakulam, Koliam, Kozhikode, and Trivandrum districts, Nedumangadu and Neyyattinkara sub-districts; Tamil Nadu state: Kanniyakumari and Tirunelveli districts.
Classification: Dravidian, Southern, Tamil-Kannada, Tamil-Kodagu, Tamil-Malayalam, Tamil
Relationships: Lexical similarity: 71%–80% between Kanikkaran varieties in Kerala, 67%–71% between Kanikkaran in Kerala and Tamil Nadu, 66%–75% with Malayalam [mal], 59%–65% with Tamil [tam].
Language_Use: Almost all in Kerala are shifting to Malayalam [mal], but those in Tamil Nadu use L1. Some of all ages.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Malayalam [mal]. Also use Tamil [tam].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 71%–80% in Kerala, 59%–68% in Tamil Nadu (2001 census).

Location: Uttar Pradesh state: Aligarh, Etawah, Farrukhabad, Kheri, and Sitapur districts; Rajasthan state: Bhilwara, Chittorgarh, Bundi and Tonk districts; Bihar state: Madubani, Purnea and Saharsa districts; Maharashtra state: Pune, Satara, Kolhapur, Sangli, Thane, Bombay, Nasik districts; Madhya Pradesh state: Pune, Satara, Kolhapur, Sangli, Thane, Bombay, Nasik districts; New Delhi.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Unclassified
Relationships: May be in the Punjabi group.
Language_Contact: Some also use Hindi [hin], with outsiders and government officials.
General_Remarks: Sometimes called a language of Roma who reportedly use certain linguistic means of disguising their language to make it unintelligible to outsiders. A Scheduled Caste who speak a dialect of Hindi [hin] in Uttar Pradesh, a dialect of Mewari [mtr] in Rajasthan, and Hindi in Bihar and Madhya Pradesh (Singh 1995b). Considered by some to be a pejorative name; no other name is used for the entire group (2019 G. Lovejoy).

Location: Mainly Goa and Karnataka states; Andhra Pradesh state: Anantapur; Maharashtra state: Latur district; Tamil Nadu and Kerala states; small border areas of last 4 states.
Official_Recognition: Statutory provincial language in Karnataka (1950, Constitution, Schedule VIII).
Classification: Dravidian, Southern, Tamil-Kannada, Kannada
Dialect_Names: Bellary, Bijapur, Gulbarga, Kumta, Aine Kuruba, Jeinu Kuruba, Nanjangud, Siddi
Relationships: About 20 dialects; Badaga [bfq] may be one.
Typology: SOV; postpositions; noun head final; gender (masculine/feminine/neuter); case-marking (7 cases); verb affixes mark person, number, gender of subject; tense and aspect; causatives; 22 consonants, 20 vowels, 2 diphthongs; non-tonal; light stress on first syllable.
Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Alu Kurumba [xua], Bellari [brw], Holiya [hoy], Irula [iru], Jennu Kurumba [xuj], Kannada Kurumba [kfi], Kodava [kfa], Kota [kfe], Kudiya [kfg], Lambadi [lmn], Mudu Koraga [vmd], Paniya [pcg], Ravula [yea], Tamil [tam], Tulu [tcy], Vaagri Booli [vaa].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L1: 60%. Literacy rate in L2: 60%.
Education: Taught in primary and secondary schools through grade 5 and as subject thereafter in Karnataka state.
Scripts: Braille script [Brai]. Kannada script [Knda], primary usage. Nandinagari script [Nand], no longer in use.
General_Remarks: A Classical Language of India since 2008.

Alternate_Names: Arleng, Karbi Karbak, Karbiarlong, Manchati, Nihang, Puta, “Mikir” (pej.), “Mikiri” (pej.), “Miquirés” (pej.), “Naga-Mikir” (pej.)
Location: Arunachal Pradesh state: Papumpare district, Balijan sub-district; Assam state: Cachar, Darrang, Karbi Anglong, Lakhimpur, Marigaon, Nagaon, and Sonitpur districts in Mikir and Rengma hills; Meghalaya state: Jaintia district; Nagaland state: Dimapur area foothills.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Karbi
Relationships: Lexical similarity: 82%–96% between dialects.
Language_Use: Other groups speak Karbi as L1, including some Dimasa.
Language_Contact: Also use Assamese [asm], among all age groups. Also use English [eng].
Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Sakachep [sch].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 54% in Assam (2001 census).
Literature: Literature. Radio. Dictionary. Grammar. Texts. Bible: 1952.

Alternate_Names: Cashmeeree, Cashmiri, Kacmiri, Kaschemiri, Keshur, Koshur
L1_Full: 6,770,000 in India (2011 census). 6,610,000 Kashmiri, 39,700 Kishtwari, and 125,000 Siraji (2011 census).
Location: Himachal Pradesh state: Chamba and Lahul Spiti districts in Kashmir valley; Jammu and Kashmir state: Anantag, Badgam, Bandipore, eastern Baramula and Kupwara, Doda, Ganderbal, Kargil, Kishtwar, Kulgam, west Leh, Ramban, and Shupian districts.
Official_Recognition: Statutory language of provincial identity in Jammu and Kashmir (1950, Constitution, Schedule VIII).
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Outer Languages, Northwestern, Dardic, Kashmiri
Dialect_Names: Bakawali, Bunjwali, Standard Kashmiri, Kishtwari (Kashtawari, Kashtwari, Kathiawari, Kistwali), Miraski, Rambani, Riasi, Shah-Mansuri, Siraji of Doda, Siraji-Kashmiri, Zayoli, Zirak-Boli, Poguli (Pogali, Pogli)
Relationships: Transitional dialects to Punjabi [pan]. Kashtawari dialect is standard, other dialects are influenced by Dogri [dgo].
Typology: SVO; gender (masculine/feminine); case-marking (5 cases); verb affixes mark person, number, object; ergativity; tense and aspect; 23 consonant and 8 vowel phonemes.
Language_Contact: Most also use Urdu [urd] (Koul and Schmidt 1983). Some also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin].
Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Bhadrawahi [bhd], Burushaski [bsk], Changthang [cna], Gujari [gju], Khah [hkh], Uyghur [uig].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L1: 88% male; 12% female over 35 years of age (Koul and Schmidt 1983). Literacy rate in L2: 55% for Jammu and Kashmir (2001 census). 83% would prefer use of Kashmiri rather than Urdu as medium in primary school, 48% in middle school (Koul and Schmidt 1983).
Education: Taught in primary and secondary schools through grade 5 and as subject thereafter in Jammu and Kashmir.
Literature: Literature. Newspapers. Radio. Videos. Dictionary. Grammar. Bible: 1899–2005.
Scripts: Arabic script, Naskh variant [Arab]. Arabic script, Nastaliq variant [Aran], primary usage. Devanagari script [Deva]. Latin script [Latn]. Sharada script [Shrd], no longer in use.

Location: Gujarat state: Bharuch, Dang, Surat, and Sabarkantha districts; Dadra and Nagar Haveli, Amboli and Dapada Panchayat areas; Maharashtra state: Raigad and Thane districts, Sahayadri Range foothills; Rajasthan state: Jhadol, Mubusha, Onga, and Samicha Parebati police station areas.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Outer Languages, Southern, Konkani
Dialect_Names: Northern Katkari, Central Katkari, Southern Katkari
Relationships: Referred to as a dialect of Marathi [mar]. 89%–96% intelligibility between dialects. Lexical similarity: 67%–75% with Marathi [mar], 77%–90% among dialects.
Language_Use: Vigorous. Home, community.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Marathi [mar].
General_Remarks: L1 in Maharashtra is Marathi [mar], in Dadra and Nagar Haveli is Kukna [kex], in Gujarat is a variety of Marathi [mar], in Rajasthan is Kathodi, a variety of Marathi [mar] (Singh 1994b:475–479).

Alternate_Names: Banhali, Khahistani, Khash, Khasha, Khashali, Kohistani, Panchali, Parbati, Paristani
Location: Jammu and Kashmir: Ramban district, Banihal, Gool, Khari, and Ramsu sub-districts; Doda, Jammu, Rajouri, Reasi, and Udampur districts.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Intermediate Divisions, Western, Pahari, Western Pahari
Typology: SOV, SVO; postpositions; no articles; gender (masculine, feminine, neuter); nouns are inflected for gender, number and case; case-marking (4 cases: nominative, dative, ergative, vocative); tense and aspect; 33 consonants and 16 vowels (8 long, 8 short).
Language_Use: Home, community. Used by all.
Language_Contact: Also use Dogri [dgo]. Also use English [eng]. Also use Kashmiri [kas]. Also use Urdu [urd].
Scripts: Arabic script, Naskh variant [Arab]. Devanagari script [Deva]. Latin script [Latn], informal use on social media.

Alternate_Names: Khael Baat, Khael Bra, Khael Braa, Khalinge Rai
Location: Sikkim state: West and South districts, scattered; West Bengal state: Darjeeling district.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Western Tibeto-Burman, Himalayan, Kiranti, Western
Typology: SOV; postpositions; adjectives, numerals, relatives before noun heads; content q-word initial; no noun classes or genders; 1 prefix, up to 2 suffixes; clause constituents indicated by case-marking; affixes indicate case of noun phrase; verbal affixation marks person and number of subject—obligatory; ergative; causatives; comparatives; passives and voice; CV, V, CCCV; nontonal; 23 consonant and 9 vowel phonemes.

Location: Arunachal Pradesh state: West Siang district, Singa sub-district, Mankota, Nuykkang, Nyering, Tashigong, and Yortung villages in Yang Sang Chu valley.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Unclassified
Relationships: Lexical similarity: 82% between Khamba varieties, 11%–14% with Tshangla (Memba) [tsj] (Joseph et al 2019).
Language_Use: Home, community. Some of all ages.
Language_Contact: Most also use Hindi [hin], especially educated people. Also use Adi [adi]. Also use Idu-Mishmi [clk]. Also use Tshangla [tsj].

Autonym: လိꩱ့်တဲးၵမ်းတီ‎ (Tai Khamti)
Alternate_Names: Hkamti, Kham-Tai, Khampti, Khamti Shan, Khantis, Tai Kham Ti
Location: Arunachal Pradesh state: Siang district, Namsai subdistrict, Barpathar, Chakham, Kheram, M. Pong, Man Khao, Memong, and Mime villages; Lohit district, Inten, Mahang, Mamareng, Nanam, Nathaw, and Ningro villages; Assam state: Lakimpur district, Barigaon, Barkhamti, Barpathar, Deotola, Sribhuyan, Tipling, and Tunijan villages; Dibrugarh district.
Classification: Kra-Dai, Kam-Tai, Tai, Southwestern
Dialect_Names: Assam Khamti, North Burma Khamti, Sinkaling Khamti
Typology: SOV; postpositional case-marking particle.
Language_Contact: Many also use Assamese [asm] (Bradley 2007a).
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 73% (2001 census).

Alternate_Names: Khamiyang, Khamjang, Shyam, Tai Khamyang, Tai Nora
Location: Assam state: Tinsukia district, Pawaimukh village.
Classification: Kra-Dai, Kam-Tai, Tai, Southwestern
Relationships: Reportedly similar to Phake [phk] of Assam and Shan [shn] of Myanmar. Lexical similarity: 64%–83% with Aiton [aio] and 48%–55% with Phake [phk].
Language_Use: Older adults only.
Language_Contact: Shifted to Assamese [asm].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 58% in Assamese [asm] (1981 census).
General_Remarks: A Scheduled Tribe. Close affinity to the Khampti of Arunachal. Several thousand Assamese may use their ethnic group name.

Alternate_Names: Dhed Gujari, Khandeshi, Khandeshi Bhili, Khandish, Maharashtra Bhil
Location: Gujarat state; Maharashtra state: Dhule district, Sakri sub-district; Nasik district, Satna sub-district; Nandurbar district, Nandurbar, and Shahada sub-districts.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Intermediate Divisions, Western, Khandesi
Dialect_Names: Dangri, Kunbi (Kunbau), Rangari, Khandesi, Kotali Bhil
Relationships: All varieties of Khandesi tested at 90% or higher intelligibility with each other. A group of Kukna in Dhule District speak Khandesi.
Language_Use: Vigorous. A group of Kukna [kex] in Dhule District also use Khandesi. Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Kukna [kex]. Also use Marathi [mar].
Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Kukna [kex].

Alternate_Names: Haria, Khadia, Khariya, Kharvi, Khatria, Kheria
Location: Jharkhand state: Ranchi district, Khunti sub-district, Kolebira and Thethaitangar Anchal; Simdega sub-district; Bilaspur, Chhattisgarh, Durg, Jashpur, Raigarh, Raipur, East Singhbhum, and West Singhbhum districts; Odisha state: Mayurbhanj, Sambalpur, and Sundargarh districts; Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Assam, Tripura, West Bengal states. Dhelki dialect mainly in northwest Gangpur (Raigarh), Jashpur, and Sundargarh; Dudh dialect is in south Gangpur (Raigarh) Ranchi, and western Sambalpur.
Classification: Austro-Asiatic, Munda, South Munda, Kharia-Juang
Language_Contact: Many also use Sadri [sck]. Also use Bengali [ben]. Also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin]. Also use Odia [ory]. Also use Santhali [sat].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 46% (1991 census).
Literature: Literature. Radio. Dictionary. Grammar. Texts. NT: 1992.
General_Remarks: A Scheduled Tribe in Bihar, Madhya Pradesh, Odisha, West Bengal. A Scheduled Caste in Tripura.

Location: Jharkhand state, East Singhbhum district, Chakulia, Dhalbhumgarh, Dumaria, Ghatsila, Musabani and Potka blocks; a few in West Singhbhum district; West Bengal state: Bankura district, Indpur, Raipur, and Ranibandh blocks; Purulia district, Balrampur, Barabazar, Bundwan, Hura, Manbazar, Puncha, and Purulia Muffasil blocks; West Medinipur district, Binpur block.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Outer Languages, Eastern, Bengali-Assamese
Relationships: A Western subdialect of Bengali [ben] (Grierson and Konow 1903–1928). Lexical similarity: 57%–90% among varieties of Kharia Thar, 53%–63% with Bengali [ben], 51%–67% with Odia [ory], 57%–75% with Lodhi [lbm].
Language_Use: Spoken by some Hill Kharia. Ethnic Hill Kharia in Odisha speak Odia [ory] as L1. Many in Jharkhand and West Bengal speak Bengali [ben] as L1. Home, village, private prayer.
Language_Contact: Most also use Bengali [ben], in outside domains. Also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin]. Also use Odia [ory]. Also use Santhali [sat].

Alternate_Names: Kahasi, Kassi, Khasa, Khashi, Khasiyas, Khuchia
Location: Assam state: Cachar, Kamrup, Lakhimpur, Nagaon, and North Cachar Hills districts; Meghalaya state: Jaintia Hills, and East and West Khasi Hills districts; Manipur, Tripura, and West Bengal states.
Official_Recognition: Statutory provincial language in Meghalaya State (1950, Constitution, Articles 345–347 inclusive), unscheduled language.
Classification: Austro-Asiatic, Mon-Khmer, Northern Mon-Khmer, Khasian
Relationships: Bhoi Khasi in East Khasi Hills, Nongpoh block, and Nonglung in East Khasi Hills, Umksning block are very different from standard Khasi, with different word order. Many varieties have only partial mutual inherent intelligibility. War dialect is separate from War-Jaintia [aml]. Cherrapunji (Sohra) is the standard. Lexical similarity: 75% between War dialect and standard Khasi.
Typology: SVO.
Language_Use: Government, courts, mass media in Meghalaya.
Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Biate [biu], Sakachep [sch], War-Jaintia [aml].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 63% in Meghalaya (2001 census).
Education: Taught in primary and secondary schools through grade 5 and as subject thereafter in Meghalaya state.
Literature: Literature. Radio. TV. Dictionary. Grammar. Bible: 1891–2016.
Scripts: Bengali (Bangla) script [Beng], no longer in use. Latin script [Latn], used since about 1842.

L1_Full: 25,800 (2011 census). Census uses Kalari as the name.
Location: Chhattisgarh state: Surguja district, at Madhya Pradesh and Uttar Pradesh borders.
Classification: Dravidian, South-Central, Gondi-Kui, Gondi
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng].
General_Remarks: Khirwar is a subgroup of the Gonds.

Location: Jammu and Kashmir state.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Outer Languages, Northwestern, Dardic, Chitral
Typology: SOV.
Scripts: Arabic script, Naskh variant [Arab]. Arabic script, Nastaliq variant [Aran], primary usage.

Alternate_Names: Kanauri, Kanaury Anuskad, Kanawari, Kanawi, Kanoreunu Skad, Kanorin Skad, Kanorug Skadd, Kinnaura Yanuskad, Kinner, Kinori, Koonawure, Kunawari, Kunawur, Lower Kinnauri, Malhesti, Milchan, Milchanang, Milchang, Tibas Skad
Location: Himachal Pradesh state: Kinnaur and Lahaul Spiti districts, Chauhra to Sangla and north along Satluj river to Morang, upper Ropa river valley villages; Rampur and Shimla area; Kashmir, Punjab, and Uttar Pradesh states.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Western Tibeto-Burman, Bodish, West Himalayish, Kinauri
Relationships: Dialect at Nichar has 79% inherent intelligibility of Sangla. Other varieties have functional intelligibility of each other. Related languages: Kanashi [xns], Chitkuli Kinnauri [cik], and Jangshung Tukpa [jna]. Lexical similarity: 76%–90% among varieties.
Typology: SOV.
Language_Use: Home. Some young people, all adults. Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Most also use Hindi [hin] (Negi 2012).
Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Chitkuli Kinnauri [cik].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 37%: men 52%, women 22%.
Scripts: Devanagari script [Deva]. Takri (Tankri, Takari) script [Takr], no longer in use.

Alternate_Names: Bhōṭiā of Upper Kanawar, Bhotea of Upper Kinnauri, Bod-Skad, Bod-skad, Bud-Kat, Bud-kat, Khunu-Töt, Mnyam, Mnyamskad, Myamkat, Myamskad, Nyamkad, Nyamkat, Nyamskad, Puh, Sangs-Rgyas, Sangyas
Location: Himachal Pradesh state: Kinnaur district, Morang sub-district, Nesang village in upper Kinnauri Sutlej river basin; Puh sub-district, Puh village; possibly Charang and Kuno villages.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Western Tibeto-Burman, Bodish, West Himalayish, Kinauri
Relationships: May be more than 1 language. Lexical similarity: 71% with Chhoyul Kinnauri [tpq], 63% with Mane village, 59% with Darcha village, 54% with Tibetan [bod].
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng].
General_Remarks: A Scheduled Tribe.

Location: Himachal Pradesh state: Kinnaur district, Charang, Kunnu, and Nesang villages.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Western Tibeto-Burman, Bodish, West Himalayish, Kinauri
Relationships: May be the same language as Bhoti Kinnauri [nes] (2020 H. Negi). Lexical similarity: 71% with Bhoti Kinnauri [nes], 30% with Gahri [bfu], 22% with Pattani [lae].

Alternate_Names: Chhitkul-Rakchham, Chitkhuli, Chitkuli, Kanauri, Kinnauri, Thebarskad, Tsitkhuli, Tsíhuli
Location: Himachal Pradesh state: Kinnaur district, Nichar subdistrict, Chhitkul and Rakchham villages in Sangla valley, Baspa river area.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Western Tibeto-Burman, Bodish, West Himalayish, Kinauri
Relationships: Lexical similarity: 46% with Kinnauri [kfk], 51% with Jangshung [jna], 43% with Shumcho [scu], 38% with Sunam [ssk].
Language_Use: Home, cultural events. Used by all.
Language_Contact: All also use Hindi [hin] (Martinez 2019). Most also use Kinnauri [kfk] (Martinez 2019).
General_Remarks: A Scheduled Tribe.

Alternate_Names: Boli, Chamang Boli, Himachali, Kinnauri Pahari, Lower Kinnauri, Oras Boli, Orasi, Ores, Pahari, Sonar Boli, “Harija” (pej.), “Harijan Boli” (pej.), “Harijan Kinnauri” (pej.)
Location: Himachal Pradesh state: throughout Kinnaur district.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Intermediate Divisions, Western, Pahari, Western Pahari
General_Remarks: Spoken by Scheduled Castes throughout Kinnaur District.

Alternate_Names: Birhor, Koda, Kola, Kora, Kuda, Kunha, Kunhar, Kunhu, Kunna, Kunrukh, Kunuk, Mirdha, Morva, Nagesia, Nageswar
Location: Jharkhand state: Palamu district; Odisha state: Sambalpur and Sundargarh districts; West Bengal state: Darjeeling and Jalpaiguri districts.
Classification: Dravidian, Northern
Language_Use: Home. Used by all.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Odia [ory].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L1: 17% (1981 census). Materials for multilingual education have been prepared in Kisan.
Education: Taught in primary schools, in 20 schools in Sambalpur district.

Alternate_Names: Koc, Kocch, Koce, Kocha, Kochboli, Konch
Location: Assam state: Goalpara and Nagaon districts; Meghalaya state: West Garo Hills district; Bihar, Tripura, and West Bengal states.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Sal, Boro-Garo, Koch
Relationships: Tintekiya in Meghalaya is intelligible with same dialect in Bangladesh; Tintekiya not intelligible with other Koch dialects; Koch-Rabha and Harigaya are mutually intelligible with Wanang; Dasgaya and Harigaya are mutually intelligible; these form a dialect chain (Koch-Rabha-Wanang-Harigaya-Dasgaya-Tintekiya). Lexical similarity: 90% between Tintekiya Koch of India and Bangladesh; Tintekiya: 44%–55% with other Koch dialects; Kock: 31%–39% with Rongdani Rabha [rah], 13%–17% with Garo [grt]. Lexical borrowing is heavier when it comes to high register vocabulary; Koch has borrowed words from Bangla [ben], Assamese [asm] and Hajong [haj].
Language_Use: Vigorous. Non-Koch in Koch villages normally speak Koch. Only 6 of the 8 endogamous groups still speak their mother tongue: Tintekiya, Wanang, Harigaya, Dasgaya, Chapra, and Koch-Rabha. Sankar and Satpariya have no known speakers. All domains. Used by all. Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Also use Assamese [asm]. Also use Bengali [ben]. Also use Boro [brx]. Also use English [eng]. Also use Garo [grt]. Also use Hajong [haj]. Also use Hindi [hin]. Also use Nepali [npi]. Also use Rabha [rah].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: Approximately 75% in any of the following languages: Assamese [asm], Bangla [ben], Garo [grt], English [eng], Hindi [hin], Rabha [rah], or Bodo [brx]. Show a growing interest toward education (Singh 1994b).
General_Remarks: Koch-Rabha belongs to Koch linguistically and ethnically but claims identity with the Rabha for political reasons.

Alternate_Names: Kaora, Kora, Korali, Korati, Kore, Mudi, Mudikora
Location: Bihar state; West Bengal state: Bankura and Bardhaman districts.
Classification: Austro-Asiatic, Munda, North Munda, Kherwari, Mundari
Relationships: Lexical similarity: 49%–55% with Santhali [sat], 61%–67% with Mundari [unr], 57%–60% with Kol [ekl]; wordlist contained 19% Bengali [ben] words.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Sadri [sck].

Location: Chhattisgarh state: Surguja district; Jharkhand state: Garhwa and Palamau districts; Uttar Pradesh state: Sonbhadra district.
Classification: Austro-Asiatic, Munda, North Munda, Kherwari
Relationships: A subgroup of Korwa [kfp] (Parkin 1991). Lexical similarity: 82%–96% between varieties, 50%–70% with Korwa [kfp].
Language_Use: Kodaku in Jharkhand shifting to a local variety of Sadri [sck]. Kodaku in Chhattisgarh retaining their mother tongue more. In Chhattisgarh most use Kodaku in home and village and it is used by children with each other.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin]. Also use Kurux [kru]. Also use Sadri [sck].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L1: 26% in Chhattisgarh (2001 census).
General_Remarks: Grouped with Korwa on Scheduled Tribes list in Chhattisgarh and Madhya Pradesh.

Alternate_Names: Coorg, Coorgi Kodava, Kadagi, Khurgi, Kodagu, Kotagu, Kurja, Kurug
Ethnic: 200,000. 100,000 in Kodagu District; 100,000 in Karnataka District and major cities.
Location: Karnataka state: Bengaluru (Bangalore), Dakshina Kannada (Mangalore), Kodagu (Coorg), and Mysuru (Mysore) districts. 50% live outside of Kodagu district in Karnataka state.
Classification: Dravidian, Southern, Tamil-Kannada, Tamil-Kodagu, Kodagu
Relationships: Historically there were 2 dialects, north and south. More recently, migration, intermarriage, and ethnic resurgence have contributed towards a single dialect in Kodagu (2020 N. Samuvel). 66% intelligibility of Malappuram [pcg]. Lexical similarity: 72% with Malappuram Paniya [pcg].
Language_Use: Vigorous. L1 of Airi, Male-Kudiya, Meda, Kembatti, Kapal, Maringi, Heggade, Kavadi, Kolla, Thatta, Koleya, Koyava, Banna, Golla, Kanya, Ganiga, and Malaya. Home, community, religion.
Language_Contact: Most also use Kannada [kan]. Many also use English [eng]. Also use Malayalam [mal].
Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Kudiya [kfg].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: More than 95% in Kannada [kan].
Literature: Literature. Newspapers. Radio. TV. Videos. Dictionary. Grammar. NT: 2017.
General_Remarks: A symbol of identity. ‘Kodagu’, situated to the west. Northern variety has emerged as standard and is used in Kodava literature (Rajyashree 2001).

Location: Manipur state: Bishnupur district, 3 villages south of Moirang; Chandel district, 2 villages near Palel; Senapati district, Saikul and Kangpokpi subdistricts, 5 villages; Nagaland state.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Western Naga
Relationships: Not intelligible with any related speech varieties (1991 P. Khasung). Lexical similarity: 62%–68% with Aimol [aim], 60%–66% with Purum [pub], 64% with Kharam Naga [kfw].
Language_Use: Purest Koireng spoken in Satu and Utonglo (2000 T. Shiekshel). Used by all. Children mix Meitei [mni] in with L1.
Language_Contact: Some also use Kom [kmm]. Also use English [eng], especially young people. Also use Meitei [mni].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 70%–80%. Older adults read Meitei, the young read English.
General_Remarks: Different from Liangmai Naga (Quoireng) [njn]. Assigned under 3 different Naga groups politically.

Alternate_Names: Hill Tippera, Kakbarak, Kohkborohk, Kokbarak, Kokborok, Tipura, Tripura, Tripuri, Usipi Mrung
Location: Assam and Tripura states.
Official_Recognition: Statutory language of provincial identity in Tripura State (1964, Official Languages Act No. 19 (as amended)), not a Schedule VIII language.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Sal, Boro-Garo, Dimasa-Kokborok, Kok Borok
Relationships: Debbarma is spoken by the royal family and is medium of communication with the other dialects; understood by all, but not vice versa.
Language_Contact: Also use Assamese [asm]. Also use Bengali [ben]. Also use English [eng].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L1: 74% (2001 census).
Education: Taught as subject in primary and secondary schools from grade 6. Taught as subject at 2 universities.
Literature: Literature. Newspapers. Radio. Dictionary. Grammar. Bible: 1998.

Alternate_Names: Kolam, Kolamboli, Kolami, Kolamy, Kolmi, Kulme
Location: Maharashtra state: Nanded, Wardha, and Yavatmal districts; Andhra Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh states.
Classification: Dravidian, Central, Kolami-Naiki
Relationships: Northwestern [kfb] and Southeastern Kolami [nit] not inherently intelligible. Neither is intelligible of Bodo Parja [bdv], Gadaba [gau], or Pottangi Ollar Gadaba [gdb]. Lexical similarity: 61%–68% with Southeastern Kolami [nit].
Language_Use: Home, community.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Marathi [mar], but with limited proficiency. Also use Northern Gondi [gno]. Also use Telugu [tel].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L1: 4%.

L1_Full: 10,000 (1989 F. Blair). 1,500 speakers of Naiki (Van Driem 2007).
Location: Maharashtra state: Chandrapur and Nanded districts; Telangana state: Adilabad district.
Classification: Dravidian, Central, Kolami-Naiki
Relationships: Not intelligible with Northwestern Kolami [kfb]. Rao (1950) reports another dialect in Chinnoor and Sirpur taluks of Adilabad District. The Naiki dialect is different from Naikri (Zvelebil 1970:13). Lexical similarity: 85%–88% with Naiki and other Southeastern Kolami dialects, 83% with the Metla-Kinwat and Utnur, 86% with Asifabad and Utnur, 60%–74% with Northwestern Kolami [kfb].
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: Low.

Alternate_Names: Bajania, Kachi, Kachi Gujarati, Katchi, Kohli, Kolhi, Koli, Kori, Kuchi, Kuchikoli, Vagari, Vagaria, Vaghri
L1_Full: 400,000 in India (1998). 100,000 Kachi Koli, 250,000 Rabari, 50,000 or more Vagri Meghwar, Katai Meghwar, and Zalavaria Koli.
Location: Gujarat state: Kachchh district, Rann, centered in Bhuj area.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Intermediate Divisions, Western, Gujarati
Dialect_Names: Kachi, Rabari (Rahabari), Kachi Bhil, Vagri (Kachi Meghwar), Katai Meghwar, Zalavaria Koli
Scripts: Arabic script, Naskh variant [Arab]. Gujarati script [Gujr], used by older people.

Location: Gujarat state: Wadhyar town area.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Intermediate Divisions, Western, Gujarati
Relationships: Mewasi and Wadiyari are almost the same linguistically and are converging as a caste. Dialects listed are distinct sociolinguistic endogamous ethnic groups. Lexical similarity: 83% with Parkari Koli [kvx], 78% with Vaghri [vgr], 76% with Kachi Koli [gjk].
Typology: 38 consonants, 13 vowels and 7 diphthongs; stress on first syllable.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng].
Scripts: Arabic script, Naskh variant [Arab]. Gujarati script [Gujr].

Location: Manipur state: Churachandpur, Seanapati, and Tamenglong districts, 22 villages.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Kuki-Chin, Northwestern
Relationships: Kolhreng may be a distinct language.
Language_Use: Aimol [aim], Koireng [nkd], and Chiru [cdf] speakers also understand Kom.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Meitei [mni].
Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Koireng [nkd].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 64% (2001 census).

Location: Andhra Pradesh state: East Godavari, Srikakulam, and Vizianagaram districts (Konda-Dora); Odisha state: Koraput district (Kubi); Assam state.
Classification: Dravidian, South-Central, Gondi-Kui, Konda-Kui, Konda
Relationships: Konda and Kubi dialects mutually inherently intelligible. Lexical similarity: 83% between Konda-Dora and Kubi dialect, 28%–36% with Telugu [tel].
Language_Use: Many ethnic Porja have adopted Telugu [tel] as L1.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Odia [ory].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 35%–44% for Vizianagaram, Srikakulam and E. Godavari districts; 29% among Kubi in Odisha (2001 census).
General_Remarks: The Porja are well established as two groups: the Pedda Kondalu and Chinna Kondalu. The Pedda Kondalu retain most of their traditional culture; however, the Chinna Kondalu have been heavily influenced by the Telugu [tel].

Alternate_Names: Amchigela, Central Konkan, Concorinum, Cugani, Kathodi, Katvadi, Konkan Standard, Konkanese, Konkani Mangalorean, Kunabi, North Konkan
L1_Full: 2,190,000 in India (2011 census). 2,150,000 Konkani, 17,200 Kudumbi, and 23,600 Malwani (2011 census).
Location: Gujarat state: Valsad district; Dadra and Nagar Haveli; Maharashtra state: Raigad, Ratnagiri, Sindhudung, and Thane districts; probably in Mumbai.
Official_Recognition: Statutory provincial language in Goa State (1950, Constitution, Schedule VIII), amended 1992.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Outer Languages, Southern, Konkani
Dialect_Names: Agri, Parabhi (Damani, Kayasthi), Koli, Kiristav, Dhangari (Dhanagari), Bhandari, Thakri (Thakari, Thakua, Thakura, Thakuri), Karhadi, Sangameshwari (Sangamesvari), Maoli (Ghati), Mahari (Dhed, Holia, Parvari), Chitpavani (Chitapavani), Malvani (Malwani), Kudumbi (Kudubi), Kudali, Bankoti (Bakoti), Bardeshi, Bicholi, Sashti, Cancona, Antruzi, Kunbi, Karwari, Siddi, Nawayathi, Kodiyali
Relationships: Dialects closely related; Chitapavani recognized as standard Konkani. Local fishermen use the Koli dialect (Hukkeri). Related to Katkari [kfu] (dialects: Kathodi, Katvadi), Varli [vav], Phudagi [phd], Samvedi [smv], Mangelas.
Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Goan Konkani [gom].
Education: Taught in primary and secondary schools through grade 5 and as subject thereafter in Goa state.
Literature: Literature. Newspapers. Radio. Videos. Dictionary. Grammar. Bible: 1997.
Scripts: Devanagari script [Deva], primary usage. Kannada script [Knda], no longer in use. Latin script [Latn], no longer in use.

Alternate_Names: Goan, Goanese Konkani, Gomataki, Konkani, Southern Kanara, “Goanese” (pej.)
Location: Maharashtra state: Ratnagari district, south coast strip; Goa, Karnataka, and Kerala states.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Outer Languages, Southern, Konkani
Dialect_Names: Bardeskari (Gomantaki), Sarasvat Brahmin, Chitpavani (Konkanasths), Daldi (Nawaits), Kudali (Malvani), Mangalore Standard Konkani (Goan)
Relationships: Daldi and Chitapavani [knn] are intermediate varieties between Goan Konkani [gom] and standard Konkani [knn].
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Konkani [knn].
Scripts: Devanagari script [Deva], official usage. Kannada script [Knda]. Latin script [Latn].

Location: Karnataka state: Dakshina Kannada, and Udupi districts; Kerala state: Kannur, and Kasargod districts; possibly Tamil Nadu state.
Classification: Dravidian, Southern, Tulu, Koraga
Relationships: Related to Tulu [tcy], Bellari [brw]. Not intelligible with Mudu Koraga [vmd], Tulu [tcy], or Kannada [kan]. Structural differences in phonology with Mudu Koraga. According to Bhat (1968), there are 4 dialects: Onti (spoken in Udupi), Tappu (in Hebri), Mudu (in Coondapur), Ande (in Mangalore).
Language_Use: Some young people, all adults.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Tulu [tcy].

Location: Kerala state: Kasaragod district.
Classification: Dravidian, Southern, Tulu, Koraga
Relationships: Distinct from Korra Koraga [kfd], Tulu [tcy], or Kannada [kan]. Structural differences in phonology with Korra Koraga.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Kannada [kan].

L1_Full: 10,700 in India (2021 Korean Ministry of Foreign Affairs), based on nationality.
Classification: Koreanic
Typology: SOV; Postpositions and particles used to indicate case, topic, subject, and object; Demonstrative, numeral, adjective, possessive, relative clause, and proper noun precede noun head; Adverb precedes verb; Sentence-final question particle; No articles; Passives; Marked for tense, aspect, and mood; 19 consonants and 10 vowels; No diphthongs; Non-tonal; Pitch-accent; Extensive use of honorifics and speech levels depending on formality and social hierarchy.
Scripts: Braille script [Brai]. Hangul and Han scripts [Kore], primary usage. Latin script [Latn], used for maps and signs.

Alternate_Names: Bondeya, Bopchi, Korki, Kuri, Kurku, Ramekhera
