Location: Madhya Pradesh state: Betul district, Betul city area and north; Hoshangabad and East Nimar (Khandwa) districts; Maharashtra state: Akola, Amravati, and Buldana districts.
Classification: Austro-Asiatic, Munda, North Munda, Korku
Relationships: Dialects in northern Maharashtra and south central Madhya Pradesh constitute one language; 82% to 97% intelligibility among them; Bouriya most widely understood. Lexical similarity: 76%–82% with Laki Bouriya dialects.
Language_Use: Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin]. Also use Marathi [mar].
Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Nihali [nll].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L1: 1%–5%. Literacy program in some villages in Chikaldara field. 50 literates reported.
General_Remarks: Different from Koraku [ksz].

Alternate_Names: Creole Portuguese, Kristi, Nɔ Ling, No Ling
Location: Maharashtra state: Korlai, 200 km south of Mumbai on west coast.
Classification: Creole, Portuguese based
Relationships: A blend of Portuguese [por] and Marathi [mar].
Language_Use: L1 of Christian farming community in upper Korlai. Intense cultural pressure from surrounding Marathi-speaking [mar] population. Home.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Marathi [mar], fluently with outsiders.

Location: Arunachal Pradesh state: East Kameng district.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Unclassified
Relationships: Lexical similarity: 9% with Hruso [hru]. Both are highly dissimilar to neighboring languages.
Language_Use: Home. Some young people, all adults.
General_Remarks: Part of the Aka ethnic group.

Location: Bihar state; Chhattisgarh state: Bilaspur, Jashpur, Korba, Raigarh, and Surguja districts; Jharkhand state: Gumla, Garhwa, and Palamau districts; Odisha state: Mayurbhanj and Sundargarh districts; Uttar Pradesh state: Mirzapur district; Andhra Pradesh, Maharashtra, and West Bengal states.
Classification: Austro-Asiatic, Munda, North Munda, Kherwari, Mundari
Relationships: Lexical similarity: 71%–92% between dialects, 50%–70% with Kodaku [ksz], 26%–36% with local Sadri [sck] spoken by Dihari Korwa. Lexical similarity with Sadri (an Indo-Aryan language) shows noticeable influence of Sadri on Korwa.
Language_Use: Some Pahadi Korwa are shifting to Sadri [sck]. Dihari Korwa of Jashpur speak a local variety of Sadri as mother tongue. Some Korwa speak Chhattisgarhi [hne] as mother tongue. Some of all ages.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Sadri [sck].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 26% for Chhattisgarh (2001 census).
General_Remarks: A Scheduled Caste in Uttar Pradesh speaking Hindi [hin] as mother tongue (Singh 1995b). Korwa divided into two groups: Pahadi (hill dwellers) and Dihari (plains dwellers). No intermarriage.

Alternate_Names: Knof, Kohatur, Kotar, Kotha, Kother-Tamil, Kotta, Kov, Kowe-Adiwasi, Kuof
Location: Tamil Nadu state: Gudalur, Kilkotagiri, Kollimalai, Kotagiri, Kundah, Sholur Kokkal, Trichicady settlements; a few in Aravankavu, Coonoor, Indunagar, Ooty, and Wellington; Chennai.
Classification: Dravidian, Southern, Tamil-Kannada, Tamil-Kodagu, Toda-Kota
Relationships: Lexical similarity: 35% with Badaga [bfq], 38% with Tamil [tam], 36% with Malayalam [mal], 24% with Toda [tcx].
Language_Use: Vigorous. Home, community. Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Also use Badaga [bfq]. Also use English [eng]. Also use Kannada [kan]. Also use Tamil [tam], with outsiders. It is the medium of instruction in school, so most children are bilingual in it.
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 75% (2001 census).
General_Remarks: Endogamous within the ethnic group.

Alternate_Names: Kavor, Kaya, Koa, Koi, Koi Gondi, Koitar, Koyato, Koyi, Raj Koya
Location: Chhattisgarh state: Bastar district; Maharashtra state; Odisha state: Koraput district, Malkangiri subdistrict; Telangana state: south of Godavari river, adjoining districts north of the river.
Classification: Dravidian, South-Central, Gondi-Kui, Konda-Kui, Manda-Kui, Kui-Kuvi
Dialect_Names: Malkangiri Koya, Podia Koya (Gotte Koya), Jaganathapuram Koya (Godavari Koya, Gommu Koya), Dorli (Chintoor Koya, Dor Koi, Dora, Dora Koi, Dorla Koitur, Dorla Koya, Korla)
Relationships: Linguistic center is Chintoor. Malkangiri and Podia are more divergent. Separate from Northern Gondi [gno], Adilabad Gondi [wsg], and Aheri Gondi [esg].
Language_Contact: Some also use Telugu [tel], but proficiency is low. Also use English [eng].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 7%.
Scripts: Devanagari script [Deva]. Latin script [Latn], reportedly preferred by Koya leaders. Oriya (Odia) script [Orya]. Telugu script [Telu].

Location: Karnataka state: Kodagu district, Madikeri taluk; Dakshina Kannada district, Sullia taluk; Kerala state: Kasargod district, Hosdurg taluk.
Classification: Dravidian, Southern, Tulu
Language_Use: Of 3 clans whose members originally spoke Kudiya [kfg], only the Thenmala retain Kudiya as their mother tongue, very few of the Poomala speak it, and none of the Adayka use the language (Joseph 2024).
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Kannada [kan]. Also use Kodava [kfa], which is spoken as the mother tongue by most members of the Poomala clan (Joseph 2024). Also use Malayalam [mal]. Also use Tulu [tcy], which is spoken as the mother tongue by all members of the Adayka clan (Joseph 2024).
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 48% for Scheduled Tribes in Karnataka; 63% for Kudiya in Kerala, 65% in Tamil Nadu (2001 census).

Alternate_Names: Bedia, Dharua, Khotta, Kurmali, Kurmali Thar, Kurumali
Location: Assam state: Darrang, Golaghat, Jorhat, and Sonitpur districts; Jharkhand state: east side; Odisha state: Keonjhar, Mayourbhanj, and Sundargargh districts; West Bengal state: Bankura Malda, west Midnapur, Nadia, and west Purulia districts.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Outer Languages, Eastern, Bihari
Relationships: Lexical similarity: 58%–89% between varieties, 61%–86% with Panchpargania [tdb], 58%–72% with Magahi (Khortha) [mag], 51%–73% with Sadri [sck], 46%–53% with Odia [ory], 41%–55% with Bengali [ben], 44%–58% with Hindi [hin].
Language_Use: Vigorous, but most young people in Odisha speak Odia [ory] among themselves rather than Kudmali. All domains. Used by all. Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Also use Bengali [ben]. Also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin]. Also use Odia [ory].
Literacy: There are Pre-degree, Degree, and Masters level programs in Kudmali.
Scripts: Bengali (Bangla) script [Beng], used in West Bengal. Chisoi script [Chis], used in West Bengal, Odisha, and Jharkhand. Devanagari script [Deva], used in Jharkhand. Oriya (Odia) script [Orya], used in Odisha.
General_Remarks: Kudmali is spoken by the Kurmi people of Assam brought to the tea gardens from Bihar, Odisha, and West Bengal.

Alternate_Names: Kanda, Kandh, Khond, Khondi, Khondo, Kodu, Kodulu, Kuinga, Kutia, Kuy
Location: Odisha state: Ganjam, Kandhamal, and possibly Koraput districts; Ganjam, Udayagiri area; Andhra Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, and Tamil Nadu states.
Classification: Dravidian, South-Central, Gondi-Kui, Konda-Kui, Manda-Kui, Kui-Kuvi
Language_Use: Vigorous. All domains. Used by all.
Literature: Literature. Radio. TV. Videos. Dictionary. Grammar. Texts. Bible: 2006.
General_Remarks: Different from Kuvi [kxv] and Koya (Koi) [kff].

Location: Odisha state: Gajapati district.
Classification: Dravidian, South-Central, Gondi-Kui, Konda-Kui, Manda-Kui, Kui-Kuvi
Relationships: Lexical similarity: 41%–73% with Kui [uki].
Language_Use: Used by all.

Location: Gujarat state: Dangs and Valsad districts; Karnataka state: Dakshina Kannada (Kanara) district; Maharashtra state: Dhule, Nasik, and Thane districts, Dadra and Nagar Haveli; Rajasthan state.
LWC_Support: Became a language of wider communication in the 18th century under Portuguese control. Used in trade, plays, songs, and communication among ethnic tribes.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Outer Languages, Southern, Konkani
Relationships: Dhule District Kukna has 98%–100% intelligibility with Khandesi [khn].
Language_Contact: Also use Khandesi [khn], especially a group of Kukna in Dhule District.
Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Khandesi [khn].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L1: 10%–30%. Some literacy work being done.
General_Remarks: May be the same as Dangi [dhn].

Alternate_Names: Kholung, Khulung, Khulunge Rai, Kulu Ring
Location: Sikkim state: Assam Lingzey, Zoom and many other places; Uttarakhand state: Dehradun; West Bengal state: Jalpaiguri district; Assam state.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Western Tibeto-Burman, Himalayan, Kiranti, Eastern
Typology: SOV; postpositions; noun head final; no noun classes or genders; content q-word initial; 1 prefix, up to 3 suffixes; clause constituents indicated by case-marking; verbal affixation marks person and number; ergativity; tense; no passives or voice; nontonal; 22 consonant and 6 vowel phonemes.

Alternate_Names: Kamaoni, Kumau, Kumauni, Kumawani, Kumgoni, Kumman, Kunayaoni
Location: Uttarakhand state: Almora, Bageshwar, Champawat, Nainital, Pithoragarh, and Udhamsingh Nagar districts; Almora and north Nainital (Central Kumaoni); Pithoragarh (Northeastern Kumaoni); southeast Nainital (Southeastern Kumaoni); west of Almora and Nainital (Western Kumaoni).
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Intermediate Divisions, Western, Pahari, Central Pahari
Dialect_Names: Central Kumaoni, Northeastern Kumaoni, Southeastern Kumaoni, Western Kumaoni
Relationships: Reportedly, eastern dialects are different. Names sometimes listed for dialects or subgroups are: Askoti, Bhabari of Rampur, Chaugarkhiya, Danpuriya, Gangola, Johari, Khasparjiya, Kumaiya Pachhai, Pashchimi, Phaldakotiya, Kumaoni, Rau-Chaubhaisi, Sirali, Soriyali. Most closely related to Garwhali [gbm] and Nepali [npi].
Language_Use: Home, community. Used by all. Positive attitudes. Central dialect is most accepted.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin], especially men, a few educated women, and school-aged children in towns and markets.
Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Byangsi [bee], Chaudangsi [cdn], Darmiya [drd], Gujari [gju], Rangkas [rgk], Rawat [jnl], Rongpo [rnp].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 72% for Uttarakhand (2001 census). Motivation for literacy not high.
Literature: Literature. Periodicals. Radio. Dictionary. Grammar. Texts. NT: 1825–2020.

Alternate_Names: Kumar, Mad, Mal, Maler, Malti, Malto, Maltu, Paharia, Pahariya
Location: Jharkhand state: Godda district, Sundar Pahardi sub-district; Pakaur district except southernmost block; Odisha state: Mayurbhanj; West Bengal state: Bankura, Barddhaman, and Murshidabad districts.
Classification: Dravidian, Northern
Relationships: Low comprehension of Mal Paharia [mkb]. Related to Kurux [kru]. Lexical similarity: 80% with Mal Paharia [mkb].
Language_Use: Vigorous. All domains. Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Also use Bengali [ben]. Also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin].
General_Remarks: Part of the Malto ethnic group.

Location: Kerala state: Kozhikode, Malappuram, and Wayanad districts, Ernakkulam, Kannur, Palakkad, and Trissur; all states in peninsular India.
Classification: Dravidian, Southern
Relationships: Reportedly cannot understand Telugu [tel] on Wayanad District radio. Lexical similarity: 48% with Telugu [tel].
Language_Use: Fairly vigorous in Wayanad District although Malayalam [mal] is used some in home and village. Some young people, all adults. Positive attitudes, especially in Wayanad District.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: Below 50% for older adults in Kerala.
General_Remarks: Kumbaran are a subcaste of Chettiars (or Adi Andhra) whose caste occupation is pottery or any work with mud or clay. Adi Andhra is a Scheduled Caste. Kusavan caste also speaks Kumbaran.

Location: Kerala state: Kozhikode district, Vythiri sub-district, Cheeyambam, Irulambam, Manaluvayal, Pakkam, and Porakady villages; Wayanad district, Pulpalli, Purakkadi, and Puthadi villages.
Classification: Dravidian, Southern
Relationships: Similar to Malayalam [mal] but with peculiar intonation and dialect virtually unintelligible to others (Shashi and Shri 1994, Menon 1996). Lexical similarity: 65% with Malayalam [mal], 61% with Aranadan [aaf], 83% with Pathiya [pty], 81% with Kalanadi [wkl].
Language_Use: Continued vitality doubtful, due to small population, no separate settlements, living with Malayalis, and similarity to Malayalam [mal]. Home.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Malayalam [mal].
General_Remarks: Common cultural origin with Kalanadiyar and Pathiyar.

Location: Andhra Pradesh state: East Godavari and Vishakhapatnam districts.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Outer Languages, Eastern, Oriya
Language_Use: Home. Some young people, all adults.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Telugu [tel], particularly in the market and for work and travel.
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 40% (1991 census).

Alternate_Names: Kowohans, Kurichchan, Kurichchia, Kurichia, Kurichiyars, Kuruchans
Location: Kerala state: Kannur, Kozhikode, and Wayanad districts, Mananthavady and Vythiri sub-districts in Wayanad.
Classification: Dravidian, Southern
Relationships: Lexical similarity: 60%–66% between dialects; Wayanad dialect 67%–71% with Malayalam [mal].
Language_Use: Shifting to Malayalam [mal], more in Kunnam than in Wayanad dialect.
Language_Contact: All also use Malayalam [mal], but less than half with good proficiency. Also use English [eng].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 68% (2001 census).
General_Remarks: A Scheduled Tribe. Consider themselves higher caste than Brahmin. An endangered language (Central Institute of Indian Languages). Further study is being done at Annamalai University.

Alternate_Names: Kamar, Karmakar, Karmokar, Kumbhakar, Kumhar, Umar
Location: Assam state: Barpeta, Goalpara, and Dhubri districts; Bihar, Madhya Pradesh, Tripura, and West Bengal states.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Outer Languages, Eastern, Bengali-Assamese
Language_Contact: Also use Assamese [asm]. Also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin].
General_Remarks: A dialect of Bengali [ben] which differs a lot from the standard (Singh et al 2003).

Alternate_Names: Alu Kurumba Nonstandard Kannada, Hal Kurumba, Pal Kurumba
Location: Tamil Nadu state: east Nilgiri Hills.
Classification: Dravidian, Southern, Tamil-Kannada, Tamil-Kodagu, Kodagu
Relationships: Lexical similarity: 80% between Alu Nonstandard Kannada and Pal varieties.
Language_Use: Some of all ages.
Language_Contact: Some also use Kannada [kan], or southern nonstandard Kannada. Also use English [eng]. Also use Tamil [tam].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 15%–25%.
General_Remarks: A Scheduled Tribe.

Location: Kerala state: Palakkad district, Attapady sub-district.
Classification: Dravidian, Southern
Relationships: Separate from Alu Kurumba [xua] and Kurumba Kannada [kfi]. Despite dissimilarity between Kurumba, Muduga [udg], and Irula [iru], each group uses their mother tongue to communicate with each other. Lexical similarity: 82% with Muduga [udg]; 61%–70% with Irula [iru], 50% with Alu Kurumba [xua], 52% with Kurumba Kannada, 55% with Malayalam [mal], 58% with Tamil [tam].
Language_Use: Vigorous. Home, village, religion. Used by all. Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Many also use Muduga [udg]. Also use English [eng]. Also use Irula [iru]. Also use Malayalam [mal]. Also use Tamil [tam].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 32% in Attapady; or 23% (27% men, 15% women), including other Kurumba in Wayanad District (1991 census).
General_Remarks: The least developed language group in Attapady. Thudukki variety is reportedly most pure.

Alternate_Names: Kadu Bhasha, Kadu Kurumba, Kurubara Bhashe, Nanga Man Pagi, Urali Kurumba
Location: Karnataka state: Chamrajnagar district, Gundlupet sub-district; Kodagu district, Somvarpet and Virarajendrapet sub-districts; Mysore district, Heggadadevanakote and Piriyapatna sub-districts; Kerala state: Wayanad district, Bathery, Mananthavady and Vythiri sub-districts; Tamil Nadu state: Nilgiri district, Gudalur and Panthalur sub-districts.
Classification: Dravidian, Southern, Tamil-Kannada, Tamil-Kodagu, Tamil-Malayalam, Tamil
Relationships: A nonstandard variety of Tamil [tam] or Kannada [kan]. May be same as Betta Kurumba dialect in Coorg District. Lexical similarity: 59%–77% among groups that are called Betta Kurumba.
Language_Use: Central Institute of Indian Languages lists Betta Kurumba as endangered. It is being studied by Annamalai University. Home, work, religion. Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 10%–15% in Tamil Nadu, 15%–20% in Karnataka, 40%–45% in Kerala. Favorable attitude toward literacy.
Scripts: Kannada script [Knda]. Malayalam script [Mlym]. Tamil script [Taml].
General_Remarks: ‘Kadu Kurumba’, jungle shepherds. ‘Betta Kurumba’, hill shepherds. 3 subdivisions: Ane (elephant) Kurumba, Bevina (neem tree) Kurumba, and Kolli (fire-brand) Kurumba.

Alternate_Names: Jen Kurumba, Jennu Kurumba, Jennu Nudi, Kattu Nayaka, Naik Kurumba, Naikan, Nonstandard Kannada, Shola Nayakan, Ten Kurumba
L1_Full: 101,000 (2011 census). 36,200 in Karnataka, 18,200 in Kerala, and 46,700 in Tamil Nadu (2011 census).
Location: Karnataka state: Mysore and Kodagu districts; Kerala state: Wayanad district. Tamil Nadu and Karnataka states’ border; east of Kerala state border; North Nilgiri Hills.
Classification: Dravidian, Southern, Tamil-Kannada, Tamil-Kodagu, Kodagu
Relationships: Possibly the same as Jeinu Kuruba dialect of Kannada [kan]. Lexical similarity: 61%–83% among varieties called Jennu Kurumba, less than 60% with Betta Kurumba [xub] dialects.
Language_Use: Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Kannada [kan]. Also use Malayalam [mal]. Also use Tamil [tam].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 46% in Tamil Nadu (2001 census). Attitudes favorable toward literacy.
General_Remarks: In Karnataka and Kerala states, they are known as Jennu Kurumba and Kattu Nayaka. In Tamil Nadu state, they are known as Kattu Nayakan.

Alternate_Names: Canarese, Kannada, Korambar, Kuramwari, Kuremban, Kuruba, Kuruban, Kurubar, Kurubas Kuruma, Kuruman, Kurumans, Kurumar, Kurumba, Kurumban, Kurumbar, Kurumbas, Kurumvari, Palu Kurumba, Southern Nonstandard Kannada
Location: Tamil Nadu state: Coimbatore district, Pollachi; Dindigul district, Sirumalai and Palani; Teni district, Cumbum Valley; Chingalpattu, Dharmapuri, Salem, and Vellore districts; Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh states.
Classification: Dravidian, Southern, Tamil-Kannada, Tamil-Kodagu, Kodagu
Language_Use: Home. Used by all.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Kannada [kan]. Also use Muduga [udg]. Also use Tamil [tam].
Literacy: Younger generation over 50% literate, older generation less.
General_Remarks: Reportedly 3 groups of Gowda: Okkili, Anuppa, and Kurumba, which may be languages or dialects of 1 language. Sometimes referred to as Alu or Palu Kurumba, but is a different language from Alu Kurumba [xua] in the hills. Kurumba and Kuruman are different Scheduled Tribes.

L1_Full: 26,000 (2004 survey). 25,000 in Wayanad; 1,000 in Gudalur of Nilgiri.
Location: Kerala state: Wayanad district, Sulthan Bathery and Vythiri sub-districts; Tamil Nadu state: Nilgiri district, Gudalur sub-districts, Cherangodu and Erumad villages, 10 hamlets.
Classification: Dravidian, Southern, Tamil-Kannada, Tamil-Kodagu, Kodagu
Relationships: Lexical similarity: 89%–92% between Mullu Kurumba varieties in Tamil Nadu and Kerala, 73%–77% with Malayalam [mal], 56%–65% with Tamil [tam], 22%–36% with Kannada Kurumba [kfi], 29%–41% with other Kurumba languages.
Language_Use: Use is declining. Home, village, religious services. Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Malayalam [mal].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 60%. Favorable motivation toward literacy.
General_Remarks: A Scheduled Tribe. Mullukuruman and Mullukurumbar are sometimes referred to as different tribes. Kuruman are in Kerala and Kurumbar in Tamil Nadu. Linguistically can be considered one group.

Location: Chhattisgarh state: Raigarh and Surguja districts; Jharkhand state: Lohardaga and Ranchi districts; Odisha state: Jharsuguda and Sundargarh districts; West Bengal state: Jalpaigiri district; Assam, Bihar, and Tripura states.
Classification: Dravidian, Northern
Relationships: Kisan [xis] and the Oraon dialect have 73% intelligibility. Oraon becoming standard. Related to Kumarbhag Paharia [kmj].
Typology: SOV; postpositions; noun head final; 2 noun classes (human, non-human); content q-word initial; 1 prefix, up to 6 suffixes; clause constituents indicated by case-marking; verbal affixation marks person, number and genders of subject and object; ergativity; tense and aspect; passives and voice; nontonal; 29 consonant and 10 vowel phonemes.
Language_Use: While there are written materials, the language is losing speakers (mostly due to urbanization). Some young people, all adults.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Sadri [sck].
Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Kodaku [ksz].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L1: 62% Oraon in Chhattisgarh, 25% in Bihar (2001 census).
Literature: Literature. Newspapers. Radio. Videos. Dictionary. Grammar. Texts. Bible: 2000.

Alternate_Names: Khod, Khondh, Khondi, Kodu, Kond, Kuvi Kond, Kuvinga, Kuwi
Location: Odisha state: Ganjam, Kalahandi, Koraput, and Phulbani districts; Andhra Pradesh state: Srikakulam, Vishakhapatnam, and Vizianagaram districts.
Classification: Dravidian, South-Central, Gondi-Kui, Konda-Kui, Manda-Kui, Kui-Kuvi
Language_Use: Dongria and Kuvi subgroups speak Kuvi as L1.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 34%—42% in for Vishakhapatnam, Vizianagaram, Srikakulam districts (2001 census).
Scripts: Latin script [Latn], experimental usage in 1916. Oriya (Odia) script [Orya], used in Odisha. Telugu script [Telu], used in Andhra Pradesh.
General_Remarks: Distinct from Kui [uki] and Koi (Koya).

Alternate_Names: Ladak, Ladakh, Ladakh Skat, Ladaphi, Ladhakhi, Ladwags
Location: Himachal Pradesh state: Kinnaur and Lahaul Spiti districts; Ladakh state: Leh district, 250 villages and hamlets.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Western Tibeto-Burman, Bodish, Central Bodish, Western
Dialect_Names: Leh (Central Ladakhi), Shamma (Lower Ladakhi, Sham, Shamskat), Nubra Ladakhi
Relationships: Perhaps 30%–40% intelligibility of Tibetan [bod]. Leh users comprehend 90% of Zangskari [zau] and Changthang [cna]. Nubra and Shamma not adequately intelligible with Leh to use the same educational, literacy, or development materials. Changthang and Zanskar, while understanding Stod Bhoti [sbu] better than Leh dialect, identify more with Leh Ladakhi culture. 58% to 85% intelligibility of Leh by Changthang, 73%–81% by Zanskar. Lexical similarity: 71%–83% with Purik [prx], 53%–60% with Tibetan, 84%–94% among 5 main dialects.
Typology: SOV; postpositions; genitives, relatives before noun heads; articles, adjectives numerals after noun heads; suffixes indicate case of noun phrase; ergative; causatives; comparative; CCVCC or CCCVV maximum; nontonal.
Language_Use: Vigorous. Used by all. Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin]. Also use Urdu [urd].
Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Brokskat [bkk], Changthang [cna], Zangskari [zau].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L1: 20%–50% (2001 census). Literacy rate in L2: 54%–65% men, 40% women. Percentage of those who can actually read with understanding is lower than census literacy rate indicates.
General_Remarks: Written Ladakhi is distinct from spoken forms. Leh dialect is acknowledged as standard spoken Ladakhi. It is the medium of Leh radio broadcasts and standard medium of communication among all Ladakh dialects, including Changthang and Zangskari (Paldan 2002).

Alternate_Names: Bangala, Banjari, Banjori, Banjuri, Brinjari, Gohar-Herkeri, Goola, Gormati, Gurmarti, Kora, Labhani, Labhani Muka, Lamadi, Lamani, Lambani, Lambara, Lavani, Lemadi, Lumadale, Singali, Sugali, Sukali, Tanda, Vanjari, Wanji
L1_Full: 5,080,000 (2011 census), including the following groups: 1,580,000 Banjari, 50,300 Gorboli, 3,280,000 Lambadi, and 171,000 Sugali (2011 census).
Location: Gujarat, Himachal Pradesh, Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Odisha, Tamil Nadu, Telangana, and West Bengal states.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Intermediate Divisions, Western, Rajasthani, Unclassified
Dialect_Names: Maharashtra Lamani, Karnataka Lamani (Mysore Lamani), Andhra Pradesh Lamani (Telugu Lamani)
Typology: SOV.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Kannada [kan]. Also use Marathi [mar]. Also use Telugu [tel].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 43% for Banjara of Andhra Pradesh. Many sources cite a much lower literacy rate for Banjara, 10%–20% (2001 census).
Scripts: Devanagari script [Deva], used in Maharashtra. Kannada script [Knda], used in Karnataka. Telugu script [Telu], used in Andhra Pradesh.
General_Remarks: A Scheduled Tribe in Odisha, a Scheduled Caste in Karnataka, Haryana, Punjab, Himachal Pradesh.

Location: Manipur state: Chandel district, 6 villages near Shuganu; 6 villages in Chalong area; 18 villages in Palel, Chandel town, and Sibong area; Nagaland state: Dimapur.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Kuki-Chin, Northwestern
Relationships: Reportedly most similar to Anal Naga [anm].
Typology: SOV; postpositions; genitives before head nouns; adjectives and numerals after noun heads; noun prefixes mark person, number of possessor; VC, CV, CVC, CCCVC.
Language_Use: Vigorous, but each successive generation not as knowledgeable about their folksongs and folktales. Used by all.
Language_Contact: A few also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin]. Also use Meitei [mni], at least passively.
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 40% in Meitei [mni]: 10 to 40 year olds (2000 S. Towar). Only 2% can read Latin script.
Scripts: Latin script [Latn]. Myanmar (Burmese) script [Mymr], used in Myanmar.
General_Remarks: A Scheduled Tribe.

Alternate_Names: Lapche, Nünpa, Rongke, Rongpa, Róng, Róngkup
Location: Sikkim state: Mangan district, Dzongu assembly constituency; West Bengal state: Darjeeling and Kalimpong districts.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Central Tibeto-Burman, Lepcha
Relationships: Classification uncertain; has been classified both in Himalayan and Naga groups.
Typology: SOV; postpositions; dual number; definite article; 32 consonants and 8 vowels.
Language_Use: In Sikkim, all ages. Language use not known in other regions.
Language_Contact: Many also use Nepali [npi]. Some also use English [eng].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 66% in Sikkim (2001 census).
General_Remarks: Lepcha is both language and name of people.

Alternate_Names: Lhoket, Lhomi dzyükki keccyok, Lhomiki keccyok, Shing Saapa, Syingsaaba
Location: West Bengal state: Darjeeling.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Western Tibeto-Burman, Bodish, Central Bodish, Central, gTsang
Typology: SOV; postpositions; noun head initial; masculine and feminine (limited class); content q-word precedes the main verb; 1 prefix, up to 3 suffixes; clause constituents indicated by case-marking; split ergativity; aspect; no passives or voice; tonal (tense-lax); 23 consonant and 8 vowel phonemes; evidentiality is a salient feature of Lhomi syntax.
Language_Use: Some young people, all adults.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 5%–25% (men).

Autonym: याक्थुङ् पान‎ (Yaakthung Paan), ᤕᤠᤰᤌᤢᤱ ᤐᤠᤴ‎ (Yakthung Paan)
Location: Assam state; Sikkim state: West district; West Bengal state: Darjeeling district.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Western Tibeto-Burman, Himalayan, Kiranti, Eastern
Typology: SOV; postpositions; genitives, articles, adjectives, numerals before noun heads; noun head final; content question word in situ; bipolar question word final; maximum of 3 prefixes, 6 suffixes; affixes indicate case of noun phrases; verb affixes mark subjects, objects, indirect objects—obligatory; verbal affixation marks person and number; split ergativity; reflexes conjugated intransitively can be used as a kind of passive; passives and voice; antipassives; causatives; comparatives; 16 consonant and 13 vowel phonemes; V, CV, CVC, CCV, CCVC; nontonal.
Language_Contact: Many also use Nepali [npi]. Some also use English [eng].
Education: Taught as subject in primary and secondary schools from grade 6 in Sikkim state. Taught as subject in tertiary schools.
Literature: Literature. Newspapers. Periodicals. Radio. TV. Videos. Dictionary. Grammar. Bible: 2022.
Scripts: Devanagari script [Deva], primary usage. Limbu (Kiranti, Sirijonga) script [Limb], dating from early 18th century.

Alternate_Names: Khispi, Kishpignag, Lish Monpa, Lishpa, Monpa
Location: Arunachal Pradesh state: West Kameng district, Lish, Lish Gompache, Lish Gompalok villages.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Central Tibeto-Burman, Kho-Bwa
Relationships: Reportedly most similar to Chug [cvg]. Lexical similarity: 59%–74% with Chug [cvg].
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Tshangla [tsj].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 62% for West Kameng District, males 71%, females 49% (2001 census).
General_Remarks: The cover term ‘Monpa’ (Moinba), man of the lower country, used to refer to several ethnically related peoples whose languages may not be related linguistically.

Location: Arunachal Pradesh state: Changlang district, Miao and Vijoynagar sub-district, 6 villages, Gandhigram being largest.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Ngwi-Burmese, Ngwi, Central
Typology: SOV; postpositions; classifiers; isolating language; no passives; aspect markers; causatives; topic markers; 28 consonants and 10 vowels; tonal (6 tones).
Literacy: Literacy rate in L1: 45%.
Literature: Literature. Newspapers. Radio. Dictionary. Grammar. Bible: 1968–1986.
Scripts: Latin script [Latn], used in 1915–1918, 1958–1966, and from 1981. Lisu (Fraser) script [Lisu], used since 1918, primary usage.
General_Remarks: The Lisu people are called Yobin or Yawyin by the Singpho [sgp] people.

Location: Jharkhand state: West Bengal state border area; Odisha state: Mayurbhanj district, Sadar subdistrict, Morada and Suliapada; Balasore district, Sora sub-district; West Bengal state: West Medinipur district, Binpur and Kharagpur-I sub-districts.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Outer Languages, Eastern, Bengali-Assamese
Relationships: Lexical similarity: 59%–67% with Oriya [ory], 56%–72% with Bangla (Bengali [ben]), 20% with Santhali [sat] and Mundari [unr], 66%–85% between varieties of Lodhi, 57%–75% with Kharia Thar [ksy].
Language_Use: Vigorous. All domains. Used by all. Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Also use Bengali [ben]. Also use English [eng]. Also use Odia [ory].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 22% in Odisha (2001 census).

Alternate_Names: Bagri Lohar, Belani, Bhubaliya Lohar, Chitodi Lohar, Chittoriya Lohar, Dhunkuria, Domba, Dombiali, Gadia Lohar, Gaduliya Lohar, Gara, Kanwar Khati, Lohari, Lohpitta, Panchal Lohar, Rajput Lohar
Location: Delhi, Gujarat, Haryana, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Punjab, Rajasthan, and Uttar Pradesh states.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Intermediate Divisions, Western, Rajasthani, Unclassified
Relationships: No significant dialect differences. May be same as Loarki [lrk] in Pakistan.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 40% (1981 census).
General_Remarks: Nomadic blacksmiths. The name ‘Gade Lohar’ refers to people who travel in bullock carts and are blacksmiths.

Location: Himachal Pradesh: Lahaul Spiti district in Lahul valley; Jammu and Kashmir state: Leh district, small border area.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Unclassified
Relationships: Different from Gade Lohar [gda].
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin].
General_Remarks: Lohar is a Scheduled Caste in Himachal Pradesh, not all of whom speak Lahul Lohar. Similar name and occupation to ‘Gade Lohar’.

Location: Assam state: Kamrup district; Meghalaya state.
Classification: Austro-Asiatic, Mon-Khmer, Northern Mon-Khmer, Khasian
Relationships: Lexical similarity: 36% with standard Khasi [kha].
Language_Contact: Also use Assamese [asm]. Also use English [eng]. Also use Garo [grt]. Also use Hindi [hin].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 10% (Singh 1994b).
General_Remarks: Previously listed as dialect of Khasi [kha]. Culturally intermediate between the Khasi and the Garo [grt].

Alternate_Names: Bihari, Magadhi, Magaya, Maghai, Maghaya, Maghori, Magi, Magodhi, Megahi
L1_Full: 20,700,000 in India (2011 census). 8,000,000 Khortha and 12,700,000 Magahi (2011 census).
Location: Bihar state: Arwal, Aurangabad, western Bhagalpur, Gaya, Jehanabad, western Munger, Nalanda, Nawada, eastern Patna, and Sheikhpura districts; Jharkhand state: Giridih, Hazaribagh, Palamu, southern Ranchi districts, and north Chota Nagpur area.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Outer Languages, Eastern, Bihari
Relationships: Greatly influenced by standardized Hindi [hin].
Language_Use: Shifting to Hindi [hin] among formally educated Magahi users and among those who have migrated to the cities (2020 M. Bhushan). Religion. Some of all ages. Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin], especially educated people, city-dwellers, and those who travel.
Literacy: Literacy rate in L1: 30%. Literacy rate in L2: 30% in Hindi [hin]. Bhojpuri [bho] can use Magahi materials.
Literature: Newspapers. Periodicals. Radio. Grammar. Texts. NT: 1826–2016.

Location: Sikkim state: South district, scattered in East district.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Western Tibeto-Burman, Himalayan, Central Himalayan, Kham-Magar, Magar
Language_Use: Home.
Language_Contact: Also use Nepali [npi].

Location: Assam state: tea estates; Bihar state; Jharkhand state: Dhanbad, Gumla, Hazaribagh, Pargana, Ranchi, Santal Lohardaga, Saraikela Kharsawan, East Singhbhum, and West Singhbhum districts in Chota Nagpur area; Odisha state: Balasore, Keonjhar, and Mayurbhanj districts; West Bengal state: Jalpaiguri and West Medinipur districts.
Classification: Austro-Asiatic, Munda, North Munda, Kherwari, Santali
Relationships: Possible dialect of Santhali [sat]. Lexical similarity: 69%–87% between varieties of Mahali, 68%–93% with Santhali [sat], 53%–59% with Mundari [unr].
Language_Use: Most in Jharkhand reported Santhali [sat], Sadri [sck] or Mundari [unr] as their mother tongue rather than Mahali. May be a threatened language. Home, village, private prayer for half the L1 speakers in Jharkhand.
Language_Contact: Also use Bengali [ben]. Also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin]. Also use Munda [unx]. Also use Mundari [unr]. Also use Odia [ory]. Also use Sadri [sck]. Also use Santhali [sat].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 12% for Jharkhand (20% male, 4% female) (1981 census); 32% for Odisha (2001 census).
Scripts: Bengali (Bangla) script [Beng]. Latin script [Latn], used in Bangladesh.
General_Remarks: Mahli are reported to speak Sadri [sck] as L1 in Jharkhand, the Thar dialect of Dhatki [mki] in Odisha, and Bengali [ben] in West Bengal.

Alternate_Names: Apabhramsa, Bihari, Maitili, Maitli, Methli, Tirahutia, Tirhuti, Tirhutia
Location: Bihar state: Muzaffarpur west, past Kosi east to west Purnia district, to Munger and Bhagalpur districts south, and Himalayan foothills north; Delhi, Kolkata, Mumbai. Cultural, religious, and linguistic centers are Janakpur, Madhubani and Darbhanga. Many settled abroad.
Official_Recognition: Statutory language of provincial identity in Bihar State (1950, Constitution, Schedule VIII), amended 2003.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Outer Languages, Eastern, Bihari
Dialect_Names: Standard Maithili, Southern Standard Maithili, Eastern Maithili (Khortha, Khotta, Kortha, Kortha Bihari), Jolaha, Central Colloquial Maithili (Sotipura), Kisan, Dehati, Thetiya (Thati)
Relationships: Caste variation more than geographic variation in dialects. Functional intelligibility among all dialects, including those in Nepal. Reportedly most similar to Magahi [mag]. Lexical similarity: 91% between Brahmin and non-Brahmin dialects; 51%–65% with Bajjika [vjk].
Typology: SOV; postpositions; noun head final; 11 noun classes or genders; content q-word in situ; genitives, articles, numerals before noun heads, adjectives before and after noun heads; 1 prefix, up to 5 suffixes; clause constituents partially indicated by case-marking (6 cases) and postpositions; verbal affixation marks person, number, gender, and honorificity of subject; nominative-accusative; object marked by position; person, gender, animate distinguished, obligatory for subject; transitives; both tense and aspect; passives and voice; causatives; comparatives; V, VC, VCC, CV, CVC, CVV, CCV, CVCC, CCVCC; non-tonal; 26 consonant and 16 vowel phonemes; stress on penultimate syllable.
Language_Use: Used by Brahmin and other high caste or educated Hindus, who influence the culture and language, and other castes. There is a Maithili Academy. Linguistics and literature taught at Patna University and at L. N. Mithila University in Darbhanga. Home, community. Mixed attitudes. Influenced by caste, ranging from superiority to resentment; non-Brahmin speech viewed as inferior.
Language_Contact: Also use Bengali [ben]. Also use Bhojpuri [bho]. Also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin]. Also use Nepali [npi].
Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Bajjika [vjk].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L1: 25%–50%. Literacy rate in L2: 25%–50%. If they can read Nepali [npi] or Hindi [hin], they can read Maithili. The educated read Hindi, Nepali, or English books for pleasure. Some literacy work in India.
Education: Taught in primary and secondary schools through grade 5 and as subject thereafter in Bihar state.
Scripts: Devanagari script [Deva], primary usage. Kaithi script [Kthi], used until the turn of the 20th century. Newa script [Newa], no longer in use, historic usage. Tirhuta script [Tirh], used until the turn of the 20th century.

L1_Full: No known L1 speakers in India (2016). Last native speaker in India, Thak Bahadur, died in 2016.
Location: Jharkhand state: Gumla district; Sikkim state: South district, Majhigaon near Jorethang, and East district, Majhitar near Rangpo; possibly Assam and West Bengal states.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Outer Languages, Eastern, Bihari
Typology: SOV; postpositions; noun head final; no noun classes or genders; content q-word in situ; 1 prefix, up to 2 suffixes; clause constituents indicated by case-marking; verbal affixation marks person and number; split ergativity based on nominal hierarchy (the first and second person pronouns do not code ergativity but the third person pronouns do); passives and voice; nontonal; 29 consonant and 6 vowel phonemes.
Language_Contact: Most shifted to Nepali [npi]. Some shifted to Sadri [sck].
Literature: Radio. Dictionary. Grammar. Texts. Bible portions: 2019.
General_Remarks: Distinct from Majhi dialect of Eastern Punjabi [pan] or Bote (Bote-Majhi) [bmj] of Nepal.

Location: Chhattisgarh state: Bilaspur district, Katghora sub-district; Raigarh and Surguja districts; Sikkim state; Uttar Pradesh state: scattered in Allahabad, Mirzapur, and Varanasi districts.
Classification: Unclassified
Relationships: Possibly a dialect of Asuri [asr].
Language_Contact: Shifting to English [eng].
General_Remarks: Reportedly speak Chhattisgarhi [hne] as L1.

Alternate_Names: Dehri, Mad, Mader, Mal, Mal Pahariya, Mal Pahoria, Maler, Malpaharia, Malti, Malto, Maltu, Manlati, Mar, Mar Paharia of Dumka, Marpaharia, Maw, Mawdo, Mawer, Mawer Nondi, Paharia, Parsi
Location: Bihar state: Banka district; Jharkhand state: Deoghar district; Dumka district, Pakaur; south Godda district; Sahibganj district, Borio, Depart village; south Santal Pargana district, Ramgarh hills; West Bengal state: Bankura, Barddhaman, and Murshidabad districts.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Outer Languages, Eastern, Bengali-Assamese
Relationships: Not inherently intelligible with Kumarbhag Paharia [kmj], Sauria Paharia [mjt], Bengali [ben], or Hindi [hin]. Part of the Malto ethnic group. Reportedly speak a variety similar to Kharia Thar [ksy] of Manbhum (Jharkhand). Lexical similarity: 85% between dialects, 59% with Mal Paharia Barmasiya.
Language_Use: Vigorous. All domains. Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Some also use Bengali [ben]. Also use English [eng].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 13% male, 3% female, average 8% (1981).

Location: Kerala state: Palakkad district, Parambikulam wildlife sanctuary; Tamil Nadu state: Coimbatore district, Annamalai hills.
Classification: Dravidian, Southern, Unclassified
Relationships: Lexical similarity: 68%–74% with Malasar [ymr], 70% with Eravallan [era], 70% with Muduga [udg], 65% with Tamil [tam], 61% with Malayalam [mal], 67%–72% with the Attapady dialect of Irula [iru], 75% with the Walayar dialect of Irula.
Language_Use: Vigorous. Home, village, religion. Used by all. Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Malayalam [mal].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 17% in Kerala, 15% in Tamil Nadu (2001 census).
General_Remarks: Mala Malasar means ‘king of the forest’. Culturally very distinct from neighboring tribal groups.

Alternate_Names: Mala Koravan, Malaikuravan, Malakkuravan, Male Kuravan
L1_Full: 18,600 (2001 census). 260 in Kerala, 18,300 in Tamil Nadu.
Location: Kerala state: Kollam, Kottayam, and Trivandrum districts, Chittar, Kattachira, and Rajanpara in Ranni Range, Pathanamthitta sub-district, Nottakal in Pathanapuram sub-district, Pampa river, Neduvanged sub-district forest tracks; Tamil Nadu state: Kanniyakumari district.
Classification: Dravidian, Unclassified
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Tamil [tam].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 53% for Kerala, 41% for Tamil Nadu (2001 census).
General_Remarks: A Scheduled Tribe. Reported to speak a dialect of Malayalam [mal] with many borrowed words and phrases from Tamil.

Alternate_Names: Hill Pantaram, Malapantaram, Malepantaram, Pandaram Basha
Location: Kerala state: Kollam and Pathanamthitta districts, some in Kottayam and Palakkad districts; Tamil Nadu state: Coimbatore, Maduari, and Villupuram districts.
Classification: Dravidian, Southern, Tamil-Kannada, Tamil-Kodagu, Tamil-Malayalam, Malayalam
Relationships: Lexical similarity: 83%–94% between varieties in Kerala, 63%–68% with Malayalam [mal], 64%–68% with Tamil [tam].
Language_Use: Home, community. Negative attitudes.
Language_Contact: Also use Malayalam [mal], with many shifting in Kerala. Also use Tamil [tam], with most shifting in Tamil Nadu.
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 48% for Kerala, 59% for Tamil Nadu (2001 census).
General_Remarks: A Scheduled Tribe.

Alternate_Names: Arayans, Karingal, Malai Arayan, Malayarayan, Malayarayar, Male Arayans, Maley Arayan, Vazhiyammar
L1_Full: No known L1 speakers. Dormant by 2000s.
Location: Kerala state: scattered in Ernakulam, Idukki, Kottayam, and Thrissur districts.
Classification: Dravidian, Southern, Tamil-Kannada, Tamil-Kodagu, Tamil-Malayalam, Malayalam
Language_Contact: Shifted to Malayalam [mal], in Kerala state.
General_Remarks: A Scheduled Tribe. Speak a variety of Malayalam [mal] as L1. Malayarayar and Mala Arayan are listed as 2 different communities in the census but are the same group. Though the Kanikkar of Trivandrum District also sometimes call themselves Malayarayar, they are entirely different (Menon 1996:198).

Location: Karnataka state; Kerala state: Palakkad district, Chittoor and Palakkad sub-districts; Tamil Nadu state: Coimbatore district, Pollachi sub-district.
Classification: Dravidian, Southern, Unclassified
Relationships: Lexical similarity: 68%–74% with Tamil [tam], 79%–83% with Walayar Irula [iru], 77%–86% with Eravallan [era], 57%–61% with Malayalam [mal], 68%–75% with Mala Malasar [ima] (2004 survey); 52%–56% with Malaryan [mjq], 77%–82% between Malasar and Kollimalakkar, Kollimalakkar 80% with Malapulaya (2006 survey).
Language_Use: Home, village, religion. Used by all. Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Malayalam [mal], especially in Kerala among the few with higher education. Also use Tamil [tam].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 36% in Kerala, 22% in Tamil Nadu (2001 census).
General_Remarks: Kollimalakkar call themselves Malasar but are different culturally, belonging to the Malayali tribe of Tamil Nadu. They migrated to Nelliyampathy area in Kerala for work many years ago.

Alternate_Names: Malai Vedan, Malavetan, Towetan, Veda Bhasha, Vedans, Vettava Bhasha
Ethnic: 33,000 (2011 census). 26,000 in Kerala and 7,000 In Tamil Nadu.
Location: Kerala state: Ernakulam, Idukki, Kollam, Kottayam, Pathanamthitta, and Trivandrum districts; Tamil Nadu state: scattered in Dindigul, Kanniyakumari, Madurai, Nilgiris, Salem, and Tirunelveli districts.
Classification: Dravidian, Southern, Tamil-Kannada, Tamil-Kodagu, Tamil-Malayalam, Malayalam
Relationships: Lexical similarity: 64%–68% with Malayalam [mal], 48%–52% with Tamil [tam].
Language_Use: Shifting to Malayalam [mal] in Kerala state, especially in Idukki district. Home, village in Pathanamthitta district. Some of all ages. Negative attitudes, especially in Kerala state.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Malayalam [mal], especially in Kerala.
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 67%–78% for Kerala, 56% for Tamil Nadu (2001 census).
General_Remarks: A Scheduled Tribe.

Alternate_Names: Alealum, Malayalani, Malayali, Malean, Maliyad, Mallealle, Malyalam, Mopla
Location: Karnataka state: Dakshina Kannada, Kodagu, and Mysore districts; Kerala and Lakshadweep states; Puducherry state: Mahe; Tamil Nadu state: Colimbatore, The Nilgiris, and Tirunelveli districts.
Official_Recognition: Statutory provincial language in Kerala State; union territories Lakshadweep and Puducherry (1950, Constitution, Schedule VIII).
Classification: Dravidian, Southern, Tamil-Kannada, Tamil-Kodagu, Tamil-Malayalam, Malayalam
Dialect_Names: Malabar, Nagari-Malayalam, Malayalam, South Kerala, Central Kerala, North Kerala, Kayavar, Namboodiri, Moplah (Mapilla), Pulaya, Nasrani, Nayar, Kasargod, Jeseri (Dweep Bhasha, Jesri), Jewish Malayalam, Nuclear Malayalam, Tiyya (Ezhava), Ernad
Relationships: Caste and communal dialects: Namboodiri, Nayar, Moplah, Pulaya, Nasrani. Mapilla is among the most divergent dialects, differing considerably from literary Malayalam.
Typology: SOV; postpositions; noun head final; gender (masculine/feminine/neuter); case-marking (7 cases); tense; 37 consonants, 11 vowels, 2 diphthongs; non-tonal; light stress on first syllable; inclusive/exclusive pronouns.
Language_Use: Cochin Jews in Kerala speak Malayalam.
Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Allar [all], Aranadan [aaf], Attapady Kurumba [pkr], Irula [iru], Jennu Kurumba [xuj], Kadar [kej], Kalanadi [wkl], Kanikkaran [kev], Kodava [kfa], Kudiya [kfg], Kunduvadi [wku], Kurichiya [kfh], Mala Malasar [ima], Malapandaram [mjp], Malaryan [mjq], Malasar [ymr], Malavedan [mjr], Mannan [mjv], Moundadan Chetti [cty], Muduga [udg], Mullu Kurumba [kpb], Muthuvan [muv], Paliyan [pcf], Paniya [pcg], Pathiya [pty], Ravula [yea], Thachanadan [thn], Ullatan [ull], Urali [url], Wayanad Chetti [ctt].
Education: Taught in primary and secondary schools through grade 5 and as subject thereafter in Kerala State, and Lakshadweep and Puducherry union territories.
Scripts: Arabic script, Naskh variant [Arab]. Braille script [Brai], used since 1998. Malayalam script [Mlym], primary usage.
General_Remarks: A Classical Language of India since 2013.

Alternate_Names: Dhivehi, Dhivehi Bas, Mahl, Malikh, Malki
Location: Lakshadweep state: Laccadives, Minicoy island; Kerala state: possibly in Trivandrum.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Outer Languages, Southern, Sinhalese-Maldivian
Typology: SOV.
Language_Use: Those in Minicoy are undergoing acculturation owing to lack of contact with remaining Divehi people and pressure to use other languages (Malayalam [mal], English [eng], and Hindi [hin]).
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Standard Arabic [arb].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L1: 95%–100%. Literacy rate in L2: 95%–100%.

Location: Madhya Pradesh state: Bhopal, Dewas, Dhar, Guna, Indore, Mandsaur, Nimuch, Rajgarh, Rathlam, Sehore, Shajapur, and Ujjain districts; Rajasthan state: Jhalawar district. Sondwari dialect geographically isolated from the others.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Intermediate Divisions, Western, Rajasthani, Unclassified
Dialect_Names: Ujjaini (Avanthika, Malvi Proper), Rajawadi, Umadwadi, Sondwari (Sondhwadi, Soudhwari), Bachadi, , Dholewari, Hoshangabad, Jamral, Katiyai, Malvi Proper, Patvi, Rangari, Rangri
Relationships: Considered the standard variety, Southeastern Rajasthani Nimadi [noe] is reportedly most similar language with 70% intelligibility. 88%–92% intelligibility of Ujjaini dialect by other dialects. Lexical similarity: 65%–89% among dialects.
Typology: SOV; nontonal.
Language_Use: Vigorous. Home, village, religion. Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Most also use Hindi [hin]. Also use English [eng].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 58% for rural Madhya Pradesh (2001 census). Government project discontinued due to low response.

Location: Odisha state: Kalahandi district, Thuamul Rampur subdivision.
Classification: Dravidian, South-Central, Gondi-Kui, Konda-Kui, Manda-Kui, Manda-Pengo
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng].

Location: Himachal Pradesh state: Mandi district.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Intermediate Divisions, Western, Pahari, Western Pahari
Relationships: Preliminary survey suggests speakers have functional intelligibility of Kangri [xnr]. People in southeast Mandi district may have more difficulty understanding Kangri. Standard Mandeali is spoken throughout the broad valley running north and south from Jogindernagar to Sundarnagar. Mandeali Pahari is spoken north around Barot, east of Uhl River. Intelligible with difficulty to standard Mandeali. May be intermediate variety between Mandeali and Kullui [kfx]. Southeast district contains transition to Mahasui [bfz]. In the west, Sarkaghat is also a bit different from standard Mandeali, perhaps forming a transition towards Hamirpur and Bilaspur areas. Lexical similarity: 89% with Palampuri dialect of Kangri [xnr], 83% with Chambeali [cdh].
Typology: SOV.
Language_Use: Used by all.
Language_Contact: Also use Eastern Punjabi [pan]. Also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin]. Also use Urdu [urd].
Scripts: Devanagari script [Deva]. Takri (Tankri, Takari) script [Takr], no longer in use.

Location: Andhra Pradesh state: Srikakulam, Vishakhapatnam, and Vizianagaram districts, scattered in East Godavari and West Godavari districts; perhaps in Tamil Nadu state.
Classification: Dravidian, South-Central, Telugu
Language_Use: It is uncertain if they are speaking Telugu [tel] or a closely related language of their own.
Language_Contact: Shifted to Telugu [tel].

Alternate_Names: Inavan petch, Mannan Pasha, Manne, Mannyod
L1_Full: 7,850 (2001 census). 7,760 in Kerala, 82 in Tamil Nadu.
Location: Kerala state: Idukki district, Devikulam, Pirmed, and Udumpanchola sub-districts; Tamil Nadu state: scattered in Madurai district.
Classification: Dravidian, Southern, Tamil-Kannada, Tamil-Kodagu, Tamil-Malayalam
Relationships: Little variation between varieties with 92% intelligibility, 70% intelligibility of Malayalam [mal]. Lexical similarity: 86%–96% between varieties, 57%–61% with Tamil [tam], 56%–64% with Malayalam [mal].
Language_Use: Home, village, religion. Some young people, all adults. Positive attitudes. Interest in language development.
Language_Contact: Also use Malayalam [mal], with many youth shifting, especially the educated and those having contact with outsiders (Shaw 2008).
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 50% for Kerala, 84% for Tamil Nadu (2001 census).
General_Remarks: A Scheduled Tribe in Kerala and Tamil Nadu. Not the same as the Scheduled Caste Mannan in Trivandrum and other adjoining districts of Kerala and Tamil Nadu who speak Malayalam. Romanized spelling is the same but the Scheduled Caste name is pronounced with retroflex double n.

Alternate_Names: Hawthai, Mira, Sabeu, Tlongsai, Zao, “Chin, Mara” (pej.), “Lakher” (pej.), “Mara Chin” (pej.), “Maraa” (pej.), “Miram” (pej.), “Shendu” (pej.)
L1_Full: 75,000 in India (2024 Executive Secretary of the Mara Autonomous District Council).
Location: Mizoram state: Siaha district, Mara Autonomous District Council and other districts. 2 towns, 60 villages. Also some population in other states.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Kuki-Chin, Maraic, Mara
Dialect_Names: Tlôsai-Siaha (“Tlongsai” (pej.)), Lôchei-Hawthai, Chapi-Ngiaphia-Sabyh (“Fàbau” (pej.), “Sabeu” (pej.), Sizô), Zyhno-Lialai-Heima (“Zawhnai” (pej.)), Vyhtu
Relationships: Same as Shendu [shl]; Shendu is an exonym for Mara. Tlôsai-Siaha dialect is the lingua franca of the Mara people.
Typology: SOV.
Language_Use: Vigorous. All domains. Used by all. Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Many also use English [eng]. Also use Mizo [lus].
Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Zyphe Chin [zyp].
Education: Taught in most primary schools through grade 8.

Location: Andhra Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Goa, Karnataka, and Madhya Pradesh states; Maharashtra state: Belgaum, Bidar, and Karnataka districts.
Official_Recognition: Statutory provincial language in Maharashtra State (1950, Constitution, Schedule VIII).
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Outer Languages, Southern
Dialect_Names: Gawdi of Goa, Kasargod, Kosti, Kudali, Nagpuri Marathi, Thanjavuri Marathi
Relationships: Complex dialect situation with many dialects. Dialects bordering other major language areas share many features with those languages. Dialects or closely related languages: Konkani [knn], Goan Konkani [gom], Deccan [dcc], Varhadi-Nagpuri [vah], and Gowlan [goj]. There is a dialect in Thanjavur District and elsewhere in Tamil Nadu influenced lexically by Tamil [tam] and Kannada [kan], with at least 100,000 speakers.
Language_Use: The Bene Israel are a Marathi-speaking Jewish group in Mumbai.
Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Ahirani [ahr], Andh [anr], Bhalay [bhx], Far Western Muria [fmu], Gowli [gok], Indo-Portuguese [idb], Katkari [kfu], Khandesi [khn], Korku [kfq], Korlai Portuguese Creole [vkp], Lambadi [lmn], Mawchi [mke], Nihali [nll], Noiri [noi], Northern Gondi [gno], Northwestern Kolami [kfb], Palya Bareli [bpx], Pardhan [pch], Pauri Bareli [bfb], Powari [pwr], Rathwi Bareli [bgd], Saraiki [skr], Tulu [tcy], Vaagri Booli [vaa], Varli [vav], Vasavi [vas], Waddar [wbq].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L1: 77% (2001 census). Literacy rate in L2: 77% (2001 census).
Education: Taught in primary and secondary schools through grade 5 and as subject thereafter in Maharashtra state.
Scripts: Braille script [Brai]. Devanagari script [Deva], primary usage. Modi script [Modi].
General_Remarks: The Habshi are Muslim, descended from East African slaves brought to western India. Are is a synonym for a Marathi caste name. Are also refers to Marathi-speaking communities in south India.

Alternate_Names: Hill Madia, Hill Maria, Madi, Madia, Madia Gond, Madiya, Modh, Modi
L1_Full: 165,000 (2000). 141,000 Maria and 23,700 Hill Maria; All Gondi speakers: 2,910,000 (2011 census).
Location: Chhattisgarh state: Bastar district, Narayanpur and Bijapur sub-districts, administrative block of 200 villages known as ‘Abujhmar block’; Maharashtra state: Garhchiroli (Chanda) district, Bhamragad, Etapalli, and Sironcha sub-districts.
Classification: Dravidian, South-Central, Gondi-Kui, Gondi
Dialect_Names: Abujmaria (Abujhmadia, Abujhmaria, Abujmar Maria, Abujmariya, Hill Maria), Adewada, Bhamani Maria (Bhamani), Etapally Maria
Relationships: Etapally Maria dialect is apparently understood by all. Distinct from Muria, Dandami Maria [daq], Northern Gondi [gno], Adilabad Gondi [wsg], Aheri Gondi [esg], and Koya [kff]. 76%–77% intelligibility of other Gondi varieties. Muria Gondi [mut] is intelligible of Abujmaria around Narainpur area but not elsewhere. Distinct from Maria dialect of Chanda District in Maharashtra (Natarajan 1985). Intelligibility 90%–100% of Bhamragarh dialect by other Maria speakers. Maria is intelligible to the Gatte Maria, an ethnic group. Lexical similarity: 59%–80% among dialects (1991 survey), 65%–98% (1999 survey).
Language_Use: All domains.
Language_Contact: Some also use Halbi [hlb], especially men who may also use a Muria variety. Also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L1: Men 5%, women below 1%. Literacy rate in L2: 25%–50%. High interest in literacy.
General_Remarks: A Scheduled Tribe.

Alternate_Names: Bastar Koya, Bison Horn Maria, Dandami Madiya, Dhuru, Gondi Madiya, Madiya, Maria Gond
Location: Andhra Pradesh state: Bijapur, Chhattisgarh, and Daksin Bastar Dantewada districts; Maharashtra state: Garhichiroli district; Telangana state: Khamman district.
Classification: Dravidian, South-Central, Gondi-Kui, Gondi
Relationships: Those in Geedam and Bailadila have 95%–98% mutual intelligibility, 81% of the Sukma variety, but 18%–21% of Maria [mrr], 18%–45% of Muria in Sukma understood the Geedam variety at 81% or lower; those in Bailadila understood Sukma at 92%. May be more than one language. Distinct from Northern Gondi [gno], Adilabad Gondi [wsg], Aheri Gondi [esg], Maria of Garhchiroli, and Koya [kff].
Language_Use: Used by all.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng].
Literacy: Literacy program in progress.
General_Remarks: A Scheduled Tribe.

Location: Mizoram and Tripura states.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Ngwi-Burmese, Burmish, Southern
Language_Use: Home, village.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng].
Scripts: Bengali (Bangla) script [Beng], used in Bangladesh. Myanmar (Burmese) script [Mymr], used in India.

Location: Rajasthan state: Barmer, Bikaner, Churu, Jaisalmer, Jalore, Jodhpur, and Pali districts; Delhi, Gujarat, Haryana, Madhya Pradesh, Punjab, and Uttar Pradesh states; thoughout India.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Intermediate Divisions, Western, Rajasthani, Marwari
Relationships: The standard form of Marwari. May or may not be different from Marwari of Pakistan [mve]. 67% intelligibility of Shekhawati [swv], 61% of Godwari [gdx], 54% of Mewari [mtr], 54% of Dhundari [dhd], 45% of Haroti [hoj], and 45% of Mewati [wtm]. 53% intelligibility of Shekawati by Marwari. Lexical similarity: 50%–65% with Hindi [hin], 69%–76% with Merwari [wry], 72%–87% between dialects, 62%–74% with Godwari [gdx], 61%–77% with Shekawati [swv].
Typology: SOV; postpositions; noun head final; content q-word in situ; clause constituents indicated by case-marking; both tense and aspect; 38 consonant and 10 vowel phonemes; nontonal.
Language_Use: Vigorous. Home, village, market, religion. Used by all. Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin], especially educated people.
Literacy: Literacy rate in L1: 5%–10%. Literacy rate in L2: 50%–75%.
Literature: Literature. Newspapers. Radio. Dictionary. Grammar. Texts. NT: 1820–2023.

Alternate_Names: Māwəchī, Mauchi, Mavchi, Mawachi, Mawchi Bhil, Mowchi
Location: Gujarat state: southeast; Maharashtra state: Dhule district.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Intermediate Divisions, Western, Bhil
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Marathi [mar].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L1: 5%–10%. Literacy rate in L2: 25%–50%.

Alternate_Names: Kaṯhe, Kathe, Kathi, Mēkhalī, Mēklē, Mailhai, Manipuri, Meetei, Meeteilon, Meitei Manipuri, Meiteilon, Meiteiron, Meithe, Meithei, Meithlei, Menipuri, Mitei, Mithe, Pōṇṇā, Ponna
Location: Assam state: Cachar and Dima Hasao; Mainly Manipur state; Nagaland state: Dimapur, Kohima, Peren, Phek; Mizoram state: Aizwal and Kolasibi; possibly some in nearby states.
Official_Recognition: Statutory provincial language in Manipur State (1950, Constitution, Schedule VIII), amended 1992.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman
Relationships: Intelligibility of Meitei in Bangladesh is difficult. Those in Bangladesh may understand India Meitei better than vice versa possibly due to more language change in Bangladesh over the years. India Meitei is more standard. Intelligibility between dialects in Bangladesh definitely sufficient to understand complex and abstract discourse. Lexical similarity: 80%–86% between dialects in Bangladesh, 65%–70% between Bangladesh and India varieties.
Typology: SOV; postpositions; articles before noun heads; 25 consonants and 6 vowels; tonal (2 tones).
Language_Contact: Also use Hindi [hin].
Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Aimol [aim], Anal [anm], Chiru [cdf], Chothe Naga [nct], Gangte [gnb], Hmar [hmr], Inpui Naga [nkf], Kharam Naga [kfw], Koireng [nkd], Kom [kmm], Lamkang [lmk], Mao Naga [nbi], Maram Naga [nma], Monsang Naga [nmh], Moyon Naga [nmo], Purum [pub], Tarao Naga [tro], Thado Chin [tcz], Thangal Naga [nki].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L1: 73% (2005 BI). Literacy rate in L2: 69% for Manipur (2001 census).
Education: Taught in primary and secondary schools through grade 5 and as subject thereafter in Manipur state.
Literature: Literature. Radio. Videos. Dictionary. Grammar. Texts. Bible: 1984–2022.
Scripts: Bengali (Bangla) script [Beng]. Braille script [Brai]. Latin script [Latn], unofficial usage. Meitei Mayek script [Mtei].
General_Remarks: Mainly rural. 7 clans (Mangang (Ningthouja), Luwang. Khuman (Khumal), Moirang, Angom, Khaba-nganba, and Sarang-leisangthem).

Location: Rajasthan state: Ajmer and Nagaur districts.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Intermediate Divisions, Western, Rajasthani, Marwari
Relationships: 82%–97% intelligibility of Marwari [mve]. Lexical similarity: 60%–73% between varieties of Merwari in Ajmer and Nagaur districts; 49%–74% with Marwari [rwr], 58%–80% with Shekhawati [swv], 44%–70% with Godwari [gdx], 54%–72% with Mewari [mtr], 62%–70% with Dhundari [dhd], 57%–67% with Haroti [hoj].
Language_Use: Vigorous. Home, village, market, religion. Used by all. Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin], especially educated people, with very good proficiency.

Location: Rajasthan state: Bhilwara, Chittoaurgarh, and Udaipur districts; Gujarat, Haryana, Delhi, Madhya Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh states.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Intermediate Divisions, Western, Rajasthani, Marwari
Relationships: 54% intelligibility with Marwari [rwr]. Lexical similarity: 81%–97% between dialects, 73%–91% with Marwari, 75%–90% with Wagri-Dhevdi, 72%–89% with Malvi [mup], 54%–72% with Merwari [wry], 57%–66% with Shekhawati [swv], 51%–73% with Godwari [gdx], 56%–64% with Dhundari [dhd], 69%–84% with Haroti [hoj].
Typology: SOV.
Language_Use: Home, village. Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Many also use Hindi [hin]. Also use English [eng].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 38% (2001 census).
General_Remarks: Different from Mewati, dialect of Haryanvi [bgc].

Location: Haryana state: Faridabad and Gurgaon districts; Rajasthan state: Alwar, Bharatpur, and Dholpur districts; Uttar Pradesh: Madhura district.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Intermediate Divisions, Western, Unclassified
Relationships: 45% intelligibility of Marwari [rwr]. Over 90% intelligibility of Alwar District dialect throughout Mewati area. Dialect in the Nuh area of Gurgaon is considered purest. Lexical similarity: 72%–77% with Hindi [hin], 63%–68% with Haryanvi [bgc], 57%–70% with Shekhawati [swv], 62%–67% with Dhundari [dhd], 52%–70% with Haroti [hoj], 68%–71% with Braj Bhasha [bra], 86%–99% between all varieties of Mewati.
Language_Use: Vigorous. Home, village, market, religion. Used by all. Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Some also use Hindi [hin]. Also use Standard Arabic [arb]. Also use Urdu [urd].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 25% (2006 SIL).
General_Remarks: People are called Meo; many Urdu [urd] loanwords.

Location: Arunachal Pradesh state: East Kameng district, Bameng and Lada sub-districts, Besai, Dongko, Drackchi, Gerangzing, Kampaa, Kojo, Nabolong, Naschgzang, Panker, Pego, Rojo, Sachung, Salang, Sekong, Wakke, and Zarkam villages; West Kemang district, Nafra sub-district, 25 villages including Chalang, Debbing, Dibrick, Dichik, Khellong, Lower Dzang, Nachinghom, Nafra, Najang, Naku, Nizong, Rurang, Upper Dzang, and Zangnaching in Bichom and Pakesa river valley.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Central Tibeto-Burman, Hrusish
Dialect_Names: Western Miji (Dammai, Dhəmmai, Dhammai, Sajalang, Sajolang), Eastern Miji (Nəmrai, Namrei)
Relationships: Generally considered in the Mirish subgroup. Reportedly completely dissimilar to any surrounding language. Lexical similarity: 54%–65% between varieties of West and East Kameng; 54%–83% between all varieties.
Language_Use: Used by all.
Language_Contact: Also use Assamese [asm]. Also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin]. Educated speak it more fluently, but all speakers know some. Also use Hruso [hru]. Also use Nyishi [njz].
Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Hruso [hru], Nyishi [njz].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 39%, males 48%, females 29% (2001 census).
General_Remarks: A Scheduled Tribe.

Alternate_Names: Eastern Mishmi, Geman Dend, Geman Deng, Kaman, Kaman Mishmi, Kman, Mījū Mishmi, Miji, Miju, Mishmi
Location: Arunachal Pradesh state: Lohit district, 25 villages, high altitudes of east, upper Lohit and Dau valleys; Assam state.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Central Tibeto-Burman, Mijish
Relationships: Conflicting reports about Miju-Mishmi similarity to Idu-Mishmi [clk] and Digaro-Mishmi [mhu]. Reportedly intelligible but recorded lexical similarity is too low for this to be possible. Ethnically related, but may not be linguistically similar. Related to Kachin, Chin and Lepcha [lep] languages (Chowdhury 1996). Some linguists believe the language is similar to Jingpho [kac]. Lexical similarity: 7% with Idu-Mishmi [clk], 10% with Digaro-Mishmi [mhu] (IICCC).
Typology: SOV; 28 consonants and 6 vowels; tonal (4 tones which reportedly have a low functional load).
Language_Contact: Some also use English [eng]. Also use Assamese [asm]. Also use Digaro-Mishmi [mhu]. Also use Hindi [hin]. Also use Nepali [npi].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 40% for Mishmi (2001 census).
General_Remarks: Different from the Miji [sjl].

Location: Chhattisgarh state: Bastar district; Odisha state: Koraput and Nabarangapur districts.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Outer Languages, Eastern, Bengali-Assamese
Dialect_Names: Batasuna, Jagdal Pur, Kosagumuda, Kotpad, Nabarang Pur, Umerkote
Relationships: Dialects have good intelligibility. Not functionally intelligible of Halbi [hlb]. Lexical similarity: 83%–95% among dialects.
Language_Use: Vigorous. Home, religion. Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Also use Desiya [dso], in Odisha. Also use English [eng]. Also use Halbi [hlb], in Madhya Pradesh. Also use Hindi [hin], in Madhya Pradesh. Also use Odia [ory], in Odisha, but with low proficiency.
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 10% in Odia [ory].
General_Remarks: Declared a General Caste by the government. Divided into 2 groups, the larger Kabirpanthi and the smaller Sakta.

Alternate_Names: Hill Miri, Miching, Mishing, Mising-Padam-Miri-Minyong, Missing, Takam
Location: Arunachal Pradesh state: Lower Subansiri district, Ziro subdistrict, villages near Pasighat, both sides of Kamla river; Upper Subansiri district, Daporizo sub-district; Assam state: Dhemaji, Dibrugarh, Golaghat, Jorhat, North Lakhimpur, Sibsagar, Sonitput, and Tinsukia districts.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Central Tibeto-Burman, Tani
Relationships: Adi [adi] may be a dialect (2021 T. Patir). Most experts on the Aranuchal Pradesh and Tani languages treat Hill Miri and Mising as separate languages belonging to different branches of the Tani subgroup (2022 ELP).
Language_Contact: Also use Assamese [asm].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 53% for Arunachal, 60 % for Assam (2001 census).
Scripts: Bengali (Bangla) script [Beng]. Devanagari script [Deva]. Latin script [Latn].

Alternate_Names: Duhlian Twang, Dulien, Hualngo, Le, Lei, Lukhai, Lusago, Lusai, Lusei, Lushēi, Lushai, Lushai-Mizo, Lushei, Mizo ṭawng, Sailau, Whelngo
Location: Assam state; Manipur state: Churachandpur district; Mizoram and Nagaland states; Tripura state: Jampui Hill range.
Official_Recognition: Statutory language of provincial identity in Mizoram State (1950, Constitution, Articles 345–347 inclusive), unscheduled language.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Kuki-Chin, Central, Mizo
Relationships: Related to Hmar [hmr], Pangkhua [pkh], and Falam Chin [cfm] (Zahao dialect).
Typology: SOV.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng].
Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Biate [biu], Chakma [ccp], Hmar [hmr], Hrangkhol [hra], Mara [mrh], Paite Chin [pck], Pankhu [pkh], Pnar [pbv], Ralte [ral].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L1: 82%. Literacy rate in L2: 74% for Manipur (2001 census).
Education: Taught as subject in primary and secondary schools in Mizoram state.
Scripts: Bengali (Bangla) script [Beng]. Braille script [Brai]. Latin script [Latn], primary usage.
General_Remarks: Mizo is a Scheduled Tribe with subgroups Lushai, Pang, Tlau, and Hualngo.

Location: Arunachal Pradesh state: West Kameng district, Kalaktang sub-district, Balimu, Kalaktang, and Tomko villages.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Western Tibeto-Burman, Bodish
Relationships: Reportedly most similar to Dirang dialect of Tshangla [tsj], average 55% intelligibility of Dirang.
Language_Use: Vigorous. Home, village, religion. Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin].
Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Bugun [bgg].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 62% for West Kameng District, males 71%, females 49% (2001 census).
General_Remarks: ’Monpa’ (Moinba), man of the lower country and refers to several ethnically-related peoples which may not be related linguistically.

Alternate_Names: Brahmi, Cuona Menba, Dwags, Monkit, Northern Monpa, Takpa, Tawan Monba
Location: Arunachal Pradesh state: Tawang district.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Western Tibeto-Burman, Bodish, East Bodish
Typology: Basic SOV.
Language_Use: Vigorous. Home, village, religion. Used by all. Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin].
Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Chug [cvg], Sherdukpen [sdp].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 32% (2001 census).
General_Remarks: Monpa (Moinba), ‘man of the lower country’, refers to several ethnically related peoples, which may not be related linguistically.

Alternate_Names: Maru, Mro, Mro-Mru, Mrung, Murung, Niopheng, Niopreng
Location: West Bengal state: Hoogly, Jalpaiguri, and Nadia districts.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Ngwi-Burmese, Mru
Typology: SOV.
Scripts: Latin script [Latn]. Mro script [Mroo], developed in the 1980s.

L1_Full: 3,370 (1991 census). National census population figures combine Muduga of Attapady with Muthuvan, who, despite the similarity of the spelling of their ethnonym, are entirely different and separated by geographic and cultural distance (Menon 1996).
Location: Kerala state: Palakkad district, Mannarkad sub-district, Attapady block, Abbannuru, Chandakulam, Chitturu, Chundakki, Kakkuppady, Kallamale, Karuvare, Koravanpady, Kottamale, Kottiyuru, Molakambi, Mukkali, Ommale, Pettikkallu, Thazhachundakki, Thekkumpanna, Ummathupadiga, and Veeranuru; Tamil Nadu state: Coimbatore and Nilgiris.
Classification: Dravidian, Southern
Relationships: Also influenced by Kannada [kan] and Tulu [tcy]. Has grammatical similarities with Tamil [tam], but cannot be treated as a dialect. It is distinct in the Dravidian family (Menon 1996:274 citing Rajendran). No dialects determined on survey. Lexical similarity: 55%–57% with Malayalam [mal], 59% with Muthuvan [muv], 60% with Tamil [tam], 75% with the Attapady dialect of Irula [iru], 82%–83% with Attapady Kurumba [pkr].
Language_Use: Vigorous, children learn it first. Home, village, religion. Used by all. Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Malayalam [mal]. Education often determines the extent of bilingualism in it, but even some higher educated Muduga are not adequately bilingual.
Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Attapady Kurumba [pkr], Kannada Kurumba [kfi].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 25% (31% men and 17% women) (1991 census). One of the least literate communities in Kerala, but 73% of survey respondents claim to be literate in Malayalam [mal].

L1_Full: 500 in India (2006 SIL). 75 families in India, 60 Mugom and 15 Karmarong. In addition, there are many seasonal workers.
Location: Himachal Pradesh state: Kinnaur, Dharmshala and Ladakh; Kullu, Manali.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Western Tibeto-Burman, Bodish, Central Bodish, Central, gTsang
Typology: SOV; postpositions; content q-word in situ; clause constituents indicated by case-marking; ergativity; no passives or voice; tonal.
Language_Use: Youth born in India still use Mugom at home. Home, with friends. Used by all.
General_Remarks: Migrate from Nepal temporarily for work, but many stay 20 to 30 years.

Alternate_Names: Conta-Reddi, Mukha Dhora, Nooka Dora, Nuka-Dora, Reddi, Reddi-Dora, Riddi
Location: Andhra Pradesh state: Srikakulam, Vishakhapatnam, and Vizianagaram districts; Adivasi Oriya, scattered.
Classification: Dravidian, South-Central, Gondi-Kui, Konda-Kui, Konda
Language_Use: Use Telugu [tel] as L1 (Singh 1994b).
Language_Contact: Also use Adivasi Oriya [ort]. Also use English [eng].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 34%–42% for Scheduled Tribes in Vishakhapatnam, Srikakulam, Vizianagaram districts (2001 census).

Alternate_Names: Heriki, Killi, hoɽo jagar, muɳɖa jagar
Location: Odisha and Jharkhand states; possibly Bihar and West Bengal.
Classification: Austro-Asiatic, Munda, North Munda, Kherwari, Mundari
Relationships: Reportedly most similar to Mundari [unr].
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Sadri [sck].
Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Birhor [biy], Mahali [mjx].
Scripts: Bengali (Bangla) script [Beng]. Devanagari script [Deva]. Oriya (Odia) script [Orya].

Alternate_Names: Colh, Horo, Kolh, Mandari, Mondari, Munari
L1_Full: 1,160,000 in India (2011 census). 1,130,000 Mundari and 27,500 Bhumij (2011 census).
Location: Jharkhand state: Ranchi district, south and west; Andaman and Nicobar Islands union territory, Assam, Himachal Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Odisha, Tripura, and West Bengal states.
Classification: Austro-Asiatic, Munda, North Munda, Kherwari, Mundari
Dialect_Names: Hasada’, Latar, Naguri, Kera’, Bhumij (Bhumij Munda, Bhumij Thar, Bhumji, Sadar Bhumij)
Relationships: 75% intelligibility of Ho [hoc]. Lexical similarity: 70%–84% with the Bhumij dialect.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Sadri [sck].
Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Birhor [biy], Mahali [mjx].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L1: 10%–30%. Literacy rate in L2: 50%–75%.
Literature: Literature. Periodicals. Radio. Dictionary. Grammar. Texts. Bible: 1910–2002.
Scripts: Bengali (Bangla) script [Beng]. Devanagari script [Deva], used in India. Latin script [Latn]. Nag Mundari script [Nagm]. Ol Onal script [Onao], used in Odisha, West Bengal, and Jharkhand in India. Oriya (Odia) script [Orya].

Location: Chhattisgarh state: Bastar district, Keshkal and Kondagaon sub-districts; Odisha state: Nabarangapur district, Raigarh sub-district.
Classification: Dravidian, South-Central, Gondi-Kui, Gondi
Relationships: 95% intelligibility between dialects; 73%–83% of Western Muria [mut]; 19%–34% of Northern Gondi [gno]; 35% of Dandami Maria [daq]. Lexical similarity: 74%–77% with Western Muria [mut], 65%–75% with Far Western Muria [fmu].
Language_Use: Vigorous. Religion, work; mixed use: home, village. Used by all. Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Also use Chhattisgarhi [hne]. Also use English [eng]. Also use Halbi [hlb]. Also use Hindi [hin]. Also use Odia [ory].
Literacy: Majority are illiterate.
General_Remarks: A Scheduled Tribe.

Location: Chhattisgarh state: Rajnandgaon district, Mahola and Manpur sub-districts; Maharashtra state: Garhchiroli district, Armori, Dhanora, Korchi, and Kurkheda sub-districts; Gondia district, Jamdi sub-district.
Classification: Dravidian, South-Central, Gondi-Kui, Gondi
Relationships: 79%–88% intelligibility of other Muria languages; 74% of Dandami Maria [daq], 0% to 34% of Northern Gondi [gno], 6%–50% of Aheri Gondi [esg] and Adilabad Gondi [wsg], 2%–70% of Maria [mrr]. Lexical similarity: 72%–80% with Western Muria [mut]; 65%–75% with Eastern Muria [emu].
Language_Use: Vigorous. Home, village, religion. Used by all. Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Also use Chhattisgarhi [hne]. Also use English [eng]. Also use Marathi [mar].
General_Remarks: A Scheduled Tribe.

Location: Chhattisgarh state: Bastar district, Narayanpur and Uttar Bastar Kanker districts; Maharashtra state: Gadchiroli.
Classification: Dravidian, South-Central, Gondi-Kui, Gondi
Relationships: 80%–96% intelligibility among dialects, 69%–73% of Eastern Muria [emu], 51%–78% of Far Western Muria [fmu]. No intelligibility of Dandami Maria [daq], Northern Gondi [gno], Adilabad Gondi [wsg], Aheri Gondi [esg] or Maria [mrr]. Lexical similarity: 72%–80% with Far Western Muria [fmu]; 74%–77% with Eastern Muria [emu].
Language_Use: All domains. Used by all.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 2% (2003 India Church Growth Mission).
General_Remarks: A Scheduled Tribe.

Alternate_Names: Mudavan, Muduva, Muduvan, Muduvar, Mutuvar, Paanti naattu peeccu
Location: Andhra Pradesh state; Kerala state: Idukki district, Devikulam sub-district, Adimali and Devikulam blocks; Ernakulam, Kannur, Kottayam, Kozhikode, and Thrissur districts; Tamil Nadu state: Coimbatore district, Udumalpet and Valparai sub-districts, Anaimalai hills; Madurai district, Cardamom hills.
Classification: Dravidian, Southern, Tamil-Kannada, Tamil-Kodagu, Tamil-Malayalam, Tamil
Dialect_Names: Western Muthuvan (Malayalam Muthuvan, Nattu Muthuvan), Eastern Muthuvan (Pandi Muthuvan, Tamil Muthuvan)
Relationships: Intelligibility 82%–87% between dialects, eastern dialect more intelligible to western than vice versa, 80% intelligibility of Malayalam [mal]. Lexical similarity: 77%–88% between dialects, 62%–67% with Tamil [tam], 58%–68% with Malayalam [mal].
Language_Use: Vigorous. Home, village, religion. Used by all. Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Malayalam [mal], especially youth. Also use Tamil [tam], especially older people.
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 24% (31% males, 17% females) (1991 census); 40% for Tamil Nadu (2001 census).

Location: Arunachal Pradesh state: Upper Subansiri district; Taksing sub-district, Dadu, Esnaya, Gumsing, Lingbing, Redi, Reding, Taying, Tongla, and Yeja villages.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Central Tibeto-Burman, Tani
Relationships: Affinity with Tagin [tgj] (Singh 1994b).
Language_Use: Home. Some of all ages.
Language_Contact: All also use Hindi [hin].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 40% in Hindi [hin].
