General_Remarks: A Scheduled Tribe.

Alternate_Names: Angami, Angamis, Gnamei, Monr, Ngami, Tendydie, Tsanglo, Tsoghami, Tsugumi
Location: Nagaland state: Kohima district; Maharashtra and Manipur states.
LWC_Support: Originated in southern China; Naga Angami people migrated to the state of Nagaland during Naga pre-colonial period. Became widespread in first half of 19th century. Used in trade, church, and media.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Angami-Pochuri
Dialect_Names: Dzuna, Kehena, Khonoma, Chakroma (Western Angami), Mima, Nali, Mozome, Tengima (Kohima)
Relationships: Tengima (Kohima) dialect is standard. Naga Chokri and Naga Khezha are eastern Angami groups with their own dialects. 2 southern varieties (Viswemal, Jakhama) are not intelligible with dialects listed. Tenyidie is an umbrella term for all the dialects spoken by the Angami people.
Typology: SOV; numerals after head nouns; postpositions; tonal.
Language_Contact: Also use Assamese [asm]. Also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin]. Also use Nagamese [nag].
Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Chokri Naga [nri], Khezha Naga [nkh], Sumi Naga [nsm].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L1: 86% (2001 census). Literacy rate in L2: 86% (2001 census). Most youth read Angami. Literacy among older people is lower.
Education: Taught as subject in primary schools.

Alternate_Names: Ao, Aorr, Cholimi, Hatigoria, Nowgong, Paimi, Uri
Location: Assam state; Nagaland state: central Mokokchung district.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Central Naga
Dialect_Names: Mongsen Khari, Changki, Chongli (Chungli), Dordar (Yacham), Longla
Relationships: Chongli and Mongsen border on mutual unintelligibility (Burling 2003).
Language_Contact: Also use Assamese [asm]. Also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin].
Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Chang Naga [nbc], Sangtam Naga [nsa], Sumi Naga [nsm].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L1: 86% (2001 census). Literacy rate in L2: 86% (2001 census).

Alternate_Names: Chang, Changyanguh, Machongrr, Mochumi, Mojung, Tśang
Location: Assam state; Nagaland state: Tuensang district, 36 villages.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Sal, Boro-Garo, Northern Naga
Relationships: Reportedly similar to Wancho Naga [nnp]. Tuensang village dialect is central and intelligible to all.
Language_Contact: Also use Ao Naga [njo]. Also use Assamese [asm]. Also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin]. Also use Nagamese [nag].

Location: Nagaland state: Mon district, 10 villages, along Myanmar border.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Sal, Boro-Garo, Northern Naga
Relationships: The 2 dialects are closely related. Kayu is reportedly similar to the Chuyo and Gakat dialects of Tase Naga [nst].
Typology: SOV; tonal.
Language_Use: Vigorous. Used by all.
Language_Contact: Many also use Konyak Naga [nbe].

Alternate_Names: Chakhesang, Chakhesang Chokri, Chakrima Naga, Chakru, Chokri, Chokri Chakhesang, Eastern Angami
Location: Nagaland state: Phek district, Cheswezumi is main village; Manipur state: some in Senapati district.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Angami-Pochuri
Language_Contact: Also use Angami Naga [njm]. Also use English [eng].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: Greater than 40% (2001 census).
General_Remarks: An eastern Angami tribe with its own language. Chokri, Khezha [nkh], and Sangtam-Pochuri [nsa] make up the Chakhesang Naga community (see separate entries).

Location: Manipur state: Bishnupur district, Lamlang Hupi village; Chandel district, 15 villages; Nagaland state: near Myanmar border.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Kuki-Chin, Northwestern
Relationships: Reportedly most similar to Tarao Naga [tro]. Reported intelligibility of Aimol [aim]. Lexical similarity: less than 60% with any neighboring languages.
Language_Use: Purest Chothe spoken in Purum Khullen. Home, village, religion. Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Meitei [mni].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 90% in Meitei [mni] (Bengali script) (2000).

Alternate_Names: Kabui, Kabui Naga, Kapwi, Koboi, Kubai
Location: Assam state; Manipur state: Imphal, Senapati, and Tamenglong Imphal districts, 16 villages; Nagaland state: Dimapur, Mahei Namchi, New Zaluke, and Peren.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Unclassified
Relationships: Considered by some to be the same language as Puimei Naga [npu]. Lexical similarity: 68% with Puimei Naga [npu].
Language_Use: Home, religion. Used by all. Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Most also use Meitei [mni]. Some also use English [eng]. Also use Rongmei Naga [nbu].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 70% in English [eng] and in Meitei [mni] (Bengali script) (2000). Literacy high among young people in Meitei and English.

Location: Manipur state: Senapati district, Kharam Pallen, Laikot, Phaijol, and Thuisenpai villages.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Kuki-Chin, Northwestern
Relationships: Lexical similarity: 71%–73% with Purum [pub], 58%–60% with Kom [kmm], 64% with Koireng [nkd].
Language_Use: Used by all.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Meitei [mni]. Also use Purum [pub].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 30% in Meitei [mni], in English [eng], or in Hindi [hin]. Most 5- to 20-year-olds have learned to read in school. Older people would like to learn to read.

Alternate_Names: Kezami, Khezha, Khezhama, Kozale, Kuzale, Közhale
Location: Nagaland state: Khezhakhonoma, Kohima, and Phek districts.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Angami-Pochuri
Relationships: An east Angami group with its own language.
Language_Contact: Also use Angami Naga [njm]. Also use English [eng].
General_Remarks: Belong to Chakhesang Naga community.

Alternate_Names: Aoshedd, Kalyokengnyu, Khiamngan, Khiemnungan, Nokaw, Tukhemmi, Welam
Location: Nagaland state: east central Tuensang district.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Sal, Boro-Garo, Northern Naga
Relationships: Dialects in Myanmar and India somewhat intelligible but have very limited contact. Lexical similarity: 67% with Gongwang dialect of Ponyo-Gongwang Naga [npg], 72%–73% with Ponyo dialect of [npg], 62%–67% with Lainong Naga [lzn], 41% with Lao Naga. Is in Konyak subgroup, but is divergent. They consider Ponyo Naga [npg] a part of Khiamniungan, though lexical similarity is only around 70%.
Typology: SOV.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L1: 30%.
General_Remarks: Main clans are Lam, Thai, Shiu, and Maya.

Alternate_Names: Khoibu, Khoibu Maring, Khoibu Maring Naga
Location: Manipur state: Chandel district mountainous regions, Khoibu, Narum, Saibol, and Yangkhul villages; Laiching.

Language_Contact: Also use English [eng].

Dialect_Names: Angphang, Hopao, Changnyu, Chen, Chingkao, Chinglang, Choha, Gelekidoria, Jakphang, Longching, Longkhai (Lungkhai, Lungkhi), Longmein, Longwa, Mon, Mulung, Ngangching, Sang, Shanlang, Shunyuo, Shengha, Sima, Sowa, Shamnyuyanga, Tableng (Angwangku, Kongon, Mohung, Wakching), Tabu, Tamkhungnyuo, Tang, Tobunyuo, Tolamleinyua, Totok

Literacy: Literacy rate in L1: 40% (2001 census). Literacy rate in L2: 40% (2001 census).

Location: Manipur state: Kangpokpi, Senapati, and Tamenglong districts, centered in Tamei sub-district, 45 villages; Nagaland state: Peren district, Tening sub-district, 6 villages.

Alternate_Names: Chizima, Choimi, Hlota, Lhota, Lotha, Lutha, Miklai, Tsindir, Tsontsii

Location: Assam state; Manipur state: Imphal district; Senapati district, 26 villages near Maram, 5 villages near Senapati.

Education: Taught as subject in primary and secondary schools.
General_Remarks: A Scheduled Tribe.

Location: Manipur state: Chandel district north border mountainous region, Tengnoupal sub-district; southeast, Laiching.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Tangkhulic
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng].

Location: Manipur state: Chandel district, Chandel sub-district, Heibunglok, Japhou, Liwa Sarei, Liwchangning, and Monsang Pantha villages; Nagaland state: near Myanmar border.

Location: Manipur state: Chandel district, 14 villages including Heigru Tampak, Khongjom, Komlathabi, Mitong, Moyon Khullen, Penaching; Nagaland state: near Myanmar border.

Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Western Naga
Relationships: Different from Zeme Naga [nzm].
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng].
General_Remarks: Adopted the designation Northern Zeme because Zeme has government recognition while Mzieme does not.

Alternate_Names: Borduria, Jaipuria, Mohongia, Namsangia, Nocte, Nokte, Paniduria

Language_Use: Home, village, religion. Used by all.

Location: Nagaland state: Kohima district, north Rengma.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Angami-Pochuri
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng].

Alternate_Names: Paola, Paumei, Pomai, Pome, Poumai, Poumei, Poumei Naga

Location: Assam and Manipur states.

General_Remarks: Were assigned as part of Rongmei Naga [nbu].

Location: Assam state: Cachar district. 35 villages; Manipur and Nagaland states.

General_Remarks: Merged ethnically with Zeme [nme] and Liangmai [njn] Naga to form the Zeliangrong community. Liangmai and Zeme are referred to collectively as Zeliang.

Location: Nagaland state: Tuensang district, Kiphire sub-district, Chare circle.

Dialect_Names: Kizare, Pirr (Northern Sangtam), Phelongre, Thukumi (Central Sangtam), Photsimi, Purr (Southern Sangtam)
Relationships: Standard based on Tsadanger village dialect. Kizare north of Meluri, and not known how much it differs from other Sangtam.
Language_Contact: Also use Ao Naga [njo]. Also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin]. Also use Nagamese [nag].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 40% (2001 census).
General_Remarks: Chokri, Khezha, and a small section of Sangtam make up the Chakhesang Naga community.

Alternate_Names: Injang, Moiyui, Mon, Mozhumi, Nzong, Nzonyu, Rengma, Rengma Naga, Southern Rengma, Unza, Western Rengma
Location: Assam state: Karbi-Anglong district, 15 villages; Manipur state; Nagaland state: Kohima district, Tseminyu sub-district.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Angami-Pochuri
Relationships: Tseminyu principal dialect main center. Southern Rengma and Northern Rengma [nnl] are reportedly inherently unintelligible.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Nagamese [nag].
Literacy: Literacy in Rengma is higher among older people. Young people are learning English.

Location: Assam state: Tinsukia district, 7 villages. Nagaland state: Kohima, Mokokchung, Tuensang, and Zunheboto districts. Dayang is near Dayang river.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Angami-Pochuri
Language_Contact: Also use Angami Naga [njm]. Also use Ao Naga [njo]. Also use Assamese [asm]. Also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin]. Also use Lotha Naga [njh]. Also use Nagamese [nag].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 50% in Assamese [asm], English [eng].

Language_Contact: Also use English [eng].

Alternate_Names: Rangpan, Tangsa, Tangsa Naga, Tangshang, Tase, Tase Naga, Tasey
L1_Full: 38,600 in India (2011 census). Includes 10,200 Tutsa (2011 census).
Location: Arunachal Pradesh state: Changlang district, Manmau, Jayrampur, Nampong, and Kharsang circles; Assam state: border area with Changlang district, 25 villages.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Sal, Boro-Garo, Northern Naga
Dialect_Names: Lungri (Longri), Shecyü (Sangche, Sangkhe, Sanke, Sankey, Sechu, Shangge, Shangkey, Shechu), Sangwal (Shangvan, Shangwan, Shängvan), Tikhak, Tonglim (Cholim, Cyawlim, Tangrim, Tonglum), Tupsa (Tutcha, Tutsa), Joglei (Jogly, Jugli, Yogli, Yukli), Yongkuk (Yongkok, Yukok), Havi (Have, Havoy, Hawi, Hawoi, Muklom), Kimsing (Cham Chang, Chamchang, Cyamcyang, Cyämcyäng, Khemsing), Lungkhe (Longkhi, Longphi), Lungchang (Longchang, Longcyang), Miti (Maitai, Maixtaix), Muklum (Moklum), Mueshaungx (Hewa, Mosang, Mossang, Mueshaung, Müxshawngx), Mungre (Morang, Mungray), Ngemu (Ngaimong, Nyemu), Phong (Nukta, Ponthai), Rera (Poerah, Rongrang, Ronrang), Hasik (Awla, Awlay, Laju, Lazu Naga, Ollo Naga), Hakhun (Haqkhun), Champang (Cyämpäng, Thampang), Haqcheng (Haqcyeng, Haqtseng), Haqchum (Haqcyum), Lama, Lochang (Loxchangx), Nocte (Nokte), Kato, Lajo (Layaw), Wancho (Väncyaw)
Relationships: Phong (Ponthai) dialect is similar to both Nocte [njb] and Tangsa. Higsho dialect is similar to Nocte. Those living closer to the Nocte identify as Nocte; those living closer to the Tangsa identify as Tangsa. May be up to 36 subtribes of Tangsa. Kimsing dialect speakers can understand all dialects well. Kimsing is similar to Tutsa. Kimsing has most speakers and is most influential.
Typology: SOV; postpositions; genitives, articles before noun heads; numerals, adjectives after head nouns; question word final; word order distinguishes subject, object, and indirect object; person agreement is marked on verbs in many but not all varieties; ergative-absolutive marked, particles indicate case after the noun; passives; tonal.
Language_Use: Vigorous in remote areas, shifting to Assamese [asm] and Hindi [hin] in town areas (2017 S. Morey). All domains in remote areas. Some of all ages. Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Also use Assamese [asm], especially in town areas. Also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin], especially in town areas. Also use Singpho [sgp].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 56% (2001 census).
General_Remarks: ‘Tangsa’, hill people.

Location: Manipur state: Chandel district, Palel sub-district, Heikakpokpi, Khuringmul Laiminei, and Leishokching villages; Ukhrul district, Sinakeithei village.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Kuki-Chin, Northwestern
Relationships: Reportedly most similar to Chothe Naga [nct], 70% intelligibility. Lexical similarity: less than 60% with any neighboring language; 43%–46% with Chothe Naga [nct].
Typology: Postpositions; genitives, articles, adjectives, numerals, relatives before noun heads; maximum affixes 2; word order distinguishes subjects, objects, and indirect objects; noun affix marks case; verb affixes mark number; no passive; causatives and comparatives; CVC.
Language_Use: Home, religion. Used by all. Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Meitei [mni].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 75% in Meitei [mni], English [eng]. Literacy program in progress. Older people can read Meitei in Bengali script. Young people prefer Latin script. Most villages have primary and junior schools; attendance is irregular.
General_Remarks: Not recognized as a separate Scheduled Tribe by the government due to its small size.

Alternate_Names: Khoirao, Khoirao Naga, Koirao, Kolya, Mayangkhang, Miyang-Khang, Ngari, Thangal, Thanggal, Tukaimi
Location: Manipur state: Senapati district, East and West Sadar hills sub-districts, Gailongde, Makeng Thangal, Mapao Thangal, Mayangkhang, Ningthoubam, Thangal Surung, Tikhulen, Tumnoupokpi, and Yaikangpou. Most are east of Barak valley.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Western Naga
Relationships: Reportedly similar to Maram Naga [nma].
Typology: Postpositions; genitives, relatives before noun head; articles, adjectives, numerals after noun head; question word initial; case marked by postpositional clitics; comparatives; CV, CVC, CVV, VC, V syllables; nontonal.
Language_Use: Used by all.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Meitei [mni].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 90% in Meitei [mni], English [eng].
General_Remarks: A Scheduled Tribe.

Location: Arunachal Pradesh state: south Changlang and east Tirap districts; Assam state: Tinsukia district.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Sal, Boro-Garo, Northern Naga
Relationships: Reportedly similar to Nocte Naga [njb] and Tase Naga [nst].
Typology: SOV; postpositions; genitives and articles before noun heads; adjectives and numerals after noun heads; maximum affixes 2; affixes indicate case of noun phrase; ergativity; CV, CVC, VC; may be tonal but it does not carry much functional load.
Language_Use: Home, village. Used by all.
Language_Contact: Also use Assamese [asm]. Also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 5%. Very few with higher education.
General_Remarks: Consider themselves separate from Nocte [njb] and Tase Naga [nst].

Alternate_Names: Banpara Naga, Joboka, Jokoba, Naga Wancho, Wancho, Wanchu
Location: Arunachal Pradesh state: southwest Tirap district, 36 villages; Assam and Nagaland states.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Sal, Boro-Garo, Northern Naga
Dialect_Names: Changnoi, Bor Muthun (Bor Mutonia), Horu Muthun, Kulung Muthun (Mithan)
Relationships: Significant variation between spoken language in upper and lower regions. Reportedly similar to Chang Naga [nbc] and Konyak Naga [nbe].
Language_Contact: Also use Assamese [asm]. Also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 25% (2001 census).
Scripts: Devanagari script [Deva]. Latin script [Latn]. Wancho script [Wcho].

L1_Full: 83,300 (2011 census). Includes 12,300 Chirr and 11,100 Tikhir (2011 census).
Location: Nagaland state: Tuensang district, between Namchik and Patkoi.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Central Naga
Dialect_Names: Tikhir, Wai, Chirr, Minir, Pherrongre, Yimchungru
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin]. Also use Nagamese [nag].

Location: Assam state: North Cachar district, upper Barak valley; Manipur state: Tamenglong district; Nagaland state: Kohima district, Jhaluke, Medzephima, and Paren sub-districts.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Western Naga
Language_Use: Used strongly for oral communication but not much in written form. Home, village, church. Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 59% in Manipur (2001 census).
General_Remarks: Merged ethnically with Liangmai [njn] and Rongmei [nbu] Naga to form the Zeliangrong community. Liangmai and Zeme are referred to collectively as Zeliang.

Alternate_Names: Bodo, Kachari Bengali, Naga Creole Assamese, Naga Pidgin, Naga-Assamese, Nagamese Creole
Location: Nagaland state: Kohima district, Dimapur sub-district; Arunachal Pradesh state border area.
LWC_Support: Naga tribes came from China through Burma by late 14th century. Developed by mid 16th century. In 1826, lingua franca of Naga Hills, widely used in almost all domains by majority of population.
Classification: Creole, Assamese based
Relationships: A variety least similar to Assamese [asm] is spoken by the Yimchenger Naga, and varieties most similar to Assamese by the Angami Naga, and around Dimapur and Kohima.
Typology: SOV; no gender; case marking (7 cases); 2 tenses, 3 aspects; 21 consonants and 6 vowels; non-tonal.
Language_Use: L1 for the Kachari in Dimapur area, a small community, and among children of interethnic marriages. Mixed attitudes, viewed by some as a threat to the indigenous languages (Longkumer 2016).
Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Angami Naga [njm], Chang Naga [nbc], Dimasa [dis], Konyak Naga [nbe], Lotha Naga [njh], Monsang Naga [nmh], Phom Naga [nph], Pochuri Naga [npo], Sakachep [sch], Sangtam Naga [nsa], Southern Rengma Naga [nre], Sumi Naga [nsm], Yimchungru Naga [yim].
Literature: Newspapers. Radio. Videos. Dictionary. Grammar. NT: 2018.

L1_Full: No known L1 speakers. The last speaker either died or shifted to Hindi [hin] or Northern Gondi [gno] by 1981 (Ishtiaq 1999).
Location: Madhya Pradesh state: Balaghat, Chhindwara, Mandla, and Seoni districts.
Classification: Dravidian, South-Central, Gondi-Kui, Gondi
Language_Contact: Many shifted to Hindi [hin]. Many shifted to Northern Gondi [gno].
General_Remarks: Nagarchi is a people group living in Seoni, Jabalpur, and Mandla districts of Madhya Pradesh who speak Hindi [hin] (Singh 1998a).

Location: Madhya Pradesh state: Barwani district; Maharashtra state: Dhule district; Jalgaon district, Chopda sub-district, north of Amalwadi; Nandurbar district, Dhadgaon sub-district, 12 villages near Toranmal.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Intermediate Divisions, Western, Bhil
Relationships: 96% intelligibility of Bareli Pauri [bfb]. This may be acquired rather than inherent (1988 S. Watters). Lexical similarity: 58%–68% with Noiri [noi] varieties, 60%–61% with Dungra Bhil [duh], 69%–73% with Bareli Pauri [bfb].
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng].
General_Remarks: Reported to speak Nimadi [noe] as L1 (Singh 1994b). Nihali [nll] and Nahali are different languages.

Location: Chhattisgarh state: Raipur, Bilaspur districts; Odisha state: Sambalpur district.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Outer Languages, Eastern, Bengali-Assamese
Relationships: A more divergent variety, related to Halbi [hlb].
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng].

L1_Full: Population unknown. May be replaced by Hindi [hin] (2006 Y. Modi).
Location: Arunachal Pradesh state.

Language_Use: Formerly a lingua franca of Arunachal Pradesh.
Language_Contact: Shifted to Hindi [hin].
Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Apatani [apt], Bugun [bgg], Zakhring [zkr].

Alternate_Names: Eastern Pahari, Gorkhali, Gurkhali, Khaskura, Nepalese, Parbatiya
Location: Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Bihar, Haryana, Himachal Pradesh, Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland, Sikkim, Tripura, Uttar Pradesh, and Uttarakhand states; West Bengal state: Darjeeling area.
Official_Recognition: Statutory provincial language in Sikkim, West Bengal state (1950, Constitution, Schedule VIII), amended 1992.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Intermediate Divisions, Eastern, Eastern Pahari
Relationships: Nepali as spoken in northern India is a creolized form with a greatly simplified grammar and many loanwords from both English [eng] and Hindi [hin] as well as a few loan words from some Sino-Tibetan languages. Speakers of standardized Nepali report intelligibility of the creolized form at 80%–90%. Speakers of the creolized Nepali who do not have access to the standardized form through formal education report very low intelligibility of the standardized form (30%–50%) (2023 R. Glustrom).
Typology: SOV; postpositions; noun head final; 11 noun classes or genders; no articles; content q-word in situ; 1 prefix, up to 5 suffixes; clause constituents indicated by case-marking (4 cases); verbal affixation marks person, number and gender of subject; split ergativity; both tense and aspect; passives and voice; causatives; non-tonal; 29 consonant and 11 vowel phonemes.
Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Adi [adi], Bantawa [bap], Byangsi [bee], Chaudangsi [cdn], Darmiya [drd], Eastern Magar [mgp], Gurung [gvr], Koch [kdq], Kullu Pahari [kfx], Lepcha [lep], Limbu [lif], Maithili [mai], Majhi [mjz], Miju-Mishmi [mxj], Sherpa [xsr], Sikkimese [sip], Thado Chin [tcz], Toto [txo], Yakkha [ybh].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L1: 30%–100%. Literacy rate in L2: 25%–75%.
Education: Taught in primary and secondary schools through grade 5 and as subject thereafter in Sikkim and West Bengal state.
Scripts: Braille script [Brai]. Devanagari script [Deva], primary usage.

Autonym: नेपाल भाषा‎ (Nepal Bhasa), नेवाः भाय्‎ (Newah Bhay)
Alternate_Names: Nevarí, Newa Bhaye, Newaah Bhaae, Pahri, “Nēwāri” (pej.), “Newari” (pej.)
Location: Bihar state: some in Bettiah; Sikkim and West Bengal states.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Western Tibeto-Burman, Himalayan, Central Himalayan, Newar
Typology: SOV; postpositions; genitives, adjectives, demonstratives before noun heads; noun heads final; 4 noun classes: animate, inanimate, common, honored (some varieties); numeral classifiers; content q-word in situ; relatives before and without noun heads; in polar questions there is a particle sentence finally; 1–3 prefixes (depends on dialect), up to 3 suffixes; clause constituents indicated by case-marking; verbal affixation marks person and number (in Dolakha, Tauthali, and Badikhel dialects) or is based on complex evidential patterns involving agency and intention (Kathmandu Valley varieties); affixes or clitics indicate case of noun phrases; ergative; causatives; comparatives; tense and aspect; no passives or voice; V, VC, CV, CVC, CCV, CCVC; non-tonal; breathy voice (some varieties); 28 consonant and 6 vowel phonemes (Kathmandu variety).
Language_Use: Some young people, all adults.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng].
Literature: Literature. Newspapers. Periodicals. Radio. TV. Videos. Dictionary. Grammar. Texts. Bible: 2015.
Scripts: Devanagari script [Deva], primary usage. Newa script [Newa], in common use during the Malla period and earlier, recent efforts to revive usage. Ranjana (Lantsa, Wartu) script [Ranj].

Location: Andaman and Nicobar Islands state: North Nicobar Islands, Car island.
LWC_Support: Originated in Myanmar (Burma); became dominant under Great Britain rule in the second half of the 19th century. Spoken by majority of population in Nicobar Islands. Used in agriculture, church, school, oral literature, music, dance, and local economy.
Classification: Austro-Asiatic, Mon-Khmer, Nicobar, Car
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 46% for Scheduled Tribes in Nicobar District. 72% for Nicobar (2001 census).

L1_Full: 10,100 (2001 census). 5,310 on Katchal, 3,410 on Kamorta, 930 on Nancowry, 430 on Trinket.
Location: Andaman and Nicobar Islands state: Camorta, Katchal, Nancowry, Nicobar Islands, Trinket islands.
Classification: Austro-Asiatic, Mon-Khmer, Nicobar, Nancowry
Dialect_Names: Camorta (Kamorta), Katchal (Kachel, Tehnu), Nancowry (Nancoury), Trinket (Trinkat, Trinkut)
Relationships: Central Nicobar once regarded as one language but no longer generally accepted. Dialects now regarded as mutually unintelligible with the exception of Trinket and Katchal (Parkin 1991).
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 46% for Scheduled Tribes in Nicobar District. 72% for Nicobar (2001 census).

L1_Full: 7,500 (2001 census). 350 on Little Nicobar Island, 7,570 total on Great Nicobar, about 400 of these are Shom Peng [sii].
Location: Andaman and Nicobar Islands state: Little Nicobar and outer Great Nicobar islands.
Classification: Austro-Asiatic, Mon-Khmer, Nicobar, Great Nicobar
Dialect_Names: Condul (Kondul), Great Nicobar, Little Nicobar, Milo
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 46% for Scheduled Tribes in Nicobar District. 72% for Nicobar (2001 census).

Location: Madhya Pradesh state: Burhanpur; Maharashtra state: Buldana district, Jamod Jalgaon sub-district.
Classification: Language isolate
Relationships: Lexical similarity: 25% between Nihal in Chikaldara taluk and Akola District and Korku [kfq] (Munda).
Language_Use: Some young people, all adults.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin]. Also use Korku [kfq]. Also use Marathi [mar].
General_Remarks: They live in or near Korku [kfq] villages in a position of subordination to the Korku people. Possibly belonged to a now extinct speech family of India. Influenced significantly by Munda and Dravidian languages. 60%–70% of vocabulary borrowed. Nihali and Nahali [nlx] are different languages.

Location: Madhya Pradesh state: Barwani, south Dhar, Khandwa, and Khargone districts; Maharashtra and Uttar Pradesh states.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Intermediate Divisions, Western, Rajasthani, Unclassified
Relationships: Dialects have 90%–100% mutual inherent intelligibility. Lexical similarity: 74%–94% among dialects, 64%–75% with Malvi [mup], 62%–77% with Hindi [hin], 56%–64% with Gujarati [guj], 49%–58% with Marathi [mar].
Language_Use: Vigorous. All domains, except with government officials. Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin], in education, but generally with low proficiency.
Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Palya Bareli [bpx], Pauri Bareli [bfb], Rathwi Bareli [bgd].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 40%.

Location: Madhya Pradesh state: Badwani district, Pansemal sub-district; Maharashtra state: Dhule district, Shirpur sub-district; Jalgaon district, Chopda sub-district; Nandurbar district, Akkalkua, Dhadgaon, and Shahada sub-districts.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Intermediate Divisions, Western, Bhil
Relationships: Barutiya people have high acquired intelligibility of Vasavi [vas] and Bareli Pauri [bfb] and Dungra Bhili [duh]. Lexical similarity: 77%–87% with Dungra Bhili [duh], 60%–71% with different Vasavi [vas] varieties, 58%–68% with Nahali [nlx] of Toranmal, 47%–54% with the Kotali dialect of Bhili [bhb]; the Barutiya dialect of Noiri, 64%–70% with Bareli Pauri [bfb]. Noiri-Barutiya variety falls between Vasavi and Bareli Pauri on a dialect continuum.
Language_Use: Vigorous. Home, village. Positive attitudes. Positive attitudes to the west. Less positive to the east.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin]. Also use Marathi [mar].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 1% in Marathi [mar].
General_Remarks: A Scheduled Tribe in Maharashtra and Madhya Pradesh. A Bhil subgroup. ‘Noira’ means ‘people who speak through the nose’.

L1_Full: No known L1 speakers. Had 300 speakers at beginning of 20th century, but extinct by end of century.
Location: Arunachal Pradesh state: northeast, near Tibet.
Classification: Kra-Dai
Typology: SOV.

Alternate_Names: Bangni, Dafla, Daphla, Lel, Nil, Nishi, Nisi, Nissi, Nyising
L1_Full: 299,000 (2011 census). 23,000 speakers of Bangni dialect (Van Driem 2007).
Location: Arunachal Pradesh state: lower Subansiri district.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Central Tibeto-Burman, Tani
Relationships: Reportedly similar to Tagin [tgj]. Apatani [apt] may be a dialect.
Language_Use: All domains.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Miji [sjl].
Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Miji [sjl], Puroik [suv].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 37%—46% (2001 census).
General_Remarks: Nisi is a Scheduled Tribe. Nisi has been used as a cover term for western Tani languages.

Location: Scattered, in Gujarat, Haryana, New Delhi, Punjab, Rajasthan and other states.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Unclassified
Relationships: Resembles Marathi [mar] with Gujarati [guj] features and borrowings from Marwari [mve] and Punjabi.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin].

Alternate_Names: Odisha, Odri, Odrum, Oliya, Oriya, Uriya, Utkali, Vadiya, Yudhia
Location: Andhra Pradesh state: Vishakhapatnam district; Chhattisgarh state: Bastar, Raigarh, and Raipur districts; Jharkhand state: Ranchi and Singhbhum districts; West Bengal state: Medinipur (Midnapore) district; Assam and Odisha states.
Official_Recognition: Statutory provincial language in Odisha State (1950, Constitution, Schedule VIII).
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Outer Languages, Eastern, Oriya
Dialect_Names: Mughalbandi (Odia Proper, Standard Odia), Ganjami (Southern Odia), Sundargadi (Northwestern Odia), North Balasore Odia, Midnapore Odia, Halbi
Relationships: Lexical similarity: 75%–76% with Sambalpuri [spv], 68% with Kamar [keq].
Typology: SOV; postpositions; gender (masculine/feminine); no articles; case-marking (7 cases); verb affixes mark person, number; passives; tense and aspect; 22 consonant and 11 vowel phonemes.
Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Bhatri [bgw], Birhor [biy], Bodo Gadaba [gbj], Chhattisgarhi [hne], Duruwa [pci], Eastern Muria [emu], Gata’ [gaq], Ho [hoc], Juang [jun], Juray [juy], Kharia [khr], Kharia Thar [ksy], Kisan [xis], Konda-Dora [kfc], Kudmali [kyw], Lodhi [lbm], Mahali [mjx], Mirgan [zrg], Pengo [peg], Sadri [sck].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L1: 64% (2001 census). Literacy rate in L2: 64% (2001 census).
Education: Taught in primary and secondary schools through grade 5 and as subject thereafter in Odisha state.
Scripts: Braille script [Brai]. Oriya (Odia) script [Orya], primary usage.
General_Remarks: A Classical Language of India since 2014.

L1_Full: No known L1 speakers. The last speaker died in 1931 (Van Driem 2001).
Location: Andaman and Nicobar Islands, west central and southwest interior Middle Andaman island.
Classification: Andamanese, Great Andamanese, Central

Location: Andaman and Nicobar Islands: Little Andaman island, Dugong Creek and South Bay.
Classification: Andamanese, South Andamanese
Relationships: Reportedly distinct from Sentinel [std].
Language_Use: Some young people, all adults.
General_Remarks: Reserved toward outsiders.

Alternate_Names: Adivasi, Adiwasi Oriya, Desiya, Kotia, Kotia Oriya, Kotiya, Tribal Oriya
Location: Andhra Pradesh state: Vishakhapatnam district, Araku valley; Odisha state.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Outer Languages, Eastern, Oriya
Relationships: Lexical similarity: 38%–42% with standard Odia [ory], 80%–85% with Desiya [dso] in Odisha.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng].
Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Bodo Parja [bdv], Bondo [bfw], Mukha-Dora [mmk], Parenga [pcj].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L1: 7%. Literacy rate in L2: 34% for Scheduled Tribes in Vishakhapatnam District (2001 census).

Alternate_Names: Kauli, Kullui, Kulu Boli, Kulu Pahari, Kului, Kulvi, Kulwali, Pahari, Pahari Kullu, Phari Kulu
Location: Himachal Pradesh state: Kullu district, Balichowk, Banjar, and Sainj sub-districts.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Intermediate Divisions, Western, Pahari, Western Pahari
Dialect_Names: Inner Siragi (Inner Seraji, Saraji, Siragi, Siraji), Kullui, Outer Seraji
Relationships: Inner Siragi is apparently different from the Siraji-Kashmiri dialect of Kashmiri [kas]. Lexical similarity: 85% or higher among dialects.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin]. Also use Nepali [npi]. Also use Tinani [lbf]. Also use Urdu [urd].
Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Gujari [gju].
Scripts: Devanagari script [Deva]. Takri (Tankri, Takari) script [Takr], no longer in use.

Location: Himachal Pradesh state: Shimla and Solan districts.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Intermediate Divisions, Western, Pahari, Western Pahari
Dialect_Names: Lower Mahasu Pahari (Baghati, Baghliani, Kiunthali), Upper Mahasu Pahari (Barari, Bishshau, Rampuri, Rohruri, Shadochi, Sharachali, Shimla Siraji)
Relationships: The Kiunthali variety appears to be understood by others, and their attitude toward it is favorable. Rampuri is also called Bushahri. Intelligibility among dialects above 85%. Lexical similarity: 74%–82% with upper dialects, 74%–95% with lower dialects.
Typology: SOV; postpositions; genitives after noun heads; nontonal.
Language_Use: Home, religion. Used by all.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin], with more proficiency among educated people.
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 80% for Shimla District, 82% for Solan (2001 census).

Alternate_Names: Mirpur, Mirpur Panjabi, Mirpur Punjabi, Mirpuri
Location: Jammu and Kashmir state: Kupware district, near Pakistan border.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Intermediate Divisions, Western, Panjabi, Western Panjabi
Scripts: Arabic script, Naskh variant [Arab]. Arabic script, Nastaliq variant [Aran], primary usage.

L1_Full: No known L1 speakers in India.
Location: Scattered.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Unclassified
Language_Use: Classical and liturgical language of the Theravada Buddhist canon. Positive attitudes.
Scripts: Devanagari script [Deva]. Myanmar (Burmese) script [Mymr]. Sinhala script [Sinh]. Thai script [Thai].
General_Remarks: Pali was a revered standard and international language because the oral sayings of Buddha were recorded in it in the first century BCE, but it died out in mainland India as a literary language in the fourteenth century.

Alternate_Names: Makkal, Malai Paliyar, Palani, Palaya, Palayan, Paliyar, Palleyan, Palliyar, Poliyar, Seramar, Tamil
Location: Karnataka state; Kerala state: Idukki district, Pirmed sub-district, Chakkupallam, Kumily, and Vandanmedu areas; Ernakulam and Kottayam districts; Tamil Nadu state: Coimbatore, Dindigul, Madurai, Pudukkottai, Ramanathapuram, Thanjavur, and Tirunelveli districts.
Classification: Dravidian, Southern, Tamil-Kannada, Tamil-Kodagu, Tamil-Malayalam, Malayalam
Relationships: Lexical similarity: 71%–75% with Tamil [tam], 62%–65% with Malayalam [mal], 79%–85% with Mala Pulayan [pcf].
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Malayalam [mal]. Also use Tamil [tam], with high proficiency.
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 44%–62% in Kerala, 50% for Hill Pulaya (2001 census).
General_Remarks: Paliya and Mala Pulaya refer to L1 as Tamil [tam], though it differs from standard Tamil.

Alternate_Names: Bedia, Bediya, Chik Baraik, Chik Barik, Pan, Pan Sawasi, Tair, Tamara, Tamaria, Tanti, Temoral, Tumariya
Location: Assam state: upper tea gardens; Jharkhand state: Ranchi and Singhbhum districts; Odisha and West Bengal states.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Outer Languages, Eastern, Bihari
Relationships: Sonahatu variety considered most pure. Lexical similarity: 77%–94% between dialects, 61%–86% with Kudmali, 68%–76% with Magahi (Khortha) [mag], 61%–70% with Sadri [sck], 48%–52% with Odia [ory], 45%–58% with Bengali [ben], 50%–60% with Hindi [hin].
Language_Use: Vigorous. Home, village, market, religion. Used by all. Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Also use Bengali [ben]. Also use Hindi [hin].
Scripts: Bengali (Bangla) script [Beng], no longer in use. Devanagari script [Deva]. Kaithi script [Kthi], no longer in use.
General_Remarks: Panchpargania means ‘5 districts’, namely Silli, Bundu, Rahe, Baranda, and Tamar parganas of Ranchi (Singh 1995b).

Location: Himachal Pradesh state: Chamba district, Pangi sub-district; Lahaul Spiti district, Udaipur on Chenab river to Chamba border at Purthi, possibly from Tandi to Sach Pass; Jammu and Kashmir state: Doda district.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Intermediate Divisions, Western, Pahari, Western Pahari
Relationships: 64% inherent intelligibility of Mandeali [mjl], 52% of Kangri [xnr], 44% of Chambeali [cdh], 50% of Bhadrawahi [bhd]; some dialect variation throughout the valley in Chamba District; Purthi reportedly most divergent. Lexical similarity: 55% with Hindi [hin], 77% with Kullu Pahari [kfx]; 45% with Bhadrawahi [bhd].
Language_Use: Vigorous. Home, village, religion. Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: A few also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 9% men, 1% women. In 1981, 9% of the men had a 5th grade education, 1% of the women; 3% of the men had an 8th grade education, fewer than 1% of the women.

Location: Karnataka state: Kodagu district; Kerala state: Kannur, Kozhikode, Malappuram, and Wayanad districts; Tamil Nadu state: west of Nilgiris hills.
Classification: Dravidian, Southern, Tamil-Kannada, Tamil-Kodagu, Tamil-Malayalam, Malayalam
Relationships: Intelligibility of Malappura Paniya by Kodava [kfa] is 66%. Lexical similarity: 79%–88% between dialects and Malappuram Paniya, 71% with Kodaku [ksz] and Kodava [kfa].
Language_Use: Home, religion.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Kannada [kan]. Also use Malayalam [mal]. Also use Tamil [tam].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 41% for Kerala, 26% for Tamil Nadu (2001 census).
Scripts: Kannada script [Knda], used in Karnataka. Malayalam script [Mlym], used in Kerala. Tamil script [Taml], used in Tamil Nadu.

Alternate_Names: Paang, Pang, Pang Khua, Pangkhu, Pankho, Pankhua, Panko, Pankua
Location: Mizoram state: Chhimtuipui and Lunglei districts, 12 villages.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Kuki-Chin, Central
Language_Contact: Also use Bawm Chin [bgr]. Also use Mizo [lus].
General_Remarks: Scheduled Tribe. A subgroup of the Mizo [lus].

Location: Andhra Pradesh state; Chhattisgarh state: Bilaspur, Raipur, and Surguja districts; Madhya Pradesh state: Balaghat, Betul, Chhindwara, Hoshangabad, Jabalpur, Mandla, and Seoni districts; Maharashtra state: Bhandara, Garhchiroli, Nagpur, Wardha, and Yavatmal districts; Telangana state: possibly in Adilbad district.
Classification: Dravidian, South-Central, Gondi-Kui, Gondi
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin], in Madhya Pradesh. Also use Marathi [mar], in Maharashtra.
General_Remarks: L1 is Gondi [gon] (Singh 1994b).

Alternate_Names: Bahelia, Chita Pardhi, Lango Pardhi, Paidia, Paradhi, Paradi, Paria, Phans Pardhi, Takankar, Takia
Location: Karnataka state: Belgaum and Bijapur districts, small border areas; Maharashtra state: Kolhapur, Sangli, Satara, and Solapur districts; Gujarat and Madhya Pradesh states: widely scattered.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Intermediate Divisions, Western, Bhil
Dialect_Names: Neelishikari, Pittala Bhasha, Takari, Haran Shikari
Relationships: Probably more than 1 language (Lango). Possibly a dialect of Bhili [bhb].
General_Remarks: A Scheduled Caste in Madhya Pradesh. Different than Paradhi, who speak Kacchi [kfr].

Alternate_Names: Gadaba, Gorum, Gorum Sama, Gorum-Parenga, Pareng, Parenga Parja, Parengi, Parenji, Poroja
Location: Odisha state: Mayurbhanj district.
Classification: Austro-Asiatic, Munda, South Munda, Koraput Munda, Sora-Juray-Gorum, Gorum
Language_Contact: Shifted to Adivasi Oriya [ort].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 17% (2001 census).
General_Remarks: Ethnonym: Gadaba, erroneously.

Location: Punjab state: Pathankot; Himachal Pradesh and Jammu and Kashmir states: where the 3 states meet in southwest Kashmir valley; Kupwara district, Changnar and Dhakki villages; Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, and Maharashtra states; New Delhi; Uttar Pradesh: Rampur district.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Iranian, Eastern, Southeastern, Pashto
Typology: SOV; noun head final; gender (masculine/feminine); no articles; case-marking (3 cases); verb affixes mark person, number, gender of subject; passives; tense and aspect; causatives.
Literature: Literature. Newspapers. Periodicals. Radio. TV. Videos. Dictionary. Grammar. Texts. Bible: 2019.
Scripts: Arabic script, Naskh variant [Arab], primary usage. Arabic script, Nastaliq variant [Aran].

Location: Kerala state: Wayanad district, Cheramkolli, Kazhambu, Mathamangalam, Thekkumpatta, and Thelampatta villages.
Classification: Dravidian, Southern
Relationships: It has been reported that they speak Malayalam [mal] mixed with Kannada [kan] words (Menon 1996:313; Shashi and Shri 1994, Vol. 11). Lexical similarity: 88% with Kalanadi [wkl], 83% with Kunduvadi [wku], 72% with Malayalam [mal], 79% with Paniya [pcg], 76%–80% with Mullu Kurumba [kpb], 70%–74% with Wayanad Kurichiya.
Language_Use: Continued vitality doubtful, due to small population, no separate settlements, living with Malayalis, and similarity to Malayalam [mal]. Home.
Language_Contact: Also use Malayalam [mal].
General_Remarks: Common cultural origin with Kunduvadiyar and Kalanadikal. Not related to the washerman caste of the same name in Travancore area. (Menon 1996).

Alternate_Names: Chamba, Chamba Lahuli, Changsapa Boli, Lahuli, Manchad, Manchati, Patni, Swangla
Location: Himachal Pradesh state: Chamba-Lahul, Lahul, Pattan, and lower Mayar valleys, some in Kullu and Manali cities; Jammu and Kashmir state: Kishtwar district.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Western Tibeto-Burman, Bodish, West Himalayish, Kinauri
Dialect_Names: Chamba-Lahuli (Western Pattani), Eastern Pattani, Central Pattani
Relationships: 3 caste dialects exist (Pandit-Rajput, Harijan and Lohar). The lower castes understand Pandit-Rajput, but not vice versa. Lexical similarity: 55%–63% between Western Pattani dialect and Tinani [lbf], 26%–39% with Bunan [bfu], 37% with Shumcho [scu], 35% with Jangshung [jna], 33% with Sunam [ssk], 31% with Chitkuli [cik] and Kinnauri [kfk], 25% with Puh and Kinnaur District varieties (Kinnaur Bhoti [nes]) of Tibetan, 22% with Chhoyul Kinnauri [tpq], 18% with Tibetan [bod], 14%–15% with the Spiti and Stod varieties of Tibetan. Average of 80% between dialects.
Language_Use: Home, village, religion. Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Some also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin], in education and trade. Half of the population speak it with good proficiency.
Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Tinani [lbf].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 50% for women (even young ones). Over 50% for men. Most young men under 30 can read (2002).
Scripts: Devanagari script [Deva]. Tibetan script [Tibt], no longer in use.

Location: Andhra Pradesh state: Guntur, Prakasam, and Sri Potti Sriramulu Nellore districts.
Classification: Dravidian, Unclassified
Relationships: Lexical similarity: 28% with Tamil [tam].
Language_Use: Home, workplace. Used by all.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng].

Location: Odisha state: Kalahandi district; Koraput district, Dasamantapur and Nandapur sub-districts; Nabarangapur district, Pappadahandi sub-district; Rayagada district, Kashipur sub-district.
Classification: Dravidian, South-Central, Gondi-Kui, Konda-Kui, Manda-Kui, Manda-Pengo
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Odia [ory].
General_Remarks: They consider themselves separate from Jhodia Poraja.

Alternate_Names: Faake, Fakial, Phakey, Phakial, Tai Phake
Location: Arunachal Pradesh state; Assam state: Dibrugarh district, Bor-phake, Man-long, Man-po-mung, Mung-lang, Nam-phake, Ning-gam, Nong-lai, Pha-neng, and Tipam-phake villages along Dihing river.
Classification: Kra-Dai, Kam-Tai, Tai, Southwestern
Relationships: Reportedly similar to Aiton [aio]. Similar to Shan [shn] of Myanmar. Lexical similarity: 48%–54% with Aiton [aio] and 48%–55% with Khamyang [ksu].
Language_Use: Used by all.
Language_Contact: Also use Assamese [asm]. Also use English [eng].

Location: Maharashtra state: Thane district.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Outer Languages, Southern, Konkani
Relationships: A more divergent dialect of, or closely related language to, Konkani [knn].

Location: Assam state: North Cachar hills, Borolokha, Dibruchera and Jatinga; Karbi Anglong district, Ulukunchi; Meghalaya state: Khasi and Jaintia hills north of War Jaintia; Mizoram state: north Aizawl district.
Classification: Austro-Asiatic, Mon-Khmer, Northern Mon-Khmer, Khasian
Relationships: Formerly considered a dialect of Khasi [kha]. Jaintia dialect has 12 spoken forms: Jowai, Shangpung, Batau, Raliang, Sutnga, Sumer, Nartiang, Barato, Rymbai, Lakadong, Mynso, and Nongtalang. All are intelligible, except for Nongtalang, which is akin to Khmer [khm]. Jowai is standard spoken form. Lexical similarity: 68% with standard Khasi.
Typology: Verb-initial.
Language_Contact: Also use Bengali [ben]. Also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin]. Also use Mizo [lus].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 62% for Synteng dialect in Meghalaya (2001 census).

L1_Full: No known L1 speakers in India.
Location: Goa state, Daman and Diu, Dadra and Nagar Haveli.
Classification: Indo-European, Italic, Romance, Italo-Western, Western, Gallo-Iberian, Ibero-Romance, West Iberian, Portuguese-Galician
Typology: SVO; prepositions; gender (masculine/feminine); definite and indefinite articles; verb affixes mark person, number; passives; tense; comparatives; 21 consonants, 13 vowels, 11 diphthongs; non-tonal.
Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Indo-Portuguese [idb].
Scripts: Braille script [Brai]. Latin script [Latn], primary usage.

Location: Madhya Pradesh state: Balaghat, Betul, Chindwara, and Seoni districts; Maharashtra state: Bhandara, Gondia, and Wardha districts.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Intermediate Divisions, Western
Dialect_Names: Bhoyar Powari (Bhomiyari, Bhoyari, Bhoyaroo, Bhuiyar, Bhuria, Bohoyeri), Vyneganga Powari, Govari of Seoni, Khalari, Koshti, Kumbhari, Marari
Relationships: Reported intelligibility between Bhoyar and Vyneganga. Balaghat District dialect considered central among Bhoyar and Vyneganga varieties. Lexical similarity: 60%–87% among dialects; 80%–83% with Koshti, Kumbhari, and Khalari sub-groups; 49%–65% with Bagheli [bfy], 46%–64% with Bundeli [bns].
Language_Use: Powari use is decreasing in the Bhoyar and Vyneganga dialect areas. Half the children learn Hindi [hin] or Marathi [mar] first. Home. Neutral attitudes.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin]. Also use Marathi [mar].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 72% for Powari-speaking districts (2001 census).
General_Remarks: Younger generation is getting education.

Location: Chandigarh state; Haryana state: Ambala and Pauchkula districts; Himachal Pradesh state: Kangra and Una districts; Jammu and Kashmir state: Jambu, Kathua, and Samba Jambu districts; Punjab state: Amritsar and Gurdaspur districts; Rajasthan state: north Ganganagar district.
Official_Recognition: Statutory provincial language in Punjab, West Bengal states; union territories Delhi, Chandigarh (1950, Constitution, Schedule VIII).
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Intermediate Divisions, Western, Panjabi
Dialect_Names: Punjabi Proper (Panjabi Proper), Majhi, Doabi, Bhatiani (Bhatneri, Bhatti, Bhatyiana), Powadhi (Puadhi, Puadi), Malwai (Malwa), Bathi
Relationships: Western Punjabi [pnb] is distinct from Eastern Punjabi, although there is a chain of dialects to Western Hindi (Urdu) [urd]. Bhatyiana dialect considered a mixture of Punjabi and Marwari [mve]. Majhi considered the purest Punjabi form (Grierson and Konow 1903–1928).
Typology: SOV; postpositions; gender (masculine/feminine); no articles; case-marking (7 cases); verb affixes mark person, number, gender of subject; passives; tense and aspect; 15 consonant and 24 vowel phonemes; tonal (3 tones: high, mid, low).
Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Bauria [bge], Bazigar [bfr], Bhattiyali [bht], Bilaspuri [kfs], Chambeali [cdh], Churahi [cdj], Dogri [dgo], Kangri [xnr], Mandeali [mjl], Sansi [ssi].
Education: Taught in primary and secondary schools through grade 5 and as subject thereafter in Punjab and West Bengal states.
Scripts: Arabic script, Naskh variant [Arab]. Gurmukhi script [Guru], primary usage. Khojki script [Khoj].
General_Remarks: Associated with Sikhs. Different from Majhi [mjz] in India and Nepal.

Location: Jammu and Kashmir state: Kathua, Jammu, and Samba districts; Punjab state: Gurdaspur district; possibly Delhi, Haryana.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Intermediate Divisions, Western, Panjabi, Western Panjabi
Typology: SOV; postpositions; gender (masculine/feminine); no articles; case-marking (7 cases); verb affixes mark person, number, gender of subject; passives; tense and aspect; 15 consonant and 24 vowel phonemes; tonal (3 tones: high, mid, low).
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng].
Literature: Literature. Newspapers. Periodicals. Radio. TV. Videos. Grammar. NT: 1819–1931.
Scripts: Arabic script, Naskh variant [Arab]. Arabic script, Nastaliq variant [Aran], primary usage, also called Shahmukhi. Khojki script [Khoj]. Lahnda (Landa) script [Qaaj], no longer in use. Latin script [Latn].

Alternate_Names: Burig, Burigskat, Purig-pa, Purigi, Purigskad, Purik, Purik Bhotia, Purik-Sham-Nubra, Purkhi, Purki
Location: Ladakh state: Kargil district, mainly Suru valley; Dras valley, some in western Himalayas.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Western Tibeto-Burman, Bodish, Central Bodish, Western
Relationships: Reportedly similar to Balti [bft].

Language_Contact: Many also use Balti [bft]. Also use English [eng]. Also use Urdu [urd].

Scripts: Arabic script, Naskh variant [Arab]. Tibetan script [Tibt], no longer in use.

Location: Arunachal Pradesh state: East Kameng, Kurung Kumey, Papumpare, and Lower Subansiri districts, along Par river, 53 villages.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Central Tibeto-Burman, Kho-Bwa
Dialect_Names: Bulu, Kojo Rojo, Rawa, Sario Saria, Chayangtajo, Kurung-Kumey, Lasumpatte
Relationships: A divergent language which may not be Sino-Tibetan. Burling (2003) groups it with Sherdukpen [sdp] and Bugun; possibly also with Lish [lsh] and Sartang [onp]. Lexical similarity: 54%–67% between varieties; 57%–68% with Chug [cvg]; less than 15% with Bugun [bgg] and Nyishi [njz].
Language_Use: Home, village. Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: All also use Nyishi [njz]. Some also use Assamese [asm]. Some also use Hindi [hin]. Also use English [eng].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 2%.
Scripts: Bengali (Bangla) script [Beng], limited usage. Devanagari script [Deva], limited usage. Latin script [Latn], primary usage.
General_Remarks: A satellite relationship to Nyishi and Bangni peoples, bonded economically. A Scheduled Tribe in India. Claim kinship with the Khoa or Bugun. Distinct in that rice is not their staple.

Location: Manipur state: Chandel district, Chandanpokpi, Khongkhang Chothe, Lamlang Huipi, Loirang Talsi, New Wangparan, Salemthar, and Zat’lang; Senapati district, Moibunglikli, Purumkhulen, Purumkhunou, Purumlikli, and Waicheiphai villages.

Relationships: 95% intelligibility of Kharam Naga [kfw]. Lexical similarity: 60%–65% with Kom [kmm], 60%–66% with Koireng [nkd], 57%–60% with Aimol [aim], 71%–73% with Kharam Naga [kfw].
Typology: SOV; postpositions; numerals, adjectives, articles after noun head; question word between subject and object; word order distinguishes subject, object, indirect object; V, CV, CVC, CVV; nontonal.
Language_Use: Vigorous. Home, village. Used by all. Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Meitei [mni], with speakers of other languages.
Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Kharam Naga [kfw].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 30%–40% (2000).

Location: Assam state: Darrang, Goalpara, and Kamrup districts; Nagaland state; West Bengal state: Alipurduar and Jalpaiguri districts; Koch Bihar district, Tafangunj sub-district; Meghalaya state: East and West Garo hills districts.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Sal, Boro-Garo, Koch
Relationships: Rongdani is the standard dialect. Lexical similarity: 73% between Maituri and Rongdani. 31%–39% with Koch [kdq].
Language_Use: The majority of the ethnic group speaks Assamese [asm] as L1; Rabha spoken only in Rongdani and Maituri. Home, prayer, market, other villages. Used by all.
Language_Contact: Also use Bengali [ben]. Also use English [eng]. Also use Garo [grt]. Also use Hindi [hin].
Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Koch [kdq].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 30%–50%. High interest in language development.
Literature: Literature. Radio. TV. Dictionary. Grammar. Bible: 2023.
Scripts: Bengali (Bangla) script [Beng]. Latin script [Latn], preferred by Catholics.

Scripts: Myanmar (Burmese) script [Mymr], informal and non-standardized use.

Location: Mizoram state: mainly Aizawl district, scattered in Chhimtuipui and Lunglei districts; Manipur and Tripura states; a few in Jampui hills.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Kuki-Chin, Peripheral, Northern
Relationships: Related to Tedim Chin [ctd], Paite Chin [pck], Thado Chin [tcz], and Zo [zom].
Typology: SOV.
Language_Contact: Shifted to Mizo [lus].
Literacy: Though literacy is high, formal education level is low (in Tripura).
General_Remarks: A subgroup of the Mizo [lus]. Spoken only in northern Mizoram villages (Singh 1995b).

Alternate_Names: Canpa, Chyanam, Johari, Kyonam, Saukas, Saukiya Khun, Shaukas
L1_Full: No known L1 speakers. The last speaker either died or shifted entirely to Kumaoni [kfy] by the 1950s.
Location: Uttarakhand state: Pithoragarh district, Darchula and Munsyari sub-districts in Johar valley, Nepal border along Mahakali valley.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Western Tibeto-Burman, Bodish, West Himalayish, Almora
Language_Contact: Shifted to Kumaoni [kfy].
General_Remarks: Identity merged with the dominant Kumaoni people. Rangkas sometimes refers to the whole group of Darmiya, Chaudangsi, Byangsi, and the now extinct Johari.

Alternate_Names: Langlo, Langlong, Langlu, Langrong, Lengreng, Riam chong, Ronglong
Location: Assam and Mizoram states; Tripura state: Joitang village.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Unclassified

Language_Contact: Also use English [eng].

Location: Gujarat state: Panchmahals district; Vadodara district, Chhota Udaipur and Kavant sub-districts; Madhya Pradesh state: Jhabua district, Alirajpur sub-district.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Intermediate Divisions, Western, Bhil
Relationships: 76% intelligibility of Bhilali [bhi]. A chain of related varieties from Bhilali to Rathawa; extremes have limited mutual intelligibility. Lexical similarity: 83% with Bhilali [bhi].
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 37% for Gujarat (2001 census).
General_Remarks: Distinct from Rathwi Bareli [bgd] in Madhya Pradesh.

Location: Karnataka state: Kodagu district; Kerala state: Kannur district; Wayanad district, Mananthavadi sub-district.
Classification: Dravidian, Southern, Tamil-Kannada, Tamil-Kodagu, Tamil-Malayalam, Malayalam
Relationships: 93%–94% dialect intelligibility between Yerava and Adiya dialects. Pani Yerava may be a dialect of Ravula or of Paniya [pcg]. Lexical similarity: 83%–98% among Yerava and Adiya varieties, 53%–61% with standard Malayalam [mal], 35%–40% with Badaga [bfq], 32%–42% with colloquial Kannada [kan], 66%–74% Pani Yerava dialect with the Adiya and Yerava dialects.
Language_Use: Vigorous. Home, village, religion. Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Kannada [kan]. Also use Malayalam [mal].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 40% for Kodagu District, Karnataka; 44% among Adiya in Kerala (2001 census). High motivation for literature, literacy.
General_Remarks: Adiyan is a Scheduled Tribe in Karnataka and Tamil Nadu. Yerava is a Scheduled Tribe in Karnataka. Pani Yeravas are not the same as the Paniya of Wayanad District.

Alternate_Names: Ch’opa, Chiutse, Ganung-Rawang, Kiutze, Krangku, Rvwang, Taron, “Hkanung” (pej.)

Typology: SOV.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng].
Literature: Newspapers. Periodicals. Dictionary. Grammar. Texts. Bible: 1986.

Alternate_Names: Ban Manus, Ban Rauts, Bhulla, Bãt-kha, Dzanggali, Jangali, Janggali, Jhangar, Raji, Raut
Location: Uttarakhand state: Pithoragarh district, north of Askot Maila, 9 villages.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Western Tibeto-Burman, Himalayan, Central Himalayan, Raute-Raji
Relationships: Extensive borrowing from areal Indo-Aryan (Kumaoni, Nepali) languages (2011 J. Fortier). Very similar to Raute [rau] and Raji [rji].
Typology: SOV; postpositions; genitives, articles, adjectives, numerals before noun heads; noun heads both initial and final; no noun classes or genders; content q-word initial; maximum number of suffixes 3; affixes indicate case of noun phrases; verb affixation marks person and number; passives; causatives; comparatives; CV, CVC; nontonal.
Language_Use: All speakers use a highly mixed variety. Due to poor socio-economic status, miniscule number of speakers, fewer domains of language use, attitude of the dominant group and lack of initiative from the state, Rawat is quickly assimilating into Kumaoni [kfy] (Rastogi 2006). Home, religion. Negative attitudes.
Language_Contact: Shifting to Kumaoni [kfy] (Rastogi 2006).
Literacy: Younger generation taking interest in literacy.
General_Remarks: Many Indo-Aryan loans. Raute are found in Kumaon where they are known as Raji (Gurung 1997).

Language_Contact: Also use English [eng].

Alternate_Names: Rang Po Bhasa, Rangkas, Rangpa, “Manchhi Bhassa” (pej.), “Marchha” (pej.), “Marchha Pahari” (pej.), “Tolchha” (pej.)
Location: Uttarakhand state: Chamoli district, Joshimath sub-district, Bampa, Gamshali, Malari, and Niti villages; Mana valley, Aut, Benakuli, Gajkoti, Hanuman Chatti, Indradhara, Pathiya-Dhantoli, and Mana. Mana and Niti valleys (Marchha), Niti valley (a few Tolchha).
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Western Tibeto-Burman, Bodish, West Himalayish, Kinauri
Relationships: A Himalayan language distinct from Tibetan [bod].
Language_Use: Rongpo speakers learn Garhwali simultaneously with Rongpo. Code switching and code mixing are very common. It is uncertain whether stable bilingualism will continue or whether Rongpo will be replaced by Garhwali or Hindi. Home, community. Used by all.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Garhwali [gbm]. Also use Hindi [hin]. Also use Kumaoni [kfy].
Literacy: Hindi used for all written communication.
General_Remarks: Many Indo-Aryan loanwords. Grierson and Konow referred to this as the Garhwal dialect of Tibetan (Grierson and Konow 1903–1928). Ranglo or Rang often used as a cover term for Byangs, Chaudangs, Darma, and Rongpo.

Location: Meghalaya state: East Garo Hills district.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Sal, Boro-Garo, Koch
Relationships: Most closely related to Atong [aot], Koch [kdq], and Rabha [rah]. Not inherently intelligible of Garo [grt].
Language_Use: Elderly only.
Language_Contact: Shifted to Garo [grt].

Alternate_Names: Chota Nagpuri, Dikku Kaji, Ganwari, Gauuari, Gawari, Goari, Jharkhandhi, Nagpuri, Nagpuria, Sadan, Sadana, Sadani, Sadati, Sadhan, Sadhari, Sadna, Sadrias Khatoya, Sadrik, Santri, Siddri, Sradri
L1_Full: 5,130,000 in India (2011 census). 19,100 Gawari, 763,000 Nagpuria, and 4,350,000 Sadri (2011 census).
Location: Bihar state: Aurangabad; Chhattisgarh state: Surguja; Jharkhand state: Chatra, Latehar, Palamu, and Ranchi districts.
LWC_Support: Lingua franca among many tribal groups and among tea-garden community of Assam, Bengal, and Bangladesh during the Assam colonial period of 1860–1890. Taught at universities at Jharkhand. Historically used in court, literature, and poetry (17th century).
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Outer Languages, Eastern, Bihari
Relationships: 77% of Oraon Sadri [sdr] of Bangladesh. Speakers name 3 registers of Sadri: Sadani (finer, respectful, formal), Common Sadri (Nagpuri), and Lower Sadri (rough). Lexical similarity: 77%–96% between dialects, 58%–71% with Hindi [hin], 47%–54% with Odia [ory], 45%–61% with Bengali [ben].
Language_Use: Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Also use Bengali [ben]. Also use Hindi [hin], especially in the market, with leaders, and for prayer and worship, but proficiency is low. Also use Odia [ory].
Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Asuri [asr], Bijori [bix], Birhor [biy], Ho [hoc], Kharia [khr], Koda [cdz], Kodaku [ksz], Korwa [kfp], Kurux [kru], Mahali [mjx], Majhi [mjz], Munda [unx], Mundari [unr], Santhali [sat], Sora [srb], Turi [trd].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 15%–25%.
Literature: Literature. Periodicals. Radio. Dictionary. Grammar. NT: 1931–2016.

Location: Assam state: Dima Hasao district, Baigao, Bangphiri, Dorbin, Langlut, Lungding, Kekrangship, Mundet, New Kekrangship, Phaijol, Tuijonte, and Tuisuonthum villages; Hailakandi and Karimganj districts, Burua, Halam punji (Pakala), Ronpur, Ronpur Khothar, Tangpui (Kalidas punjee), and Zailien villages; West Karbi Anglong district, Khilimulong, Langkarcha, Socheng, and Umpho villages; Meghalaya state: Jaintia Hills district, Mongor, Rumphung, and Saithsma villages; Nagaland state: Kohima district, Khelma village; Manipur, Mizoram, and Tripura states.

Language_Contact: Also use Bengali [ben]. Also use Biate [biu]. Also use Dimasa [dis]. Also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin]. Also use Hmar [hmr]. Also use Hrangkhol [hra]. Also use Karbi [mjw]. Also use Khasi [kha]. Also use Nagamese [nag]. Also use Thado Chin [tcz].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 25%.

Location: Chhattisgarh state: Jagdalpur, Raigarh, and Raipur districts; Odisha state: Balangir, Bargarh, Boudh, Deogarh, Jharsuguda, Kalhandi, Nuvapada, Sambalpur, Sonpur, and Sundargarh districts.

Relationships: Lexical similarity: 75%–76% with Oriya [ory].
Language_Use: All domains. Used by all. Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng].

Location: Maharashtra state: Palghar district, Vasai-Virar.

Relationships: A divergent dialect of, or closely related language to Konkani [knn]. Shares many features with Gujarati [guj].
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng].

Location: Haryana state: Sirsa district; Punjab state: Bathinda and Muktsar districts; Rajasthan state: Hanumangarh district; scattered elsewhere in Delhi, Himachal Pradesh, Jammu and Kashmir, Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh, and Uttar Pradesh states.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Western Hindi, Hindustani, Sansi
Relationships: Intermediate between Eastern Punjabi [pan] and Hindustani (see Hindi [hin]). Sometimes identify themselves as Marwari [rwr]. Related to Rajasthani [mwr], Sindhi [snd], Eastern Punjabi. Lexical similarity: 71% with Urdu [urd], 83% with the Sochi dialect of Sansi [ssi](1998). Numerous phonological and morphological borrowings from Eastern Punjabi [pan], Hindi [hin], and Gujarati [guj] (Gusain 2002).
Language_Use: Not being passed on to the next generation. Much mixing of Hindi [hin], Eastern Punjabi [pan], or Gujarati [guj] (Gusain 2002). Home only. Adults only.
Language_Contact: Some shifting to Eastern Punjabi [pan]. Some shifting to Gujarati [guj]. Some shifting to Hindi [hin].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: Below 5%.
General_Remarks: Bhils by caste. Called a Gypsy language. They have an argot called Farsi. Gusain (2002) classifies this as a Rajasthani dialect. Socially separate from surrounding groups. Governed by their own social norms and economy. Losing some tribal characteristics but are not yet integrated into the national mainstream (Gusain 2002).

L1_Full: No known L1 speakers in India.
Official_Recognition: Statutory language of national identity (1950, Constitution, Schedule VIII).
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan
Typology: SOV; both prepositions and postpositions; noun head final; 3 genders; content q-word in situ; up to 3 prefixes, up to 5 suffixes; clause constituents indicated by case-marking; verbal affixation marks person, number and genders of subject and object; dual number; non-ergative; tense and aspect; passives and voice; comparatives; non-tonal; 34 consonant, 8 vowels, 2 diphthongs.
Language_Use: Used in liturgy, cultural ceremonies, and rituals.
Education: Taught as subject in primary and secondary schools. Taught as subject in tertiary schools.
Literature: Literature. Newspapers. Periodicals. Radio. Dictionary. Grammar. Texts. Bible: 1822.
Scripts: Devanagari script [Deva]. Grantha script [Gran]. Kawi script [Kawi]. Myanmar (Burmese) script [Mymr]. Newa script [Newa]. Sharada script [Shrd]. Siddham script [Sidd], no longer in use. Sinhala script [Sinh].
General_Remarks: Sanskrit has 2 individual historical languages, both of which are assigned codes in the ISO 639-3 standard: Classical Sanskrit (cls) and Vedic Sanskrit (vsn). Historically, Vedic Sanskrit is the more ancient of the 2 and is primarily associated with the ancient religious texts, the Vedas. Classical Sanskrit came out later and is the standardized form associated with literature, philosophy, and science. For almost 2000 years, Sanskrit exerted enormous influence over many languages, most importantly both the Indo-Aryan and the Dravidian languages of the Indian sub-continent.

Location: Bihar state: Bhagalpur and Munger districts; Jharkhand state: Hazaribagh and Manbhum districts; Odisha state: Balasore district; West Bengal state: Bankura and Birbhum districts; Assam, Mizoram, and Tripura states.

General_Remarks: Language of Santhal tribals of Chota Nagpur Plateau (comprising the states of Jharkhand, Bihar, Odisha, Chhattisgarh).

Location: Arunachal Pradesh state: West Kameng district, Rupa (Kupa), Shergaon, and Thungrao villages; Maharashtra state: Jigaon; Assam state.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Central Tibeto-Burman, Kho-Bwa
Relationships: Lexical similarity: 49%–60% with Sartang. Burling (2003) groups it with Puroik [suv] and Bugun [bgg] and possibly also with Lish [lsh] and Sartang [onp].

Language_Contact: Also use Hindi [hin]. Also use Tawang Monpa [twm].
Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Bugun [bgg].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 15% (20% male, 7% female) (Muanthanga 1998).
General_Remarks: Separated from the Sartang by war.

Autonym: शेर्वी तम्ङे‎ (sherwi tamnge), ཤར་པའི་སྐད་ཡིག‎ (shar pa’i skad yig)
Alternate_Names: Serwa, Sharpa, Sharpa Bhotia, Sherwi tamnye, Xarba, Xiaerba

Location: Jammu and Kashmir state: Bandipore and Kargil districts, Dras and Kishenganga valleys, Gurais area.

Scripts: Arabic script, Naskh variant [Arab]. Arabic script, Nastaliq variant [Aran], primary usage.
General_Remarks: Open to education and jobs outside the area. Distinct from Brokskat [bkk], but Brokskat is also used semiofficially to refer to a highly divergent variety of Shina spoken by Buddhists.

Alternate_Names: Bhutia, Dandzongka, Danjongka, Danyouka, Denjong, Denjong-skad, Denjongke, Denjongkha, Denjongkä, Denjongpa, Denjonka, Denjonke, Denzong Ke, Denzongke, Denzongpe Ke, Denzongpeke, Dranjoke, Dranjongke, Drendzongké, Lachengpa, Lachungpa, Lhoke, Sikami, Sikkim Bhotia, Sikkim Bhutia, Sikkimese Bhutia

Relationships: Partially intelligible of Dzongkha [dzo] of Bhutan. Lexical similarity: 65% with Dzongkha [dzo] of Bhutan, 42% with Tibetan [bod].
Language_Use: Some young people, all adults. Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Most also use Nepali [npi], for education and trade (Yliniemi 2019). Some also use Central Tibetan [bod], which is viewed as appropriate for religion. Also use English [eng] (Yliniemi 2019). Also use Hindi [hin] (Yliniemi 2019).
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 68% for Bhutia in Sikkim (2001 census).

Location: Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Delhi, Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Odisha, Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu, and Uttar Pradesh states.

Dialect_Names: Bhatia, Jadeji, Kayasthi, Lari, Lasi, Thareli, Thari, Viccholi, Visholi
Typology: SOV; noun head final; gender (masculine/feminine); case-marking (8 cases); verb affixes mark person, number, gender of subject; passives; tense and aspect; 24 consonant and 15 vowel phonemes.

Language_Contact: Shifting to Hindi [hin]. Also use English [eng].
Education: Taught in primary and secondary schools through grade 5 and as subject thereafter in Rajasthan state.
Scripts: Arabic script, Naskh variant [Arab], primary usage. Devanagari script [Deva], used in India. Gurmukhi script [Guru], used in India. Khojki script [Khoj].

Language_Contact: Most also use Assamese [asm]. Also use English [eng].
Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Tangsa Naga [nst], Turung [try].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: Less than 40%.
General_Remarks: Many loans from Khamti [kht]. Kachin refers to a cultural, rather than a linguistic group.

Location: Himachal Pradesh state: Shimla district, southeast section; Sirmaur district.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Intermediate Divisions, Western, Pahari, Western Pahari
Relationships: Difficult intelligibility between Dharthi and Giripari; and between Upper Mahasui and Giripar. Dharthi dialect more influenced by Hindi. In south Shimla District, Kiunthali and Sirmauri are used interchangeably. Reportedly a different variety of Sirmauri in Sirmaur District. Lexical similarity: 56%–70% with Dharthi and Giripari, with considerable variation within each dialect; Giripari 67% with Lower Mahasui, 65% with Upper Mahasui, 61% with Jaunsari [jns].
Language_Use: Home, village. Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin], with high proficiency among educated people, and a wide range of proficiency among uneducated people, but older, uneducated women have very limited proficiency.
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 60% for Sirmaur District (2001 census).
Literature: Newspapers. Radio. TV. Videos. Grammar. NT: 2017.
Scripts: Devanagari script [Deva]. Takri (Tankri, Takari) script [Takr], special variety used informally (Masica 1991).
General_Remarks: Dharthi is spoken in Giriwar area, Giripari in Giripar area.

L1_Full: 248,000 (2011 census). Each listed district has communities of at least 5,000.
Location: Tamil Nadu state: North Arcot, Chengai-Annai, Dindugul, Madurai, Ramanathapuram, Salem, Thanjavur, Tiruchchirappalli, and Tirunelveli districts; Chennai, Deccan, Madurai, Salem, and Thanjavur cities; Andhra Pradesh and Karnataka states.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Intermediate Divisions, Western, Gujarati
Relationships: Indo-Aryan elements reveal Gujarati [guj] relationship; some structure from Dravidian, lexicon from Telugu [tel] and Tamil [tam]. An Indo-European island surrounded by Dravidian languages. The 3 main populations in Salem, Thanjavur, and Madurai cities had between 67% and 97% inherent intelligibility among themselves. Lexical similarity: 77%–96% between all varieties. The 3 main populations: 84%–96%. Southern dialects have 83% or higher lexical similarity with Thanjavur variety.
Language_Use: Vigorous. Home, prayer.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Tamil [tam].
Scripts: Devanagari script [Deva]. Saurashtra script [Saur], a modern version developed in the late 1800s, used for centuries. Tamil script [Taml], primary usage. Telugu script [Telu].
General_Remarks: Most are weavers; nonweavers are generally better educated. System of exogamous clans.

Location: Himachal Pradesh state: Lahaul Spiti district, Spiti sub-district; Jammu and Kashmir state: southeast Leh district.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Western Tibeto-Burman, Bodish, Central Bodish, Central, Western
Relationships: Not intelligible of Ladakhi [lbj]; low intelligibility of Stod Bhoti [sbu]. All areas of Spiti understand each other. Lexical similarity: 41% with the Lhasa Tibetan dialect of Central Tibetan [bod], 57% with Ladakhi (Leh) [lbj], 57% with Stod Bhoti [sbu] from Darcha.
Language_Use: Home, Community, Religion. Some young people, all adults.
Language_Contact: Many also use Hindi [hin].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 65% in Hindi [hin]. Most literates read Hindi. Some older people and Buddhist monks and nuns, read Tibetan.

Alternate_Names: Lahul Bhoti, Stod, Stod-Kad, Tod, Tod-Kad

Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Western Tibeto-Burman, Bodish, Central Bodish, Central, Western

Language_Use: Home, community, religion. Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Many also use Hindi [hin], for trade and education. Many speak Hindi but are less proficient than those in other Lahul communities. Also use English [eng].
Literacy: Desire for literacy in Stod Bhoti.

Location: Chhattisgarh state: Jashpur, Koriya, and Surguja districts; Korba and Raigarh districts’ border areas.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Intermediate Divisions, Eastern, East Central

Language_Use: Vigorous. All domains. Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng].

Location: Bihar state: Katihar, Kishanganj, and Purnea districts; West Bengal state: Dakshin Dinajpur and Uttar Dinajpur districts.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Outer Languages, Eastern, Bihari
Relationships: Reportedly very similar to Maithili [mai] (2019 N. Choudhary). Preliminary survey results show intelligibility of Nepali Rajbanshi [rjs]. Lexical similarity: 70%–74% with Hindi [hin], 67%–71% with the western variety of Kamtapuri [rkt] spoken near Dinajpur, 77%–86% with varieties of Surjapuri.
Language_Use: Vigorous. Home, village. Used by all. Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: Low (2006 M. Toulmin). Different scripts in Nepal and India.
General_Remarks: Possible alternate names are Chaupal, Choupal, and Suraji, but surveyors did not find these terms used. Historically more closely related to Kamtapuri [rkt] and Rajbanshi [rjs] than Hindi [hin], a relationship borne out by greater morphological similarity. (2006 M. Toulmin).

Alternate_Names: Bengali of Cachar, Sileti, Siloti, Srihattia, Sylheti Bangla, Sylheti Bengali, Sylhetti, Syloti, Syloty
Location: Assam state: Barak valley region, Cachar, Hailakandi, and Karimganj districts; Tripura state: North Tripura district; possibly Nagaland, Kolkata.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Outer Languages, Eastern, Bengali-Assamese

Scripts: Bengali (Bangla) script [Beng]. Latin script [Latn]. Syloti Nagri script [Sylo].

Language_Use: Vigorous. Home, cultural activities, market. Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng].

Location: Andhra Pradesh state: Chittoor and Sri Potti Sriramulu Nellore districts, east Puducherry enclaves; Karnataka state: Chamarajana district; Kerala state: south; assorted border areas; Tamil Nadu state.
Official_Recognition: Statutory provincial language in Tamil Nadu State; union territories Puducherry, Andaman and Nicobar Islands (1950, Constitution, Schedule VIII).
Classification: Dravidian, Southern, Tamil-Kannada, Tamil-Kodagu, Tamil-Malayalam, Tamil
Dialect_Names: Adi Dravida, Aiyar, Aiyangar, Arava, Burgandi, Kongar, Madrasi, Madurai, Tamil, Sri Lanka Tamil, Malaya Tamil, Burma Tamil, South Africa Tamil, Tigalu, Harijan, Sanketi, Hebbar, Mandyam Brahmin, Secunderabad Brahmin
Relationships: Burgandi are nomadic. Aiyar and Aiyangar are Brahmin dialects. Southern dialect around Madurai is literary standard. Eastern dialect is colloquial standard (Zvelebil 1998). Sanketi dialect in Karnataka used by immigrants from Madurai and Shenkotta in Tamil Nadu. Lexicon greatly influenced by Kannada.
Typology: SOV; postpositions; gender (rational, non-rational); no articles; case-marking (8 cases); verb affixes mark person, number, gender of subject; passives (affective, effective); tense; no comparatives; 18 consonants, 10 vowels and 2 diphthongs; non-tonal; stress on first syllable; inclusive/exclusive pronouns.
Language_Contact: All also use Kannada [kan] (Gowda 1976).
Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Alu Kurumba [xua], Attapady Kurumba [pkr], Eravallan [era], Irula [iru], Jennu Kurumba [xuj], Kadar [kej], Kanikkaran [kev], Kannada Kurumba [kfi], Kota [kfe], Malankuravan [mjo], Malapandaram [mjp], Malasar [ymr], Moundadan Chetti [cty], Muthuvan [muv], Paliyan [pcf], Paniya [pcg], Sourashtra [saz], Toda [tcx], Vaagri Booli [vaa].
Education: Taught in primary and secondary schools in Tamil Nadu state.
Scripts: Arabic script, Naskh variant [Arab], no longer in use. Braille script [Brai]. Tamil script [Taml], primary usage.
General_Remarks: A Classical Language of India since 2004.

Relationships: Lexical similarity: 60%–64% with Malayalam [mal], 50%–54% with Tamil [tam], 66%–72% with Mullu Kurumba [kpb].

Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 30% (2004 survey). Literacy rate much lower than state literacy rate.
