Location: Sikkim and Uttar Pradesh states; West Bengal state: Darjeeling district.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Western Tibeto-Burman, Himalayan, Kiranti, Western
Typology: SOV; postpositions; noun head final; content q-word in situ; no prefixes, up to 4 suffixes; clause constituents indicated by case-marking; verbal affixation marks person and number; ergativity; tense; passives and voice, but rare; tonal; 29 consonant and 16 vowel phonemes.
Language_Use: Most ethnic Thulungs in Darjeeling do not speak Thulung but Nepali [nep].
Literature: Literature. Newspapers. Periodicals. Radio. Videos. Dictionary. Texts. NT: 2017.

Alternate_Names: Bhotia, Bod, Central Tibetan, Phoke, Pohbetian, Poke, Skad, Tebilian, Tibate
Location: Himachal Pradesh state: Tibet border; Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Delhi, Sikkim, and Uttarakhand states.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Western Tibeto-Burman, Bodish, Central Bodish, Central
Dialect_Names: Aba (Batang), Dartsemdo (Tatsienlu), Dru, Gtsang, Hanniu, Kongbo, Nganshuenkuan (Anshuenkuan Nyarong), Panakha-Panags, Paurong
Typology: SOV; noun head initial; definite and indefinite articles; ergativity; comparatives; 28 consonant and 16 vowel phonemes; tonal (4 tones); 2 levels of honorifics.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng].
Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Byangsi [bee], Chaudangsi [cdn], Chug [cvg], Darmiya [drd], Jad [jda], Sikkimese [sip], Zakhring [zkr].
Literature: Newspapers. Periodicals. Radio. Dictionary. Grammar. Bible: 1948.
Scripts: Braille script [Brai]. Marchen script [Marc]. Phags-pa script [Phag]. Tibetan script [Tibt], Uchen and Umed styles.
General_Remarks: In Himalayan countries, ‘Bhotiya’, people of Tibetan origin, and is applied to various languages.

Alternate_Names: Gondhla, Gondla, Lahauli, Lahouli, Lahuli, Rangloi, Teenan, Tinan Lahuli
Location: Himachal Pradesh state: Lahaul Spiti district, lower Chandra, Rangloi, and Tinan valleys; Gondhla is main village.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Western Tibeto-Burman, Bodish, West Himalayish, Kinauri
Relationships: Lexical similarity: 63%–56% with Pattani [lae], 32%–37% with Bunan [bfu], 21% with the Spiti [spt] and Stod [sbu] varieties of central Tibetan [bod], 62% with Tandi village, 34% with Shumcho [scu], 32% with Jangshung [jna], 31% with Kanauri and Sunam [ssk], 13% with Tibetan [bod].
Language_Use: Home, village, infrequently in religion.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin]. Also use Pattani [lae].
Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Kullu Pahari [kfx].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: High.
General_Remarks: Lahuli applies to Lahul inhabitants; Spiti refers primarily to a place. Not a tight linguistic designation. Well educated.

Location: Assam state: Kamrup, Karbi Anglong, Lakhimpur, Nagaon, and Sibsagar districts; Meghalaya state: Khasi Hills district.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Sal, Boro-Garo, Boro-Tiwa
Language_Use: Quite a few in Brahmaputra valley adopted Assamese [asm] as L1. Resurgent interest to learn the mother tongue; approved by the state in 2004 to be taught as a subject up to class 4. Home, market. Some of all ages.
Language_Contact: Many also use Assamese [asm]. Also use English [eng].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 62% for Assam (2001 census). Literacy rate higher in the plains. In the hills, equally low among men and women.

Location: Tamil Nadu state: Kunda and Nilgiri hills.
Classification: Dravidian, Southern, Tamil-Kannada, Tamil-Kodagu, Toda-Kota
Relationships: Lexical similarity: 24% with Kota [kfe], the most similar language.
Language_Use: Vigorous. All domains. Used by all. Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Tamil [tam].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 66%–79% (2001 census).
General_Remarks: A Scheduled Tribe.

Location: West Bengal state: Jalpaiguri district, Dhunchipara, Panchayatpara, and Subhapara areas, Totopara village on Indo-Bhutan border.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Sal, Dhimalish
Relationships: Not inherently intelligible of Dhimal [dhi] of Nepal. Lexical similarity: low with Dhimal [dhi].
Typology: SOV; postpositions; genitives, demonstratives, relatives before noun heads; nontonal.
Language_Contact: Also use Bengali [ben]. Also use Hindi [hin]. Also use Nepali [npi].

Alternate_Names: Cangluo Menba, Central Monpa, Dirang, Memba, Menba, Monba, Monpa, Motuo, Sangla, Sharchopkha, Tsangla
L1_Full: 11,200 in India (2007). 8,200 in Kameng District; 3,000 in West Siang.
Location: Arunachal Pradesh state: West Kameng district, Dirang area; Assam state: Udalguri district, Mechuka and Tuting sub-districts, Bishing Mechuka, Bona, Dorgling Halung, Galling, Korfu, Namsu, Opu, Sangti, Tempang, and Tuting villages; possibly West Siang district.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Western Tibeto-Burman, Bodish
Relationships: Lexical similarity: 11%–14% with Khamba [kbg] (Joseph et al 2019).
Typology: SOV; singular-dual-plural personal pronouns; case-marking (3 cases); tense and aspect; 31 consonants and 5 vowels; nontonal; evidentiality (mirativity).
Language_Use: Used by all.
Language_Contact: Some also use English [eng]. Also use Adi [adi]. Also use Hindi [hin].
Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Chug [cvg], Khamba [kbg], Lish [lsh].
Scripts: Tibetan script [Tibt], Uchen style, used in India.
General_Remarks: A Scheduled Tribe. Chowdhury (1996) separates Memba (Tshangla) and Khamba as different tribes in Siang District, both separate from Monpa, in Kameng District.

Alternate_Names: Tal, Tallu, Thalu, Thulu, Tilu, Tullu, Tuluva Bhasa
Location: Karnataka state: Dakshina Kannada and Udupi districts; Kerala state: Kasargod district; scattered in other states.
Classification: Dravidian, Southern, Tulu
Dialect_Names: Northwest Tulu (Mangalore, Udipi), Northeast Tulu (Belthangadi, Kerala), Southwest Tulu (Kasaragod, Manjeswara), South Central Tulu (Bantwal, Puttur), Southeast Tulu (Sullia Subrahmanya), Brahmin Tulu, Common Tulu
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin]. Also use Kannada [kan]. Also use Marathi [mar].
Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Korra Koraga [kfd], Kudiya [kfg].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 80%–83% in Dakshina Kannada [kan] for Udupi districts.
Literature: Literature. Periodicals. Radio. Videos. Dictionary. Grammar. NT: 1847–2000.
Scripts: Kannada script [Knda]. Tulu-Tigalari script [Tutg], philosophical texts and religious verses are sometimes written in this script.

Location: Chhattisgarh state: Raigarh district, and scattered throughout; Jharkhand state: Gumla, Lohardaga, and Ranchi districts, Chotanagpur area; Odisha state: Sambalpur and Sundargarh districts; West Bengal state: Bankura, Birbhum, Murshidabad, and Nadia districts.
Classification: Austro-Asiatic, Munda, North Munda, Kherwari, Santali
Language_Contact: Shifted to Sadri [sck].
General_Remarks: A Scheduled Caste. Speak Sadri [sck] as L1 in Jharkhand, Mundari [unr] in West Bengal, Odia [ory] in Odisha (Singh and Manoharan 1993). Turi spoken only in Chotanagpur (Breton 1997). A Turi caste in Gujarat is not related linguistically.

Location: Assam state: Golaghat, Jorhat, and Karbi Anglong districts, Balipathar, Basapathar, Gahorisuwa, Na Kthong, Pahukatia, Rengmai, and Tipomia villages.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Sal, Jingppaw-Asakia, Jingphaw
Relationships: Closely related to Singpho [sgp]. Turung has a smaller Tibeto-Burman vocabulary and a higher proportion of lexical items of Tai origin than Singpho (Morey 2010).
Language_Contact: Most also use Assamese [asm] (Morey 2015). Also use Singpho [sgp], especially among the elderly.

L1_Full: No known L1 speakers. Survived into the 1990s.
Location: Kerala state: Alleppey, Ernakulam, Idukki, Koliam, Kottayam, Palakkad, Pathanamthitta, Thrissur, and Trivandrum districts.
Classification: Dravidian, Southern, Unclassified
Language_Contact: Shifted to Malayalam [mal].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 72–82% (2001 census).
General_Remarks: Prefer to be considered Malayalis rather than Ullatan. Ulladan and Kochu Velan are both Scheduled Tribes.

L1_Full: No known L1 speakers. Survived into the 2000s.
Location: Kerala state: Idukki district, Memari and Vanchivayal villages.
Classification: Dravidian, Southern, Tamil-Kannada, Kannada
Relationships: Shares features with Tamil [tam], Irula [iru], and Kannada [kan] (Lal 1991). Lexical similarity: 60%–71% with Malayalam [mal], 54%–58% with Tamil [tam].
Language_Contact: Shifted to Malayalam [mal].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 73% (2001 census).
General_Remarks: A Scheduled Tribe. Irali Urali is a dialect of Irula [iru] in Tamil Nadu. Urali Kurumba is an alternate name for Betta Kurumba [xub] in Wayanad District, Kerala.

Location: Jammu and Kashmir state: widespread use by Muslims; Maharashtra state: Hyderabad (Dakhini).
Official_Recognition: Statutory provincial language in Telangana state (2017, Telangana Official Languages Act, Act 9, Section 2b, 1966 (Amended by Telangana Official Languages Bill, Act 30)), co-official with Telugu [tel]. Statutory provincial working language in Bihar, Uttar Pradesh states (1950, Constitution, Schedule VIII), limited to official correspondence, notices and other communication. Statutory language of provincial identity in Jammu and Kashmir State (1957, State constitution, Article 145).
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Western Hindi, Hindustani
Dialect_Names: Dakhini (Dakani, Dakkhini, Deccan, Desia, Mirgan), Pinjari, Rekhta (Rekhti)
Typology: SOV; postposition; noun head final; gender (masculine/feminine); no articles; direct and oblique cases; verb affixes mark person, number, gender of subject; passives; tense and aspect; causatives; 35 consonants, 21 vowels; non-tonal; stress on penultimate syllable.
Language_Contact: A few also use Standard Arabic [arb]. Also use Bengali [ben]. Also use Bhojpuri [bho].
Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Balti [bft], Bhadrawahi [bhd], Bhattiyali [bht], Bilaspuri [kfs], Burushaski [bsk], Chambeali [cdh], Changthang [cna], Churahi [cdj], Dogri [dgo], Eastern Balochi [bgp], Gujari [gju], Kangri [xnr], Kashmiri [kas], Khah [hkh], Kullu Pahari [kfx], Ladakhi [lbj], Mandeali [mjl], Mewati [wtm], Purig [prx], Saraiki [skr].
Education: Taught in primary and secondary schools through grade 5 and as subject thereafter in Andhra Pradesh state and Telangana state.
Scripts: Arabic script, Naskh variant [Arab]. Arabic script, Nastaliq variant [Aran], primary usage. Braille script [Brai]. Devanagari script [Deva], used in India (Ahmad 2011).

Location: Jammu and Kashmir state: Srinagar; Ladakh, Leh.
Classification: Turkic, Eastern
Typology: SOV; postpositions; genitives, adjectives, numerals, relatives before noun heads; question words initial; word order distinguishes subjects and indirect objects, topic and comment; 8 noun cases shown by suffixes; verb suffixes mark subject person, number, second person marks plural and 3 levels of respect; passive, reflexive, reciprocal and causative; comparatives; 25 consonant and 15 vowel phonemes; CV, CVC, CVCC syllables; non-tonal; stress on final syllable; vowel harmony; evidentials.
Language_Use: Elderly only.
Language_Contact: Shifted to Kashmiri [kas].
Scripts: Arabic script, Naskh variant [Arab], official and primary usage in China, also used in Afghanistan. Cyrillic script [Cyrl], used in Kazakhstan, past usage in China. Latin script [Latn], used in China and Turkey.
General_Remarks: Border disputed with China.

Alternate_Names: Guvvalollu, Haki Piki, Hakkipikkaru, Karikkorava, Kuruvikkaran, Marattiyan, Narakureavar, Narikkorava, Narikoravar, Rattiyan, Shikarijanam, Vaghri, Vaghriwala, Vagri, Wagri Vel, Wogri Boli
Location: Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, and Maharashtra states, and Pondicherry union territory; Tamil Nadu state: Cuddalore, Tiruvannamalai, Vellore, and Villupuram districts.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Unclassified
Relationships: Lexical similarity: 36% with Marathi [mar], 40% with Hindi [hin].
Language_Contact: Most also use Hindi [hin]. Some also use Kannada [kan]. Some also use Marathi [mar]. Some also use Tamil [tam]. Some also use Telugu [tel].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: Very low.
General_Remarks: The people are called by various names meaning ‘bird catchers’. Semi-nomadic.

Location: Manipur state: Churachandpur district, 30+ villages; Assam, Meghalaya, and Tripura states.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Kuki-Chin, Peripheral, Northern, Sizang
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 60% in Manipur (2001 census).
General_Remarks: Zomi is a collective name by which Tedim Chins [ctd] of Myanmar, Paite [pck] and Vaiphei of Manipur generally identify themselves.

Alternate_Names: Berar Marathi, Berari, Dhanagari, Kumbhari, Madhya Pradesh Marathi
Location: Andhra Pradesh state: Adilabad and Nizamabad districts; Madhya Pradesh state: Balaghat and Chhindwara districts; Maharashtra state: Akola, Amravati, and Buldana districts.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Outer Languages, Southern, Unclassified
Dialect_Names: Brahmani, Govari, Jhadpi, Kosti (Rangari), Kunban (Kohli), Kunbi, Mahari (Dhedi), Raipur
Relationships: Regarded by some as a dialect of Marathi [mar].

Location: Maharashtra state: Nasik and Dhule districts; Thane district, Dahanu and Talasari sub-districts; Gujarat state: Valsad district, Dharampur sub-district, Dadra and Nagar Haveli; far north Thane district and south Gujarat state (Davari).
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Outer Languages, Southern, Konkani
Relationships: Sometimes classified as a dialect of Gujarati [guj] or Bhili [bhb]. Lexical similarity: 61%–93% among dialects, 60% with Marathi [mar], 65% with Kukna [kex].
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Gujarati [guj]. Also use Marathi [mar].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 32% for Gujarat (2001 census).
General_Remarks: Each dialect group is endogamous. Patrilocal.

Alternate_Names: Adiwasi Bhil, Bhilori, Keski Bhil, Padwi Bhilori, Vasava, Vasava Bhil, Vasave
Location: Gujarat state: Bharuch and Surat districts, south Akkalkuwa and Dhadgaon sub-districts, north of Tapti river; Satpudas; central and north Nandurbar and Nawapur sub-districts south of Tapti; Maharashtra state: Nandurbar district, Tapti river area.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Intermediate Divisions, Western, Gujarati
Dialect_Names: Dehvali (Dehwali, Kolche), Ambodi (Ambodia, Ambodia Bhil), Dogri (Dhogri, Dhogri Bhil, Dungri), Khatalia (Khatali), Kot (Kotni)
Relationships: Not intelligible of Pauri Bareli [bfb] or Bhili [bhb]. 77%–93% intelligibility between Dubli [dub], Dehvali, Dogri, Khatalia, and Kot varieties. Vasavi Dungri 79% intelligible of Dungra Bhil [duh].
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Marathi [mar], but with low proficiency.
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: Low.
General_Remarks: Subgroup of Bhil ethnic group. Vasava is the people name.

Location: Kerala state: Ernakulam, Kottayam, and Thrissur districts, Parana and Perumuzhi, Moovatupuzha sub-district on Idamala river, Idyara range; Chalakudi river area near Ittyani.
Classification: Dravidian, Unclassified
Language_Use: Some young people, all adults.

Alternate_Names: Od, Orh, Vadari, Vadda Beldar, Werders, Wodde
Ethnic: In India, Pakistan, Nepal, and Sri Lanka about 3 million (2003 IMA).
Location: Andhra Pradesh and Karnataka states; Maharashtra state: Jalgaon district.
Classification: Dravidian, South-Central, Telugu
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Hindi [hin]. Also use Marathi [mar]. Also use Telugu [tel].
Literacy: Some literate in Telugu [tel]or Marathi [mar].

Alternate_Names: Bhili, Bhilodi, Mina Bhil, Vagadi, Vagari, Vagdi, Vaged, Vageri, Vagi, Wagadi, Wagari, Waghari, Wagholi, Wagri
Location: Andhra Pradesh state: Jhabua; Gujarat state: Panchmahals and Sabarkantha; Rajasthan state: Banswara, Dungarpur, and south Udaipur districts.
LWC_Support: Became widespread in the 19th century, mainly concentrated in Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, Gujarat, and Maharashtra. Promoted by the government of Rajasthan for educational purposes. Used in trade, at home (among older people), in education, mass media, short stories, literature, farming, and hunting.
Classification: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Intermediate Divisions, Western, Bhil
Relationships: Dialect intelligibility above 95%. Intelligible of Adivasi Garasia [gas] of Bhiloda. Wagdi Banswara highly intelligible of Bhilodi of Gujarat. Wagdi highly intelligible of Patelia [bhb] of Gujarat. Lexical similarity: 84% with Patelia dialects; 75%–80% with Marwari [rwr] dialects; 79%–93% with Adiwasi Garasia dialects; 79%–87% with Rajput Garasia dialects.
Typology: SOV; postpositions; genitives after noun heads; nontonal.
Language_Use: A regional language in Vagad Desh. Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Some also use Hindi [hin], with proficiency adequate for market.
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 25%–50%.
General_Remarks: Vagri is a Scheduled Tribe in Gujarat.

Location: West Bengal state: Darjeeling district, Pankhabari area.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Western Tibeto-Burman, Bodish, Central Bodish, Unclassified
Typology: SOV; postpositions; content q-word in situ; clause constituents indicated by case-marking; ergativity; no passives or voice; tonal (Thudam dialect).

Location: Assam state; Meghalaya state: Jaintia and Khasi Hills area.
Classification: Austro-Asiatic, Mon-Khmer, Northern Mon-Khmer, Khasian
Typology: SVO; prepositions; articles before noun heads; CV, CVC, CVV, V, VCV, CCV, CCVC; nontonal.
Language_Use: Vigorous. Home, community. Used by all.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Khasi [kha].
Use_as_L2: Used as L2 by Biate [biu].
General_Remarks: Separate from War dialect of Khasi [kha].

Alternate_Names: Kolkata Sign Language, W.B. Sign Language, WBSL
L1_Full: 120,000 (2016 R. Johnson). Estimated 37,000–197,000 current deaf signers, out of 400,000–600,000 who could learn and use WBSL (2016 R. Johnson).
Location: West Bengal state: scattered.
Classification: Sign language, Deaf community sign language
Relationships: Most similar to Indian Sign Language [ins], and especially close to the ISL variety called Bangla Sign Language in Bangladesh, which on some criteria might be considered the same language as WBSL (Johnson and Johnson 2016). Related to other sign languages in south Asia; see comments on Indian Sign Language [ins] in India.
Language_Use: All domains. Used by all.
General_Remarks: Apparently originated in Calcutta Deaf and Dumb School founded in 1893, then spread to as many as 7 deaf schools in West Bengal and East Bengal (now Bangladesh) by 1932. Some variation among 14 or more current schools, plus borrowing from other regions in India (Johnson and Johnson 2016).

Location: Sikkim state: North district; West Bengal state: Darjeeling district.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Western Tibeto-Burman, Himalayan, Kiranti, Eastern
Typology: SOV; postpositions; noun head final; no noun classes or genders; content q-word in situ; 1 prefix, up to 10 suffixes (depending on analysis); clause constituents indicated by case-marking; verbal affixation marks person and number; ergativity; tense and aspect; passives and voice; nontonal; 22 consonant and 5 vowel phonemes.
Language_Use: Younger generation uses Nepali [npi] (Singh).
Language_Contact: Shifting to Nepali [npi].

Alternate_Names: Erukala, Eruku Bhasha, Korava, Korchi, Kurru Bhasha, Kurutha, Yarukula, Yerkula, Yerukala, Yerukala-Korava, Yerukla, Yerukula-Bhasha
Location: Karnataka, Kerala, and Maharashtra states; Telangana state: Karimagar and north Nizamabad districts; Tamil Nadu state: Chengai Anna, Coimbatore, Nilgiri, Periyar, and Salem.
Classification: Dravidian, Southern, Tamil-Kannada, Tamil-Kodagu, Tamil-Malayalam, Tamil
Relationships: Lexical similarity: among varieties ranges from 53%–81%, 33%–38% with Irula [iru], 28%–45% with Ravula [yea], 27%–45% with Tamil [tam].
Language_Use: Vigorous language use. In Andhra Pradesh: home, community, religion; in Rayalseema and Telengana regions, wider use. Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Some also use Telugu [tel], with higher proficiency in Andhra Pradesh and among educated adults. Also use English [eng].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 26% (1991 census).
General_Remarks: Some people called Yerukula speak Telugu [tel] as L1. Traditionally nomadic.

Alternate_Names: Charumba, Eastern Mishmi, M’ye, Meye, Meyor, Zaiwa
Location: Arunachal Pradesh state: Anjaw district, Dong, Kaho, Khroti, Kundun, Mulam Kembring, Musai, Tinai, Tinam, and Walong villages.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Central Tibeto-Burman, Keman
Relationships: Similar to Miju-Mishmi [mxj].
Typology: SOV; postpositions; verb affixes mark person and tense/aspect.
Language_Contact: Most shifting to Central Tibetan [bod]. Most shifting to Hindi [hin]. Also use Nefamese [nef].

Location: Jammu and Kashmir state: Kargil district south end, in Himalayas and Indus river valley; Zaskar mountains.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Western Tibeto-Burman, Bodish, Central Bodish, Western
Relationships: 73%–81% intelligibility of Leh Ladakhi [lbj] with high standard deviation indicating some acquired intelligibility; 90% intelligibility of Stod Bhoti [sbu] of Darcha village.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng]. Also use Ladakhi [lbj].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: Speakers in Ladakh region have highest rate.

Alternate_Names: Jou, Yo, Zo, Zohâm, Zokam, Zome, Zoukam
Location: Assam state; Manipur state: Chandel district, Singngat sub-district, Sugnu area; Churachandpur district.
Classification: Sino-Tibetan, Tibeto-Burman, Kuki-Chin, Peripheral, Northern, Sizang
Typology: SOV.
Language_Use: Positive attitudes.
Language_Contact: Also use English [eng].
Literacy: Literacy rate in L2: 62% in Manipur (2001 census).
General_Remarks: Although Zomi, derived from ‘Zo’, is gaining ground as an ethnic nomenclature amongst the Northern Chins, the Zo tribe is uniquely distinct in preservation of their culture and customs since ancient times.
